HB 2095.digest: Any driver who operates a vehicle in a manner that proximately causes the injury or death of a vulnerable user of a public way is presumed to have acted negligently in any tort action alleging liability for the injury or death, but the driver may rebut this presumption by proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the driver was not negligent. The presumption of negligence only applies when the vulnerable user was injured or killed by the driver while the vulnerable user was present on a sidewalk or shoulder, or in a crosswalk, bicycle lane, or other designated lane, path, or area established by state or local law for the use of vulnerable users of a public way. In cases that involve both driver and nondriver defendants, the presumption of negligence applies only against driver defendants. The presumption of negligence does not apply to a driver of an emergency vehicle who operates the emergency vehicle within the course and scope of the driver's employment or official duties directly related to the emergency vehicle. In any legal action alleging liability for the injury or death of a vulnerable user, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence: that the plaintiff was a vulnerable user of a public way who was injured or killed in a qualifying area; the plaintiff's damages; and that the driver's negligence was a proximate cause of the plaintiff's damages. A prevailing plaintiff is entitled to recover actual damages, statutory damages of $1,500, and reasonable attorneys' fees and actual costs, including expert fees. A prevailing plaintiff may also recover punitive damages if the driver has previously been found civilly or criminally liable for injuring or killing a vulnerable road user while operating a vehicle. Educational Requirements for Law Enforcement Officers, Prosecutors, and Judges. By July 1, 2027, the Washington State Criminal Justice Training Commission (CJTC), in consultation with the Washington Association of Prosecuting Attorneys, must develop and provide educational classes and materials regarding the offense of negligent driving with a vulnerable user victim to all law enforcement officers who enforce traffic laws or respond to traffic injuries or fatalities, and to all prosecutors who enforce traffic laws or who initiate civil infraction or criminal proceedings in response to traffic injuries or fatalities. Classes and materials must be provided to all covered law enforcement officers and prosecutors within three months of the beginning of their employment and at least once every three years thereafter. Covered officers and prosecutors must complete these classes and materials within six months of beginning their employment and every three years thereafter, but only if the CJTC makes the classes and materials available. Classes and materials for law enforcement officers must be designed to be delivered in a manner that minimizes disruption of officer duties. Classes and materials for prosecutors and judges must be designed to qualify for some continuing legal education credits. By January 1, 2028, the Washington State Administrative Office of the Courts must develop and provide similar educational classes and materials to all judicial officers and judges pro tempore in Washington who hear cases involving violations of traffic laws or which involve traffic injuries or fatalities. This requirement is subject to the availability of amounts appropriated for this specific purpose. Law Enforcement Reporti

HB 2100.digest: High Earners Payroll Expense Tax on Large Operating Companies . Beginning July 1, 2026, a payroll expense tax is levied on large operating companies engaged in business within Washington. The tax is 5 percent of the total annual employee wages that exceed the Social Security wage limit. The tax is imposed on the employer. A “large operating company” is a company that employs more than 20 people, maintains more than $5 million in gross receipts or sales, and maintains an address in the United States. The payroll expense tax does not apply to any employer with total employee wages equal to or less than $7 million for the prior calendar year. An employer may not make any deductions from employee wages to pay for the tax. The tax is administered by the Employment Security Department (ESD). The ESD must annually set the employee wage amount excluded from payroll expense tax equal to the maximum wages subject to tax for Social Security. A credit is allowed against the state payroll expense tax for any eligible city payroll expense tax paid by the employer. The amount of credit is equal to the total amount of eligible city payroll expense tax remitted to the city during the prior state tax reporting period. The credit may not exceed the tax that would be owed for the city payroll expense tax in effect on January 1, 2024. "Eligible city payroll expense tax" means a tax that is measured by annual employee compensation and imposed by a city, as of January 1, 2024. Beginning January 1, 2027, the ESD must collect penalties and interest on delinquent taxes in the same manner as required for the PFML program. Other administrative and regulatory provisions include: employer reporting and records retention requirements; successor liability provisions; the process to handle delinquencies and collection of unpaid taxes; filing of liens; authorization for the ESD to settle claims for tax interest and penalties; and administrative appeals and judicial review. Well Washington Fund . The Well Washington Fund Account (WWFA) is created in the state treasury. Beginning July 1, 2027, 51 percent of revenues from the payroll expense tax will be deposited into the WWFA. Moneys may only be spent after appropriation and may only be used for higher education programs, health care, cash assistance programs, and energy and housing programs. The remainder of the tax revenues will be deposited into the State General Fund. The Well Washington Fund Oversight and Accountability Board (Board) is established and will consist of 25 members. The Board members shall include: ten total members from the House of Representatives (House) who will be selected from each of the two major caucuses from the following five committees (or successor committees): Appropriations, Early Learning and Human Services, Health Care and Wellness, Environment and Energy, and Housing; ten total members from the Senate, who will be selected from each of the two major caucuses from the following five committees (or successor committees): Ways and Means, Human Services, Health and Long-term Care, Higher Education and Workforce Development, and Environment, Energy, and Technology; and. five members, appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the Senate, that have expertise on the intersection of federal and state funding in the following five areas of public policy: higher education, health care, cash assistance programs, housing, and the environment. HB 2102.digest: A court may not impose costs on a defendant except as specifically authorized by statute. Language generally authorizing courts to impose costs, and references to specific types of costs that may be imposed, are deleted. "Costs" are defined as any amount imposed for the costs associated with a defendant's arrest, prosecution, detention, or supervision in connection with a criminal offense. The definition of "indigent" for purposes of determining whether LFOs may be imposed or waived is revised to include a person with income at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty level. Provisions that allow a court to impose the following costs, fees, or assessments are eliminated or repealed: criminal filing fee imposed upon conviction or guilty plea; jury demand fee; costs of court-appointed counsel for defendants who are indigent and able to contribute; jail booking fee and costs of incarceration; costs of appeal imposed by the superior courts, Court of Appeals, and Supreme Court; costs of electronic monitoring required as a condition of probation or release from custody; costs for administering a deferred prosecution program; monthly assessment for misdemeanant probation services; monthly assessment for participation in a work crew and costs of urinalysis or breathalyzer monitoring; and costs related to accepting credit card payments for LFOs. Restitution . A court must, rather than may, refrain from imposing, or relieve an offender of the requirement to pay, full or partial restitution and accrued interest to any insurer or state agency, if the court finds the offender does not have the current ability to pay. The statute that provides for accrual of interest on restitution imposed in a judgment, and that addresses standards for waiver of accrued interest on LFOs, is repealed. Future Ability to Pay . An offender's future ability to pay is removed from consideration when the court: determines whether to waive or not impose restitution owed to an insurer or state agency based on ability to pay; sets the minimum monthly restitution payment amount; and determines whether the time period for enforcing the LFO judgment should be extended for an additional 10 years. Unenforceable Debts for Costs, Fees, and Interest . A previously imposed judgment against an offender for any costs, fees, and interest on restitution or other LFOs eliminated or repealed by the act is not enforceable. The court must not accept payments for such costs, fees, or accrued interest on restitution or other LFOs after the effective date of the act. Such debts are considered null and void and satisfied and paid in full. A clerk or court administrator is not required to take any action or alter any record except by judicial order. Upon motion, the court must waive all uncollectible portions of the offender's LFOs. The presiding judge of a superior court or court of limited jurisdiction may establish an administrative process to waive outstanding debt for uncollectible LFOs other than restitution. A clerk or court administrator may seek a judicial order to waive uncollectible outstanding debt for costs and fees, other than restitution, and for accrued interest on LFOs. A motion filed by a clerk or court administrator seeking to waive these debts does not constitute the practice of law.

HB 2105.digest: Notices . Receipt of a Notice of Inspection. Beginning October 1, 2026, an employer must post and distribute notices to its workers and their representatives within five days of receiving an NOI of Forms I-9 and any related worker records from a federal agency, which includes the United States Department of Homeland Security, United States Department of Justice Immigrant and Employee Rights Section, the United States Department of Labor, and any other agency enforcing civil immigration laws or employment eligibility requirements. The notice must include certain information in English and the five most commonly used non-English languages in the state, such as the name of the federal agency, the date of the NOI, the types of records sought, and contact information for a statewide organization that provides advocacy related to immigrant and refugee rights. The notice must also include a copy of the NOI. While an employer may use its own notice, the Attorney General (AG) must develop and publish a model notice for employers to use without requiring translation services, subject to certain requirements in the bill. The model notice must be published by September 1, 2026. An employer that uses the model notice is considered to have satisfied the required elements. The notice of the NOI must be posted in conspicuous places on the premises of the employer where notices to workers are customarily posted. The employer must also transmit the notice directly to workers using the primary method of communication typically used by the employer, which must include at least one of the following: hand delivery to the worker; mail with proof of delivery; email with proof of transmission; or text message sent telephonically, which may include a link to a notice maintained on a web page, with proof of transmission. Inspection Results. Beginning October 1, 2026, an employer must distribute notices to affected workers and their representatives within five days of receiving the results of any inspection of Forms I-9 and any related worker records. This applies to any worker identified by the federal agency as lacking federal work authorization or any worker whose Form I-9 has been identified as having deficiencies. The notice must include a copy of the written notice from the federal agency, as well as the following information in the language most regularly used to communicate between the employer and the affected worker: a description of any deficiencies or other items identified in the results notice related to the affected worker; the time period for correcting any potential deficiencies; a mutually agreed upon time and date, or options for times and dates, for a meeting with the employer to correct any identified deficiencies; and notice that the worker has the right to representation during any meeting scheduled with the employer. The notice must be transmitted directly to the affected workers using the primary method of communication typically used by the employer, similar to the notice of the NOI. Poster. By September 1, 2026, the AG must develop and publish a poster for employers to inform workers of the notice requirements in English and the five most commonly used non-English languages in the state. The poster must include space for an employer to provide information on where they will post required notices. HB 2144.digest: Notice Requirements to Employees . An employer must provide written notice to an employee if the employer uses, or intends to use, electronic monitoring to assist the employer in conducting performance evaluations of the employee. If the employee is represented by a union, notice must also be provided to the employee's exclusive bargaining representative. For new hires, the notice must be provided at the time the job offer is made. For employers already using electronic monitoring for performance evaluation purposes, written notice must be provided within 30 days of the effective date of the act. For employers not yet using electronic monitoring for performance evaluation purposes, written notice must be provided at least 30 days prior to implementing the use of electronic monitoring. An employer is not prohibited from implementing electronic monitoring prior to providing the required notice if: the implementation of technology is necessary: (1) to prevent imminent harm to an employee or any person; (2) to prevent imminent theft, property damage, or other economic harm to the employer; or (3) in response to an emergency event involving the employer or to a state of emergency; and the employer notifies the employee as soon as practicable and follows up with a written notice within 30 days. The notice must include a statement saying that the employer uses technology to electronically monitor its employees. If the employer uses computer monitoring software, keystroke tracking, cameras or other video or photographic technology, audio recording or listening devices, artificial intelligence systems, or Global Positioning System (GPS) or other positioning technology for the primary purpose of monitoring for job performance, the employer must include a general list of the type of technology being used. The notice must also include a statement saying whether the employer has a verification process that includes meaningful human review to confirm data gathered by the electronic monitoring. Law enforcement agencies and firefighting agencies are not considered "employers" and therefore are excluded from the bill. Violations of Notice Requirements . An employee may file a complaint with the Department of Labor and Industries (Department) for violations of the requirement. If the Department investigates, it may issue either a citation and notice of assessment if the employer violated the notice requirement or a closure letter if the employee's allegation cannot be substantiated. A citation and notice of assessment must order the employer to comply with the notice requirements within 30 days, and if the employer complies, the Department may not issue civil penalties. If the employer does not comply with the order within 30 days, the Department may determine that the violation was willful and must order the employer to pay a civil penalty of $100 to $5,000. For repeat willful violations, the civil penalty can be no less than $5,000. The Department may waive or reduce civil penalties at any time. An employee may also bring a private cause of action against the employer for failing to provide the required notice. A prevailing employee is entitled to statutory damages of $100 to $5,000, plus other relief such as actual damages, reinstatement, injunctive relief, and other appropriate remedies. HB 2145.digest: Prohibitions . A manufacturer or third party acting on behalf of a manufacturer may not deny, restrict, or prohibit the acquisition of a 340B drug by, or delivery of a 340B drug to, a covered entity, a contract pharmacy, or any location authorized by a covered entity to receive such 340B drug, unless federal law prohibits receipt of the 340B drug. A manufacturer or third party acting on behalf of a manufacturer may not require a covered entity to submit any claims, utilization, purchasing, or other data as a condition for allowing the acquisition of a 340B drug by, or delivery of a 340B drug to, a covered entity, a contract pharmacy, or any location authorized by a covered entity to receive such 340B drug, unless federal law requires such data sharing. Enforcement . A covered entity may file a civil action against a manufacturer or a third party acting on behalf of a manufacturer for a violation of the bill's requirements relating to acquisition and delivery of 340B drugs. A court may enjoin violations and award a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per day for each violation, as well as reasonable attorneys' fees and costs. For actions brought by the Attorney General to enforce the bill's requirements relating to the acquisition and delivery of 340B drugs, a violation of the bill is deemed to affect the public interest and constitute an unfair or deceptive act in trade or commerce for purposes of the Consumer Protection Act. Reporting . A covered entity must annually report the following information, separated out by payer type, to the Department of Health (DOH) concerning the covered entity's participation in the 340B Program for the previous calendar year: certain identifying information for the covered entity; the aggregate acquisition cost and the aggregate payment amount received for all 340B drugs obtained under the 340B Program and dispensed or administered to patients; the aggregate payment made to contract pharmacies; the number of claims for prescription drugs as included in the aggregate payment amount received for all 340B drugs; how the covered entity uses any savings from participating in the 340B Program; the aggregate payments made to any other entity that is not a covered entity or a contract pharmacy for managing any aspect of the covered entity's 340B Program; the aggregate payment made for any other administering expense for the 340B Program; the aggregate number of prescription drugs dispensed or administered to patients for which a payment was reported as part of the aggregate payment amount received for all 340B drugs; the percentage of the covered entity's claims that were for prescription drugs obtained under the 340B Program; and the number and percentage of low-income patients that were served by a sliding fee scale for a prescription drug dispensed or administered under the 340B Program. A manufacturer must annually report the following information to the DOH concerning the manufacturer's participation in the 340B Program for the previous calendar year: the amount of all reductions in price available from the manufacturer, other than reductions in price required under the federal 340B statute; certain information regarding overcharges by manufacturers that exceeded the 340B ceiling price; and the average 340B discount on each of the top 25 340B drugs dispensed in the state by each manufacturer, including the percentage of the discount imposed due to inflationary rebate, and the discount if it were not capped with

HB 2152.digest: Hospitals, nursing homes, and hospice care centers (collectively "facilities") must allow the medical use of cannabis by qualifying patients with a terminal condition while the patient is on the facility's premises. Nursing homes operated by a residential habilitation center are exempt from the medical use of cannabis requirements. As applied to hospitals, the requirement does not apply to emergency departments, patients receiving emergency care, or any patient of the hospital who has not been admitted to the hospital to receive inpatient services. A "terminal condition" is defined as an incurable and irreversible condition that, within reasonable medical judgment, will cause death within a reasonable period of time. Each facility must adopt a policy related to the medical use of cannabis on its premises. The policies must: prohibit smoking or vaping as a method of use; require the patient's medical use of cannabis to be included in the patient's medical records; require patients with a terminal condition to provide a copy of their authorization; require the patient or the patient's designated provider to be responsible for acquiring, retrieving, administering, and removing medical cannabis; require medical cannabis to be stored securely in a locked container in the patient's room, a designated location, or with the patient's designated provider; prohibit health care professionals and facility staff from administering medical cannabis or retrieving medical cannabis from storage; prohibit sharing medical cannabis between patients and visitors; and require the patient or the patient's designated provider to remove remaining cannabis and direct the facility to dispose of any remaining medical cannabis in accordance with procedures governing medical waste. Compliance with the medical use of cannabis requirements may not be a condition for a facility's licensure. Facilities may suspend compliance with the medical use of cannabis requirements if the federal government initiates an enforcement action against a hospital related to its compliance with the medical use of cannabis requirements or issues a rule or other notification that expressly prohibits the medical use of cannabis in health care facilities. The status of cannabis as a Schedule I controlled substance under federal law does not allow a facility to prohibit the medical use of cannabis on its premises. The act is named "Ryan's Law."
HB 2152.digest_source: WA Substitute House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2152.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to permitting the medical use of cannabis by qualifying patients in specified health care facilities;
HB 2152.title: Cannabis/health facilities

HB 2157.digest: Operating Standards for Developers of High-Risk Artificial Intelligence Systems . A developer of a high-risk AI system is required to use reasonable care to protect consumers from known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination arising from the intended and contracted uses of the AI system. Subject to certain exceptions, a developer may not provide a high-risk AI system to a deployer or other developer unless the developer makes available: a statement disclosing the intended uses of the system; documentation disclosing certain information, including: the known or reasonably known limitations of the system; the purpose of the system and its intended outputs, benefits, and uses; a summary describing how the system was evaluated for performance and for mitigation of algorithmic discrimination; and a description of how the system should be monitored when used to make a consequential decision; and any additional documentation that is reasonably necessary to assist the deployer or other developer in understanding the outputs and in monitoring for risks of algorithmic discrimination. A developer that makes a high-risk AI system available to a deployer or other developer is required to also make available certain information to enable the deployer, other developer, or a third-party contractor to complete required impact assessments. Subject to certain exceptions, a developer of a high-risk generative AI system must ensure that the outputs of such system: (1) are identifiable and detectable in an accessible manner; (2) comply with applicable accessibility requirements; and (3) apply such identification at the time the output is generated. Operating Standards for Deployers of High-Risk Artificial Intelligence Systems . A deployer of a high-risk AI system is required to use reasonable care to protect consumers from known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination. A deployer may not deploy a high-risk AI system to make a consequential decision unless the deployer has implemented a risk management policy and program. Subject to certain exceptions, a deployer that uses a high-risk AI system to make a consequential decision must have also completed an impact assessment. The impact assessment must include certain required contents, including information about the system's purpose and deployment context, the risks of algorithmic discrimination, the intended use cases, the system's inputs and outputs, system customizations, performance metrics, transparency measures, monitoring and safeguards, and the system's validity and reliability, among other information. At or before the time that a deployer uses a high-risk AI system to interact with a consumer, the deployer is required to disclose to the consumer that the consumer is interacting with an AI system. The disclosure must include certain other information, including the purpose and nature of the system, the nature of the consequential decision, deployer contact information, and a description of the AI system in plain language. A deployer that uses a high-risk AI system to make a consequential decision must send the decision to the consumer without undue delay. If the decision is adverse to the consumer and based on personal information beyond information that the consumer provided, the deployer must disclose the principal reasons for the decision, including the degree to which the high-risk AI system contributed to the decision. HB 2158.digest: The 2018 RULONA is amended to specify a process for remote notarization of a tangible record not physically present before the notary and to authorize remote oaths or affirmations, as well as remote acknowledgement of a tangible record physically present before the notary. Remote Notarization of a Tangible Record Not Physically Before the Notary. To allow for remote notarization of a tangible record not physically present before the notary, the following process is specified for confirming that the record before the notary is the same record in which the remotely located individual made a statement or on which the individual executed a signature: The remotely located individual must sign the tangible record and a declaration stating that the record is the same record on which the notary performed the notarial act by means of communication technology. The notary must record the individual signing the tangible record and declaration in the required audiovisual recording. The individual must send the tangible record and declaration to the notary not later than three days after the notarial act was performed. After receiving the tangible record and declaration from the individual, the notary must execute a certificate of notarial act, which must include a statement that the notary witnessed the individual sign the tangible record and declaration by means of communication technology. A notarial act performed in compliance with this process meets the requirement to execute the certificate of notarial act contemporaneously with the performance of the notarial act and is effective on the date the remotely located individual signed the declaration. Remote Oaths or Affirmations . Unless otherwise provided by other state law, an electronic records notary public located in Washington is authorized to use communication technology to administer an oath or affirmation to a remotely located individual if the notary: identifies the remotely located individual, either through personal knowledge, by means of an oath or affirmation from a credible witness, or by using at least two different types of identity proofing; creates an audiovisual recording of the individual taking the oath or affirmation; and retains the recording in a designated repository for a period of at least 10 years. Remote Acknowledgement of a Tangible Record Physically Present Before the Notary. An electronic records notary public located in Washington may use communication technology to take an acknowledgement of a signature on a tangible record physically present before the notary if the record is displayed to and identified by the remotely located individual during the required audiovisual recording. Miscellaneous Provisions . In addition to existing rules regarding performance of a notarial act, the DOL is directed to adopt rules regarding methods for an electronic notary public to confirm the identity of a tangible record. By allowing its communication technology or identity proofing to facilitate a notarial act for a remotely located individual or by providing storage of audiovisual recordings, the provider of communication technology, identity proofing, or storage appoints the DOL Director as the provider's agent for service of process in any civil action in Washington related to the notarial act.

HB 2165.digest: False Identification as a Peace Officer . The offense of False Identification as a Peace Officer is established as a gross misdemeanor. A person commits the offense if: the person claims to be a peace officer or creates an impression that the person is a peace officer; the person does an act with intent to convey the impression that the person is acting in an official capacity, such as using a vehicle, wearing an article of clothing, or possessing or displaying an item bearing an insignia of a law enforcement agency; and a reasonable person would believe the person is a peace officer. Definitions . A "peace officer" is any general authority, limited authority, or specially commissioned Washington peace officer, reserve officer, or federal peace officer. An item that contains the word "police," "sheriff," "constable," "marshal," or "trooper," or the title of a federal government agency employing federal peace officers, constitutes an item bearing an insignia of a law enforcement agency. Defenses and Exceptions . It is a defense to False Identification as a Peace Officer that the person identified by an item as a peace officer was commissioned by a law enforcement agency in that capacity when the item was issued to them by the agency, and the person is still authorized by the agency's policies to display or use the item. The criminalization of conduct constituting False Identification as a Peace Officer does not prohibit: possession of an item bearing an insignia of a law enforcement agency by any person who inherits or receives the item as part of a ceremony or other commemoration of a deceased person's service as a peace officer, or any person who was commissioned by the agency as a peace officer and keeps the item after retirement from the agency, to the extent authorized by the agency's policies; or depiction of law enforcement for matters of cultural, historical, political, religious, educational, newsworthy, or public interest, including, but not limited to, use in works of art, commentary, satire, and parody protected by the state or federal constitutions. Criminal Impersonation in the Second Degree . The means by which a person commits Criminal Impersonation in the second degree that specifically involves impersonating a law enforcement officer is eliminated. The two remaining means of committing the offense, related to impersonating the armed forces or knowingly distributing a forged digital likeness, are not affected.
HB 2165.digest_source: WA Engrossed Substitute House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)

HB 2172.digest: The abandonment by WSDOT of portions of state highways longer than two miles or including a bridge must occur pursuant to an agreement between WSDOT and the relevant city or county or through a determination by the Legislature in duly enacted legislation. The Legislature is required to make the final determination regarding the status of an existing state highway portion that exceeds two miles in length or includes a bridge, if it is planned for decommissioning and an agreement regarding its disposition between WSDOT and the relevant city or county cannot be reached. The RJT process at the Commission is expanded to include jurisdiction over WSDOT abandonments that exceed two miles in length. A prerequest conference with the requesting parties is added to the Commission's RJT process requirements to ensure the eligibility of transfer requests. The Commission must provide analysis regarding potential costs, risks, and impacts of route transfers and abandonments in its annual report to the Legislature required by the RJT process. The criteria for changes to the state highway system are updated to require strong connectivity, continuity, and functional characteristics when compared to routes already part of the state highway system. The criteria for rural state highways are modified to include connections to or between United States Census Bureau designated places or cities. The criteria for urban state highways are modified to include highways in a United States Census Bureau designated place or city. WSDOT's existing authority regarding state highway designations for city streets and county roads is made subject to the abandonment process created in the bill regarding the abandonment of portions of state highways longer than two miles or including a bridge.

HB 2174.digest: The legislative body of a county, city, or town, or the Secretary of the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT), may create a Crash Prevention Zone (CPZ) identifying public roads where there have been a multitude of collisions that have caused serious injuries or fatalities to provide time for authorities to investigate and implement safety improvements in the designated areas. With the approval of a city or town, a county may designate a CPZ that includes roadways that include public roads within the county, city, or town. A county may establish roadways managed by the WSDOT within a CPZ. The WSDOT may establish a CPZ without the approval of a county, city, or town. Prior to establishing a CPZ, the WSDOT, county, city, or town must hold a public hearing where members of the public may view and comment on a map of the designated CPZ. Once a CPZ is established, the establishing jurisdiction or the WSDOT must conduct an engineering and traffic investigation of the public roads in the CPZ to identify safety improvements. The Washington State Patrol and local law enforcement agencies must coordinate increased enforcement of traffic laws within the CPZ in a manner intended to reduce accident risks. A person who is found to have committed any traffic infraction relating to speed restrictions or an infraction associated with a vehicle collision within the CPZ must receive a monetary penalty of $73, provided that signs stating that penalties are increased within the CPZ are posted. The $73 penalty received must be deposited into an account created for the CPZ. Funds in the account may be used for engineering and traffic investigations, creation and installation of road signs, safety improvements, and increased law enforcement presence within the CPZ. The CPZ must be dissolved once safety improvements have been implemented. The CPZ may also be dissolved at the discretion of the city, county, or the WSDOT at the recommendation of the WSDOT, or by a petition of 10 percent of the property owners, residents, or business owners within the CPZ or an abutting property. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill authorizes the creation of crash prevention zones (CPZ) rather than accident risk zones. A county, city, town, or the Secretary of the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) may create a CPZ within their jurisdiction by identifying public roads where there have been a multitude of collisions that have caused serious injuries or fatalities, rather than accidents. A county may establish roadways managed by the WSDOT within a CPZ. The WSDOT may establish a CPZ without the approval of a county, city, or town. The monetary penalty assessed for traffic infractions within CPZs is $73, rather than double the normal penalty assessed, provided that signs are posted within the CPZ stating that penalties are increased. The $73 must be deposited into the CPZ account, rather than half of the monetary penalty assessed. The CPZ account must be administered and maintained by the jurisdiction in which the infraction occurred.

Award Matching Funds . Commerce is required to award matching funds through a competitive process. HB 2191.digest: Liability for Unpaid Wages and Benefits . Liability is extended to certain property owners when a direct contractor or subcontractor on a construction project fails to pay an unrepresented employee's wages or benefits. Liability is extended to direct contractors when a subcontractor fails to pay. Property owners and direct contractors are jointly and severally liable for a subcontractor's failure to pay. This extended liability does not apply to state, local, or tribal governments. When a construction project takes place on property that is the property owner's principal residence or on property with five or fewer residential or commercial units on a single tract, the owner is exempt from liability, but a direct contractor is still liable. Personal liability is established for officers, directors, and managers of a company when that company is liable for a direct contractor's or subcontractor's failure to pay wages or benefits, regardless of willfulness. Enforcement . An unrepresented employee or an authorized third-party representative may file a civil suit against a property owner, direct contractor, or subcontractor. Recoverable damages include: unpaid wages, fringe benefit contributions, compensation for missed meal and rest periods, reimbursements, interest, penalties, double damages, noneconomic damages, attorney fees, expert witness fees, and costs incurred in connection with the suit. Penalties and double damages are mandatory and awarded regardless of willfulness. There is a three year statute of limitations for filing a civil suit. Right to Cure . Owners and direct contractors may avoid liability by correcting an alleged violation within 21 days of receipt of notice by certified mail. Retaliation Protections . Retaliation and discrimination against an employee for complaining, testifying, or raising concerns are prohibited. The unrepresented employee or an authorized third party representative may seek relief in court. Using a person's immigration status to impact wage and hour rights is a violation of this prohibition. Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors . A property owner or direct contractor cannot avoid liability by claiming that a person is an independent contractor unless the person qualifies as an independent contractor under state law. A rebuttable presumption that a person performing labor is an employee, not an independent contractor, is established. Requirement for Subcontractors to Share Payroll Information Upon Request . A subcontractor is required to provide payroll information, and certain other information, to property owners and direct contractors upon request. Workers' personally identifying information may be shared by direct contractors or subcontractors only to the extent necessary to comply with state or federal law.

HB 2198.digest: Credential is defined as a state-issued permit, license, certification, or other regulatory approval required for an individual, business, or organization to engage in a regulated or commercial activity. Credentials include regulatory approvals tied to business, occupational, professional, or environmental activities. Statewide Credential Catalog and Central Online Repository of Credential Information . The Office for Regulatory Innovation and Assistance (ORIA), in consultation with Washington Technology Solutions (WaTech), must create a statewide credential catalog and central online repository of credential information. The catalog and repository must be maintained as the single authoritative source for state-issued credential information. The catalog and repository must be designed so that information is searchable, machine-readable where practicable, and readily accessible by members of the public. Each executive branch agency must prepare, maintain, and regularly update entries in the statewide credential catalog for all credentials issued by the agency. Each catalog entry must include certain information, including: a description of the credential; the amount of any application, credential, or program fee; credential requirements; instructions for application submission; review and processing times; citations to applicable statutory or regulatory authority; appeal processes for denied applicants; and tools and assistance for completing applications. In consultation with WaTech, ORIA must establish guidance for catalog entries, technical standards, data formats, and submission. Additionally, ORIA and WaTech must provide agencies with any templates and technical assistance necessary to support implementation. Agency Reporting Requirements . On or before March 1 of each year, executive branch agencies that issue credentials must submit a report to ORIA that includes application counts, processing times, and other identifying or statistical data required by ORIA. The information must be consistent with the credential catalog. Reporting requirements apply to: applications that have been received on or after January 1, 2025; applications determined to be complete on or after January 1, 2025; and applications for which the agency issued a final decision on or after January 1, 2025. An agency may exclude inactive applications from its report. An agency must obtain approval from ORIA for exceptions to the reporting requirement when data is unavailable and provide documented justification demonstrating it is not a result of agency failure to collect required information. Each agency shall ensure that the information included in its report is consistent with the information in the credential catalog. The Office for Regulatory Innovation and Assistance must establish guidance for agency reporting requirements, including reporting metric calculations, approved alternate processing or reporting methodologies, and circumstances where data may be excluded. Exceptions to certain reporting requirements may be approved by ORIA when necessary to ensure accuracy, accommodate statutory timelines, or reflect program-specific operational requirements. Published Decision Times . After consultation with ORIA and the Governor’s Office, each cabinet agency must establish deadlines for credential application review and decisions. Each cabinet agency must incrementally establish decision times for the credentials it issues, which must be completed by January 1

Residential settings included in the review must include residential habilitation centers, state-operated living alternatives, and contracted community-based residential settings, including group homes, group training homes, residential supported living, companion homes, and other similar settings. For each setting, the review must include the following information, per calendar year, for clients assessed by the DSHS as having a high behavior acuity level, a high medical acuity level, or both, according to the developmental disabilities assessment: the number of calls to 911 due to client behavioral management needs or crisis intervention; the number of emergency room visits where the client was medically cleared for discharge but remained in the hospital due to lack of an available provider acceptance based fully or partially on behavioral or safety concerns; and the number of instances where a client's residential placement was terminated due to the client's behavioral challenges, resulting in a transfer to state custody, incarceration, or homelessness. The review must also include the annual census of high behavioral and medical acuity clients in each setting, and the percentage of the overall client census that these clients represent for each setting. Additionally, the review must compare staff retention rates across each setting. The JLARC must compile its review findings into a report to the Legislature by December 1, 2027. As part of its report, JLARC must recommend a methodology for collecting and analyzing the information included in the review on an ongoing basis, including recommended minimum viable measures, data standardization techniques, and other methods for accurately comparing and portraying data across included settings. The DSHS must produce an ongoing annual report to the Legislature of the data measures included in the JLARC review. The report must also be posted to the DSHS website in order to allow families, guardians, and other members of the public to view aggregate data on emergency service utilization and placement stability for contracted residential settings as compared to state-operated residential settings for DSHS clients with developmental disabilities. In producing the annual reports, the DSHS must collect and organize the data in a manner that is informed by the methodology recommended by JLARC. The first report must be completed by September 1, 2028, and must include updated data starting from January 1, 2027. The report must be updated on an annual basis with updates completed by September 1 of each year. HB 2206.digest: Conformity with the Uniform Military and Overseas Voters Act . The UMOVA is substantially adopted to conform Washington voting laws with federal laws relating to service and overseas voters. Because Washington's voting statutes and rules already implement federal voting rights for United States citizens who are active service or overseas voters, there are few substantive changes made to state statute. Service and Overseas Voters—Definition . In addition to those identified under state statute as service and overseas voters, the following individuals are included in the definition of service and overseas voters: overseas voters who, before leaving the United States, would have been last eligible to vote in the state had the voter been of voting age and, except for the state residency requirement, otherwise satisfy the state's voter eligibility requirements; and overseas voters who were born outside the United States and, except for the state residency requirement, otherwise satisfy the state's voter eligibility requirements if two conditions are met. First, Washington must be the last place where a parent, legal guardian, or family member of the voter is, was, or would have been eligible to vote. Second, the voter has not previously and is not currently registered to vote in any other state. Voter Registration . If a voter registration application is received within 20 days prior to an election and the service or overseas voter provided an email address, a notification must immediately be sent to the voter with details on how to obtain a ballot by email or online. The county auditor must request an email address from each service and overseas voter who registers to vote, which is exempt from disclosure under the Public Records Act. The email address may be used only for official communication with the voter about the voting process, including transmitting ballots and election materials, and verifying the voter's mailing address and physical location. The request for an email address must describe the purpose for which the email address may be used and include a statement that any other use or disclosure of the email address is prohibited. A service and overseas voter who provides an email address may make a standing request for electronic delivery of a ballot for all elections held in which the voter is eligible to vote while registered as a service or overseas voter. Processing Ballots . The Secretary, in coordination with county auditors, must implement an electronic free-access system by which a service or overseas voter may determine by phone, email, or internet whether the voter's federal post card application or other registration, or military-overseas ballot has been received and accepted. Electronic Transmission System . The Secretary must establish an electronic transmission system through which a service or overseas voter may apply for and receive voter registration materials, military-overseas ballots, and other voting-related information. The system must be capable of accepting both a federal post card application and other approved electronic registration applications sent to the appropriate election official.

HB 2206.title: Uniformed & overseas voting

HB 2207.digest: Bonded and Nonbonded Beer Warehouse License . A bonded and nonbonded beer warehouse license is established for beer warehouses. The license authorizes, to the extent allowed under federal law and under rules adopted by the LCB, the storage and handling of beer in bond and the storage and handling of tax-paid beer not in bond. Under this license, a licensee may maintain a warehouse for the storage and handling of federally authorized beer off the premises of a brewery or entities otherwise licensed and permitted in Washington. Beer may also be transferred in bond from out-of-state manufacturers to the extent allowed by federal law and the LCB's rules. Beer may be stored and handled and is not for processing or bottling in the beer warehouse. An applicant must designate clearly in its license application the sections of the warehouse that are bonded and nonbonded with a physical separation between such spaces. Only beer in bond may be stored in the bonded sections of the warehouse and only beer that has been removed from bond tax-paid may be stored in nonbonded areas of the warehouse. The proprietor of the warehouse must maintain a plan for tracking beer being stored in the warehouse to ensure compliance with relevant bonding and tax obligations. It is provided that nothing prohibits the storage of non-alcohol products in a bonded or nonbonded section of the warehouse. The fee for the license is $150 per year, unless an applicant is already licensed as a bonded wine warehouse, in which case there is no fee for a license. There is also no fee for a bonded wine warehouse license if an applicant first holds a bonded and nonbonded beer warehouse license. The LCB must adopt similar qualifications for a beer warehouse as are required for obtaining other liquor licenses including brewery licenses. A licensee must be a sole proprietor, a partnership, a limited liability company, or a corporation. One or more domestic breweries, microbreweries, beer manufacturers, or beer certificate of approval holders may operate as a partnership, corporation, business co-op, cotenant, or agricultural co-op for the purpose of obtaining a bonded and nonbonded beer warehouse license or storing beer in the facility under a common management and oversight agreement free of charge or for a fee. Beer in bond and beer that is being removed from a beer warehouse tax-paid may be removed from a beer warehouse licensed under this section for the purpose of being: (1) exported from the state; (2) shipped to a licensed Washington beer distributor; or (3) returned to a brewery or another beer warehouse. The ownership and operation of a beer warehouse facility may be by a person or entity acting in a commercial warehouse management position under contract for licensed persons or entities on their behalf. A license applicant must demonstrate the right to have warehoused beer under a valid federal permit held by a licensee who maintains ownership and title to the beer while it is in storage in the beer warehouse. The LCB must adopt rules requiring a beer warehouse to be physically secure, zoned for the intended use, and, except as otherwise authorized, physically separated from any other use. The operator or licensee operating a beer warehouse must submit to the LCB a monthly report of movement of beer to and from a warehouse licensed under this section in a form prescribed by the LCB. The LCB may adopt other necessary procedures by which such warehouses are licensed and regulat

HB 2210.digest: Counties, cities, towns, school districts, fire districts, and port districts (eligible jurisdictions) that have voters in only one county may choose to use ranked choice voting (RCV) for their elections. An eligible jurisdiction that opts to use RCV must adopt it prior to December 31, 2032. Jurisdictions that adopt RCV before the effective date of the act may continue to use RCV to conduct their elections. An eligible jurisdiction that has voters in more than one county may choose to use RCV if another eligible jurisdiction that lies entirely within at least two counties of the original district uses RCV, or if RCV is ordered to remedy a violation of the Washington Voting Rights Act. Certain requirements for RCV ballot design, vote tabulation, and implementation are established, including provisions for duplicated rankings, skipped rankings, write-in candidates, and types of RCV elections. For single-winner contests, which include elections in which multiple positions with the same title are treated as separate offices, the winner is determined using the instant runoff voting (IRV) method. For multi-winner contests in which the positions are not dealt with as separate offices, the winners are determined using the single transferable vote (STV) method. For single-winner contests, jurisdictions that adopt RCV must hold a primary election to winnow the list to five candidates. The primary election is not conducted using RCV. For multi-winner contests, jurisdictions that adopt RCV may not hold a primary election. Jurisdictions that adopt RCV before the effective date of the act are not required to comply with these requirements for primaries. The Office of the Secretary of State is required to adopt rules by May 1, 2027, to specify procedures for administering an election that includes voters in more than one county and procedures for tabulating votes under the IRV and STV methods. Ranked choice voting must be implemented on a date chosen in consultation with the county auditor within two years following the adoption of RCV, unless a court orders a specific date. The costs of implementing RCV that are borne by a county are apportioned to the jurisdiction that is using RCV. Any jurisdiction that adopts RCV must, in coordination with the county auditor, create a public education campaign to inform voters about unique elements of the new voting process. In jurisdictions where federal, state, or local law requires services for voting in languages other than in English, educational materials must be translated into each required non-English language. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill clarifies that jurisdictions that adopt ranked choice voting (RCV) before the effective date of the act may continue to use RCV to conduct their elections. The substitute bill modifies which RCV implementation requirements do not apply to jurisdictions that adopt RCV before the effective date of that act. In the substitute bill, the only RCV requirements that do not apply to these jurisdictions are the specific requirements related to primaries.

HB 2211.digest: "Medically tailored meals" are defined as fresh or frozen meals that are designed by a qualified medical professional for the treatment of a person's medical conditions. Qualified medical professionals include health care providers whose credential include the authority to establish and tailor nutrition care plans to meet a client's needs. If the Department of Social and Health Services or the Health Care Authority contracts with entities to provide medically tailored meals to enrollees of medical assistance programs, the agencies must, to the extent possible, prioritize vendors that are nonprofit organizations or small businesses that are able to provide locally sourced, fresh, whole foods, or from-scratch prepared meals. Medically tailored meal vendors must comply with the client's nutrition care plan and have a qualified medical professional review and approve the menus provided in response to a nutrition care plan. The term "locally sourced" is defined as either: (1) agricultural commodities grown, raised, harvested, caught, or otherwise derived, fully or in part, within Washington; or (2) prepared, processed, assembled, cooked, or packaged, fully or in part, within Washington. Medically tailored meals provided to enrollees of medical assistance programs must: align with evidence-based nutritional practice guidelines for treating the client's specific condition; offer accommodations in dietary needs, allergy restrictions, and cultural preferences; prioritize local, whole foods or from-scratch prepared meals; provide at least 500 calories or otherwise meet a client's medically appropriate energy needs; and provide one-third of the recommended dietary reference intakes for carbohydrates and protein, as established by the Food and Nutrition Board of the National Academy of Medicine.

HB 2211.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to medically tailored meals;

HB 2212.digest: Beginning July 1, 2028, a person may not sell or offer for sale a new commercial or industrial washing machine unless it is equipped with or contains a microfiber filtration system that meets specified standards (qualifying microfiber filtration system) and bears a visible label with a statement regarding the qualifying microfiber filtration system. A qualifying microfiber filtration system must be active across all washing cycles of a washing machine, have a mesh size of 100 micrometers or less, be independently third-party certified to remove at least 87 percent of microfibers, and either be built into a newly-manufactured washing machine or packaged with and capable of installation with a new washing machine. Owners and operators of commercial or industrial washing machine sold prior to July 1, 2028, must equip those washing machines with a qualifying microfiber filtration system by July 1, 2034. Owners and operators of commercial or industrial washing machines must also ensure that the filter is checked regularly and is functional, and that captured lint is disposed of in a solid waste collection container. After July 1, 2030, Ecology may adopt a rule requiring new residential washing machines to be capable of filtering microfibers, but only if either: at least one other state, either bordering Washington or representing a meaningful percentage of nationwide residential washing machine sales, has a law in effect requiring new residential washing machines to be capable of filtering microfibers; and the costs associated with requiring microfiber filtration will not result in an increase in the median retail price of new residential washing machines by more than 10 percent or will have a median cost of less than $70. An Ecology rule to require microfiber filtration in residential washing machines must take effect no earlier than one year after adoption. Ecology may adopt rules to implement, administer, and enforce requirements related to washing machine microfiber filtration. Ecology may issue corrective action orders to persons out of compliance with microfiber filtration requirements and may impose civil penalties of up to $5,000 for initial offenses and up to $10,000 for repeat violations. Orders and penalties issued by Ecology are appealable to the Pollution Control Hearings Board.

HB 2212.title: Washing machine microplastic

HB 2217.digest: The first-time offender waiver sentencing alternative is replaced with options for the court to grant a pretrial deferral or suspended sentence to first-time offenders, subject to specified eligibility criteria. Eligibility Criteria . A defendant is eligible to participate in the pretrial deferral or receive the suspended sentence for one or more applicable current charges or convictions if the defendant has never been previously convicted of a felony or participated in a program or deferred prosecution for a felony in adult criminal court, and the defendant's current charge or conviction is not for: a violent offense, except Robbery in the second degree or Assault in the second degree; a sex offense; or a felony Driving Under the Influence or Physical Control offense. A defendant may only participate in the pretrial deferral or receive the suspended sentence once, except that a defendant who initially participates in the pretrial deferral remains eligible to receive the suspended sentence for the same underlying offense or offenses if the pretrial deferral is revoked. Granting the Pretrial Deferral or Suspended Sentence . Prior to empaneling a jury, the defendant may make a motion to defer entry of conviction and sentencing. If the court finds that the defendant meets the eligibility criteria as a first-time offender, the court may grant the motion and continue the case for a period not to exceed one year. There is a strong presumption that the court will grant the motion to eligible defendants. Before entering the deferral, the defendant must: acknowledge that either the written police report or the stipulated facts agreed to by the parties, if later admitted as evidence, may be entered and used to support a finding of guilt and to impose a sentence if the defendant fails to comply with terms of supervision; waive the rights to trial, speedy sentencing, call and confront witnesses, and testify and present evidence; and acknowledge the direct consequences that will happen if found guilty. Alternatively, following a trial that results in a finding of guilt, or following the revocation of a pretrial deferral described above, the defendant may make a motion for a suspended sentence. If the court finds that the defendant meets the eligibility criteria as a first-time offender, the court may grant the motion by imposing a standard sentence and entering an order suspending execution of the sentence for a period not to exceed one year. There is a strong presumption that the court will grant the motion to eligible defendants. Under either the pretrial deferral or suspended sentence, the court may impose up to six months of community custody, or up to one year of community custody if the court also orders treatment. In addition to any other conditions of community custody, the court may order the defendant to: pay all court-ordered legal financial obligations, unless the defendant is indigent; or perform community restitution work. Revoking the Pretrial Deferral or Suspended Sentence . If the prosecutor alleges that the defendant is not substantially complying with the terms of the pretrial deferral or suspended sentence any time prior to the conclusion of community custody, the prosecutor may file a motion for revocation after providing the defendant with written notice of the alleged violations and disclosure of all evidence to be offered. The court must hold a hearing on the motion to determine whether the defendant has willfully failed to s

HB 2218.digest: Worker's Choice of Provider . An employer must inform an injured worker that the worker has a right to seek initial treatment or emergency medical treatment from a provider of the worker's choice and that the worker has a right to seek further treatment from a provider of the worker's choice within the medical provider network. An employer may not require or induce an injured worker to seek treatment from a specific provider or clinic. An employer is not prevented from providing on-site medical care at the worker's own choice. The Department must investigate any allegation that an employer attempted to require or induce an injured worker to seek treatment from a specific provider or clinic. A violation by a self-insured employer is a violation of the statutory duty of good faith and subjects the employer to penalties. A violation by a non-self-insured employer subjects the employer to penalties for claim suppression. If an injured worker is unable to find a provider in the medical provider network, the worker may seek care from a nonnetwork provider under certain circumstances. If a worker lives in a county with a population of 500,000 or more, and the worker cannot find a provider willing to treat the worker within 15 miles of the worker's home, then the worker may seek care outside the network. A worker who lives in a county with a population of less than 500,000 may seek care outside the network if the worker cannot find a provider within 30 miles of the worker's home. The worker may provide notice to the Department or self-insured employer, and the Department or self-insured employer must provide a declaration certifying this fact within seven days. Coverage Decisions and Treatment Guidelines . A provider may deviate from the Department's coverage decisions, treatment guidelines, policies, or national guidelines when medically appropriate. Utilization Review . Utilization review must be completed within 10 business days from the date that the utilization review provider receives all requested information necessary to make the treatment recommendation, or else the treatment must be authorized. If it is uncertain whether authorized treatment is related to a workplace injury or occupational disease, the Department shall adjudicate whether the condition is related by issuing an order within 30 days of the deadline for completion of the utilization review. Continued Treatment . If the Department denies an application to reopen a permanent partial disability claim, the Department may authorize continued treatment when necessary to protect the worker's life or for the administration of medical and therapeutic measures. Continued monitoring of cancer is covered at a frequency recommended by the worker's oncologist. Written Notice When Removing a Provider from the Medical Provider Network . When the Department removes a provider from the medical provider network, it must be done in writing. The provider may appeal to the Washington State Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals.
HB 2218.digest_source: WA House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2218.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to access to medical care in workers' compensation;
HB 2218.title: Workers' comp. medical care

HB 2219.digest: Minimum licensing requirements for child care and preschool programs must include a zero tolerance policy for imminent physical harm, defined as the presence of high-potency synthetic opioids or drug manufacturing equipment in the licensed facility or program space, and must expressly require that the premises of all licensed settings are absent of high-potency synthetic opioids, drug manufacturing equipment, and drug paraphernalia. Upon violation of the zero tolerance policy, the DCYF must issue an immediate summary suspension of the licensee's child care license. Statutory guidelines are established for periods of mixed-ratio time at child care centers in which children of different age groups may be combined. Child care centers are authorized to have up to 2.5 hours per day of mixed-ratio time, or four hours per day if at least 90 minutes of that time is reserved for meal and rest breaks for staff. The mixed-ratio time may be used on a schedule established by the child care center. The staff-to-child ratio and group size for the youngest child in the mixed group must be maintained during mixed-ratio time. No private right of action is action is created by the statutory child care licensing standard requirements. The DCYF must waive the preservice orientation requirement when an individual has previously completed the applicable orientation, and: it has been less than five years since completion of the orientation; the orientation and licensing process have not substantially changed since the date of completion; and the individual has not had a break in service either as a licensed child care provider or working in a licensed child care facility.
HB 2219.digest_source: WA Engrossed Substitute House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2219.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to enhancing the operational efficiency of child care providers;
HB 2219.title: Child care providers

HB 2220.digest: For hearings in relation to a certification action of a peace officer, corrections officer, or tribal police officer, a six-member hearings panel will hear the case and make the final administrative decision. A simple majority is required for any action. If the hearings panel is unable to reach a majority decision, the administrative law judge presiding over the hearing must enter an initial order on the matter. The new member on the six-member hearings panel must be an additional peace officer, corrections officer, or tribal police officer at or below the level of first line supervisor with at least 10 years' experience, respective of whether the hearing is related to a certification action of a peace officer, corrections officer, or tribal police officer. The CJTC must adopt rules to implement the new requirements related to certification action hearings. Beginning July 1, 2027, the chief, administrator, or sheriff of every law enforcement agency and police department must submit biennial reports to the CJTC with the following: the total number and date of certification of each peace officer employed; peace officer training records, including the number of required hours of training for each required subject, the number of peace officers required to complete each training subject, and the number of trainings successfully completed by each required subject; and the number of peace officers, managers, or administration employees decertified, and the reasoning for decertification. Beginning July 1, 2028, the CJTC must submit biennial reports to the Governor and the Legislature summarizing the reports submitted by law enforcement agencies and police departments. The CJTC must prepare and make available materials and resources necessary for peace officers and officials who administer public safety laws and law enforcement services. These materials must also be distributed to city and county officials, police chiefs, and sheriffs. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill, compared to the original bill: removes the new clear and convincing standard of proof in a hearing for a revocation or suspension of a peace officer or corrections officer's certification; removes the new definitions of "probation," "retraining," "revocation," and "suspension"; increases the size of the hearings panel from five to six members for hearings related to a certification action of a tribal police officer, in addition to increasing the size of the hearings panel for hearings related to a certification action of a peace officer or corrections officer; provides that, if the hearings panel for a certification action is unable to reach a majority decision, the administrative law judge presiding over the hearing must enter an initial order on the matter; and requires the CJTC to adopt rules to implement the new requirements for certification action hearings.
HB 2220.digest_source: WA House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)

HB 2220.title: CJTC oversight

HB 2221.digest: The WDFW must designate an ungulate population as "at-risk" and initiate predator mitigation within 60 days if any population within the federal delisting area experiences a reduction of 25 percent or more below its 10-year rolling average. "Ungulate" means mule deer, white-tailed deer, elk, moose, mountain goat, mountain caribou, and bighorn sheep. "Predator" includes bears, cougars, and wolves. If an ungulate population is designated at-risk, the WDFW must implement predator mitigation actions, including: seasonal or geographic predator reduction around sensitive ranges; translocation of gray wolves within Washington; and targeted removal or nonlethal mitigation. The WDFW must also monitor ungulates to determine population increases over time. Mitigation actions must continue until mule deer and white-tailed deer populations meet or exceed 2004 harvest levels for two consecutive years and exceed their 10-year rolling average. The WDFW must conduct and resume annual population counts of white-tailed deer in partnership with sportsmen. Survey methods must be collaboratively designed and publicly transparent. A report of the population counts and the annual deer season harvest reports must be published annually by March 31 or two weeks before the current seasons can be set. The WDFW must report ungulate population trends, at-risk designations, mitigation actions, and progress toward 2004 population benchmarks annually to the Legislature by March 31.

Cities over 500,000 are exempt from levy reduction requirements. The 25 cent portion of one of the fire protection district property tax levies that could be protected from prorationing is excluded from the $5.90 aggregate tax rate limit for a fire protection district formed using the alternative resolution method. Notice of a hearing on a resolution to form a fire protection district may be published on a city website or local newspaper, and additional notice may be provided by mail or by any other means the city deems necessary to notify affected persons. A fire protection district formed using the alternative resolution method can contract with the city for services, including information, technical, financial, and human resource functions.

HB 2225.digest: Notifications and Engagement with Minors . An operator must provide a clear and conspicuous disclosure that an AI companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human. If the operator knows that the user of an AI companion chatbot is a minor, or if the AI companion chatbot is directed to minors, the operator is required to: notify the user that the chatbot is artificially generated and not human; implement reasonable measures to prevent its AI companion chatbot from generating or producing sexually explicit content or suggestive dialogue with minors; and implement reasonable measures to prohibit the use of manipulative engagement techniques, which cause the AI companion chatbot to engage in or prolong an emotional relationship with the user. Required notifications must be provided at the beginning of the interaction and at least every three hours during continued interaction. If the operator knows the user is a minor, or if the AI companion chatbot is directed to minors, the required notifications must also be provided every hour during continued interaction. An operator must implement reasonable measures to prohibit and prevent AI companion chatbots from claiming to be human and from otherwise generating any output that refutes or conflicts with required disclosures. Required Protocols . An operator may not make available or deploy an AI companion chatbot unless it maintains and implements a protocol for detecting and addressing suicidal ideation or expressions of self-harm by users. The protocol must: include reasonable methods for identifying expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm; provide automated or human-mediated responses that refer users to appropriate crisis resources; and implement reasonable measures to prevent the generation of content encouraging or describing how to commit self-harm. An operator must disclose on their website, and within any mobile or web-based application through which the AI companion is made available, the details of the required protocols, including safeguards used to detect and respond to expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm and the number of crisis referral notifications issued in the preceding calendar year. Enforcement . Violations of the bill's requirements are deemed to affect the public interest and constitute an unfair or deceptive act in trade or commerce for purposes of the Consumer Protection Act. Definitions . The bill provides definitions for several terms, including "AI companion chatbot" and "operator."
HB 2225.digest_source: WA Engrossed Substitute House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)

HB 2225.title: AI companion chatbots

HB 2233.digest: Film plastic carryout bags with a thickness of up to 10 mil are restricted. The pass-through charge for paper carryout bags is increased from 8 cents to 20 cents. Restrictions on prohibited types of carryout bags apply to the sale, distribution or shipment of restricted bags manufacturers and distributors of carryout bags, in addition to the provision of such bags by retail establishments to customers. Penalties are established for violations by manufacturers and distributors of up to $2,000 for a first violation, up to $5,000 for a second violation, and up to $10,000 for a third and subsequent violations. Violations by retail establishments remain subject to penalties of up to $250. Retail establishments that use a third-party platform must list applicable pass-through charges associated with each customer order on the platform and must collect the pass-through charge from the customer through the platform. Handleless bags are not carryout bags subject to restrictions on film plastic or pass-through charges if they are used by consumers inside stores or by retail establishments within a delivered or picked-up carryout bag. Carryout paper bags may meet D8410, a second type of ASTM composting standard, in order to be deemed capable of composting and therefore eligible to be used as a paper carryout bags. Retail establishments are prohibited from collecting both pass-through charges and any remaining difference between the pass-through charge and the establishment's customary price for a paper carryout bag from anyone using a voucher or electronic benefits card issued through the WIC program or state administered cash and food assistance support programs. This prohibition applies regardless of whether the card was used for all or part of a transaction.
