HB 2236.digest: The Commission is empowered to make loans and mortgage loans, but not loans or mortgage loans for owner-occupied residential home purchases or refinancing, except for certain down payment assistance loans. Except for these down payment assistance loans, the Commission may not originate or make residential mortgage loans directly to natural persons for the purchase or refinancing of owner-occupied single-family housing. The Commission is not intended to function as a retail mortgage lender, nor is it authorized to compete with private financial institutions in the origination of residential mortgage loans to individual homebuyers. Instead, the Commission's mortgage lending authority is intended solely to streamline financing for multifamily and other non-owner-occupied housing. The length of time that the Commission attorney may serve is increased from two years to four years. The requirement that the SFC be notified in advance of the issuance of bonds by the Commission is removed. The Housing Finance Program and Housing Finance Plan are repealed.

HB 2237.digest: Deputy State Fire Marshal Compensation . The minimum monthly salary paid to deputy state fire marshals must be competitive with local firefighting agencies within Washington, guided by the results of a survey undertaken in the collective bargaining process during each biennium. The salary levels must be guided by the average of compensation paid to the corresponding rank from the firefighting agencies of Seattle, Vancouver, Spokane, Snohomish, Tacoma, South King County, and King County. Compensation must be calculated using base salary, premium pay (pay received by more than a majority of employees), education pay, and longevity pay. By September 1, 2026, and every four years thereafter, the Office of Financial Management (OFM) is required to conduct an evaluation of the seven firefighting agencies listed above to ensure the continued competitiveness of deputy state fire marshal salaries. This evaluation must be reported to the Governor and the appropriate fiscal and state government committees of the Legislature. The OFM may replace one of the seven firefighting agencies with another if the OFM determines that a different agency would be more relevant. The State Fire Service Policy Board . By December 1, 2026, the State Fire Service Policy Board must submit a report to the appropriate committees of the Legislature that examines the benefits of, and issues arising from, establishing the State Fire Marshal's Office as separate and independent of the Washington State Patrol.
HB 2237.digest_source: WA House Bill Analysis 2026 (Summary of Bill)
HB 2237.last_action: First reading, referred to State Government & Tribal Relations.

HB 2237.title: Deputy state fire marshals

HB 2238.digest: The Director of the Department of Agriculture (Director) must exercise all the powers and perform all duties necessary to monitor food system performance and coordinate statewide food security, working collaboratively with other government agencies, tribes, nonprofit organizations, research institutions, and industry experts with roles related to agricultural resilience and food access. When evaluating food system performance, the Director must consider metrics that, at a minimum, relate to monitoring and quantifying certain regulatory costs. Beginning June 30, 2030, the WSDA must report every four years on the competitiveness of Washington's regulatory landscape relative to peer state competitors for commodity types prevalent in Washington's agricultural economy. The WSDA must develop a statewide food security strategy (strategy) by recommending measures the Legislature could take to make food more affordable, and related measures that have the potential to reduce the number of Washingtonians in need of food assistance to the extent that relevant data is available. The strategy must define statewide food security in terms of food access, agricultural viability, and supply chain resilience and develop a monitoring system for annually updating certain food system data across these three indicators. Agricultural viability metrics must include tracking the cost of fuel and labor using certain available or voluntarily provided data.

HB 2239.digest: Establishing a Family Burial Ground . A natural person may designate an area of land the person owns as a "family burial ground," which is defined as an area of private land designated for the burial of human remains, and in which interment may be, but is not required to be, restricted to a group of persons who are related to each other by birth, marriage, or adoption. "Family burial ground" includes any mausoleums or columbaria constructed on a family burial ground. If a property is co-owned by two or more persons, written consent of all co-owners is required before a family burial ground may be established on the property. A family burial ground may not be established on property co-owned by a combination of natural persons and legal entities. A family burial ground may not comprise more than 10 percent of the area of the parcel upon which it is established and is subject to specified setback requirements. The owner of the property on which a family burial ground is located may not offer plots in the family burial ground for sale or charge fees in connection with the burials. Before the sale of the property, the owner must inform buyers of the existence of the family burial ground on the property and disclose the existence of the family burial ground in the seller's disclosure statement. Mausoleums and Columbaria on a Family Burial Ground . A mausoleum, columbarium, or similar structure constructed on a family burial ground must be constructed with such material and workmanship as to ensure its durability and permanence and must be of class A fireproof construction. A mausoleum, columbarium, or similar structure must also be constructed and installed in compliance with all applicable building permitting laws, public health laws, and laws governing class A construction. A violation of these requirements is a civil infraction. Reporting Interments in a Family Burial Ground . Within 30 days of an interment in the family burial ground, the owner must record the interment with the county auditor and provide specified information about the deceased person and the location of the grave, mausoleum, or columbarium. The property owner must also report each interment to the DAHP. Relocation of Human Remains from a Family Burial Ground . The owner of the property on which a family burial ground is located may relocate human remains from the family burial ground with the written consent of one of the following surviving family members of the decedent, in the order named: surviving spouse or state registered domestic partner; surviving children; surviving parents; or surviving siblings. The surviving family member who gives consent has the right to designate another lawful place for disposition of human remains in which the relocated human remains will be reinterred. If the property owner is unable to obtain the consent required for relocation of remains from a surviving family member, the property owner may petition the superior court for an order authorizing the relocation. In cases where the relocation is authorized by the superior court, the property owner has the right to designate another lawful place in which the relocated remains will be reinterred. However, in designating a place to reinter the remains, the property owner must make all reasonable efforts to consult with any surviving family members of the person whose remains will be relocated. Upon obtaining the required consent or court authorization, the property owner must obtain a per

HB 2240.digest: A rental agreement may be delivered and executed electronically, as well as by hand delivery, first-class mail, or email. If an occupant provides the owner of the self-service storage facility with an email, the owner must send the rental agreement by both email and first-class mail. If an occupant does not sign a delivered rental agreement, the occupant's continued use of the storage space for more than 30 days from the date of notice constitutes acceptance of the rental agreement with the same effect as if the agreement was signed. An occupant may not use a self-storage facility after the owner has delivered a written notice of the termination or nonrenewal of the self-service storage facility. The occupant must be given at least 25 days after receipt of the notice to remove all personal property. Prior to the occupant's removal of personal property, the owner may place reasonable restrictions on the occupant's use of the self-service storage facility, including denying access except for the occupant to remove personal property during the owner's office hours. The rental agreement may contain a provision notifying the occupant of the owner's right to dispose of personal property remaining at the self-service storage facility more than five days after the rental agreement's termination or nonrenewal. The owner may dispose of any personal property remaining at the self-service storage facility after the date provided in the written notice. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill adds a provision requiring the owner of a self-service storage facility to provide an occupant with a rental agreement by first-class mail and email if the occupant provides an email address. In addition, the amount of notice that an owner has to provide an occupant with when a rental contract is being terminated or nonrenewed is increased from 15 days to 25 days.

HB 2242.digest: Immunization Recommendations . The Department of Health (Department) is authorized to issue immunization recommendations and guidance. The Department must consider the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as well as experts and expert organizations that the Department deems relevant and based on reasonable scientific evidence and judgment. The recommendations or guidance are not subject to rulemaking requirements, however, the Department must post them on its website. Health Plan Coverage for Preventive Services . The requirement that nongrandfathered health plans provide coverage for certain identified preventive services applies to those plans issued on or after April 1, 2026, rather than June 6, 2024. The requirement that the coverage for preventive services applies to recommendations and guidelines as they existed on January 8, 2024, is extended to recommendations and guidelines as they existed on June 30, 2025. The revised date applies to: (1) items or services that have a rating of A or B in the recommendations of the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF); (2) preventive care and screenings for infants, children, and adolescents provided for in comprehensive guidelines supported by the United States Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA); and (3) preventive care and screenings for women provided for in comprehensive guidelines supported by HRSA. Health plans must also provide coverage as required by the Insurance Commissioner (Commissioner) in rule for these items, services, care, and screenings. The coverage must be provided consistent with federal rules and guidance in effect on June 30, 2025, and rules adopted by the Commissioner. The requirement that health plans provide coverage for immunizations for routine use in children, adolescents, and adults recommended by the ACIP is replaced with a requirement to cover immunizations that have a recommendation from the Department. The coverage for immunizations must be consistent with Department guidance. The authority for health plans to discontinue coverage for preventive items or services that are removed from the applicable recommendations or guidelines is eliminated. The requirement that health carriers annually determine whether additional items or services must be covered without cost-sharing or whether other items are no longer required to be covered is eliminated. Health carriers may apply medical management techniques to the extent that the Department's immunization recommendations and other preventive services recommendations and guidelines in effect June 30, 2025, rather than January 8, 2024, are not specific regarding frequency, method, treatment, or setting. For health plans that are qualifying health plans for a health savings account, the health carrier may apply cost sharing to preventive services at the minimum level necessary to be able to claim tax-exempt contributions and withdrawals, regardless of the status of federal preventive service requirements. The Commissioner is authorized to modify coverage requirements for preventive items, services, care, and screenings based on the addition of preventive services or other changes to USPSTF or HRSA recommendations and guidelines. The rules must be as or more favorable to enrollees with respect to coverage of preventive services than the recommendations and guidelines in effect on June 30, 2025. W

The Office of the Long-Term Care Ombuds must establish procedures for disclosure that comply with federal requirements for disclosure by state long-term care ombudsman programs. Procedures must provide for the exercise of discretion that favors disclosure. Grand Jury Reports. The location of an archaeological site or resource disclosed to the Department of Archaeology and Historic Preservation constitutes a public record but is exempt from public disclosure. Blood Sample Analyses. The state toxicologist's blood sample analyses are no longer confidential. Accident Reports. Accident reports and supplemental reports may be disclosed if all personally identifying information, including names, addresses, license plate numbers, driver's license numbers, photos, and social security numbers, of individuals involved in the accident are redacted. Department of Social and Health Services and Department of Children, Youth, and Families Records. The analyses and data on children with behavior problems from the Department of Social and Health Services and the Department of Children, Youth, and Families are open to public disclosure. Department of Financial Institution Investigations. The requirement that no employee of the Department of Financial Institutions disclose any non-public information or information related to an investigation is eliminated. Office of Financial Management Efficiency Surveys. Efficiency survey reports created by the Office of Financial Management are no longer confidential. Birthing Center Information. Disclosure of information received by the Department of Health concerning birthing centers is no longer prohibited. Nonprofit Interrogatories. Interrogatories, and the answers to those, sent by the Office of the Secretary of State to ascertain whether a corporation has complied with the Nonprofit Miscellaneous and Mutual Corporation Act are not exempt from public disclosure. Family Court Proceedings. The authority of a court to close the files of a family court proceeding if the court deems that publication would be contrary to public policy or morals or injurious to the interests of children is eliminated.

HB 2245.digest: Consumer-Owned Utilities and Affected Market Customers Subject to the Clean Energy Transformation Act . Consumer-owned utilities (COUs) are those utilities that have at least one, instead of more than one, retail electric customer in Washington. Port districts engaged in the business of distributing electricity are COUs subject to complying with the Clean Energy Transformation Act (CETA). A public utility district (PUD) with one retail electric customer, if the customer remains the same as of January 1, 2026, and the PUD continues to receive 100 percent of its electricity needs from the Bonneville Power Administration, is not a COU and is thus not subject to the CETA standards. Affected market customers are more broadly defined as consumers of electricity, rather than customers of an electric utility, and these consumers of electricity are those that generate any electricity, rather than 100 percent of their electricity, for their or their lessee’s needs, or both. Additionally, the purchases of electricity that partially define an affected market customer are modified so that these purchases are from an entity that is not an electric utility, rather than from entities that are not the directly interconnected utility. A residential customer of an electric utility that, before May 7, 2019, generated electricity to meet less than 100 percent of its own needs and continues to consume electricity with the same or greater percentage of nonemitting electric generation and electricity from renewable resources for the same end uses is not an affected market customer and is thus not subject to the CETA standards. An affected market customers' retail electric load that must comply with the CETA standards is specified as the amount of megawatt-hours of electricity purchased from an entity that is not an electric utility or generated by the affected market customer for its own consumption. Affected Market Customer Compliance and Enforcement . The Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC) must enforce compliance with CETA on the UTC's own motion or if requested. Affected Market Customer Compliance Reporting . The UTC must adopt rules establishing reporting requirements for affected market customers to demonstrate compliance with CETA. To the extent practicable, these requirements must be consistent with required disclosures to retail electric customers. The UTC may waive compliance reporting for affected market customers that: (a) only procure electricity from nonemitting electric generation or renewable resources; and (b) generate electricity using de minimis amounts of fossil fuels for emergency backup requirements. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: Compared to the original bill, the substitute: specifies that a public utility district (PUD) with only one retail electric customer in the state is not subject to the Clean Energy Transformation Act (CETA) standards, as long as the single customer remains the same as of January 1, 2026, and the PUD continues to receive all of its electricity from the Bonneville Power Administration; and specifies that a residential customer of an electric utility, that, prior to May 7, 2019, generated electricity to meet less than all of its own needs and continues to use electricity with the same or greater percentage of nonemitting electric generation and electricity from renewable resources for the same end uses, is not an affected market customer and is thus not subject to the CETA standards.

HB 2245.title: Consumer-owned utilities

HB 2246.digest: Extending Application of Imitation Firearm Violation . Charter schools, state-tribal education compact schools (STECs), the School for the Blind (WSSB), the Center for Deaf and Hard of Hearing Youth (CDHY), and educational service districts (ESDs)—except when the ESD is acting in its capacity as an institutional education provider—may suspend or expel an elementary or secondary student (student) for up to one year if the student acts with malice and displays an instrument that appears to be a firearm on public elementary or secondary school premises. Public Premises Definition . For purposes of firearm-related violations, "public elementary or secondary school premises" means any premises, transportation, or facility areas owned, operated, or used exclusively by a school district, charter school, STEC, the WSSB, the CDHY, or an ESD—except when the ESD is acting in its capacity as an institutional education provider. Return to School, Readmission, and Extracurricular Participation . For firearm-related violations, a school district may prohibit or limit a disciplined student's return to the school or educational setting from which the student was suspended or expelled. In contrast, the following entities may deny readmission to a student disciplined for a firearm-related violation: charter schools, STECs, the WSSB, the CDHY, and ESDs—except when the ESD is acting in its capacity as an institutional education provider. The school district, ESD, or other school that disciplined the student may also prohibit or limit the student's participation in, or attendance at, extracurricular or other activities. Governing Board Decision and Reconsideration . For students disciplined for firearm-related violations, a decision to prohibit or limit a student's return, or to deny readmission, must be made by the school district board of directors or other applicable governing board upon recommendation of the superintendent or other school administrator. The student's parents or guardians may request reconsideration by the board. The board may grant the request for reconsideration, but any decision regarding the granting of reconsideration, or made following reconsideration, is final. Reengagement Meetings and Reengagement Plans . For students disciplined for firearm-related violations, the reengagement meeting must include a discussion about whether the student will be reenrolled full time at the school or educational setting from which the student was suspended or expelled, or provided comparable services in another setting. The reengagement plan must be reevaluated with the student and the student's parents or guardians every six months until the student is reenrolled full time at the educational setting from which the student was suspended or expelled.

HB 2247.digest: Veterinarian-Client-Patient Relationship . A veterinarian-client-patient relationship is the basis for interaction between veterinarians and their clients and patients, and it exists when the following conditions are met: the veterinarian has assumed responsibility for clinical judgment regarding the animal's health, and the client has agreed to follow the instructions of the veterinarian; the veterinarian has sufficient knowledge of the animal to initiate, at a minimum, a general or preliminary diagnosis of the animal's medical condition; and the veterinarian is readily available for follow-up evaluation or has arranged for emergency coverage and continuing care. To establish sufficient knowledge of an animal, such that a veterinarian-client-patient relationship exists, a veterinarian must have physically examined the animal within the last year, unless circumstances exist where telehealth is permitted. To establish sufficient knowledge in cases involving several animals, such as at farms, the veterinarian must be personally acquainted with the keeping and care of the animals. When a veterinarian-client-patient relationship has been established, the relationship extends to all veterinarians employed or practicing at the same premises as the veterinarian who established the most current relationship. A veterinarian-client-patient relationship may be terminated under specified conditions. Telehealth . Once a veterinarian-client-patient relationship has been established, ongoing care may be provided via telemedicine if certain conditions are met. If such a relationship has not been established, allowable telehealth services are limited to: teleadvice; teletriage in an emergency situation; telemedicine for the purpose of prescribing sedation in certain circumstances; dispensing drugs prescribed by another veterinarian in certain circumstances; and poison control services. A veterinarian providing care through telehealth must meet specific requirements. A veterinarian providing care for animal patients under the telehealth exceptions for establishing knowledge of a patient may deny treatment because a physical examination is necessary, and must: be licensed as a veterinarian in Washington; to the extent practicable, have or establish an association with practices that are registered in Washington; notify the client that prescription drugs or medications may be available at a pharmacy; provide the client with the veterinarian's identity and clinic address; and encourage the owner of the animal to schedule an in-person follow-up examination if there are concerns about the animal's health that cannot be addressed through telehealth.

Entity Filings: Provisions addressing the SOS's requirement to "record" an entity filing are revised to instead provide that the SOS must document the date of receipt of an entity filing. References to "filing" an entity filing are changed to "processing" an entity filing. Nonprofit corporations and limited liability partnerships formed under Washington law are required to file an initial report within 120 days of their formation. Fifty dollars of an entity's annual license fee must be deposited with the State Treasurer and the remainder of the fee must be deposited in the SOS's Revolving Fund. Foreign Entities: If a registered foreign entity changes its name, the foreign entity must include a copy of the name change document filed in the entity's home jurisdiction when it files an amendment to its foreign registration statement. Employing a remote worker who resides in Washington is added to the list of activities of a foreign entity that do not constitute doing business in the state. Trademark Registration . The provision requiring the SOS to issue a new certificate in the name of a trademark assignee is removed. International Student Exchange Visitor Placement Organizations . The SOS must establish procedures for reinstatement of an international student exchange visitor placement organization's registration. Apostille and Authentication Services . The SOS may not certify or attest to the signature of a notary public on an individually created document that can or should be issued as a certified copy from a city, county, or state entity.

HB 2250.digest: Eligibility for hospital charity care is limited to only Washington residents. The term "resident" includes a person, including an emancipated person under the age of 18 and a married person under the age of 18 who is capable of indicating intent, who currently lives in Washington and: intends to reside in Washington indefinitely; entered the state looking for a job; or entered the state with a job commitment. A child under the age of 18 may be considered a resident if they live in Washington or the child's parent or caretaker meets the criteria for being a resident. There is no minimum time period for living in Washington prior to meeting the criteria for residency. Residents may leave Washington for over a month and not lose their residency status if they: (1) intend to return to Washington once the reason for leaving is complete and this intent can be verified and (2) have not been determined eligible for Medicaid or state-funded health care coverage in another state, except for incidental or emergency health care. While a person who enters Washington for health care is not a resident and is not eligible for charity care, a person receiving emergency care under the federal Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act or the person's guarantor will be considered a resident. A person who receives a state supplemental payment is considered a resident of the state making the payment. A person who receives federal payments for foster care or adoption assistance is considered a resident of the state in which the person physically resides. A person's immigrant status may not be considered when determining a person's residency.

HB 2251.digest: Climate Commitment Act Accounts . The CIA, NCSA, and CC Account are repealed. The Climate Commitment Act Operating Account (Operating Account) and Climate Commitment Act Capital Account (Capital Account) are created. The Carbon Emissions Reduction Account is renamed as the Climate Commitment Act Transportation Account (Transportation Account). The remaining balance of the repealed accounts, as well as any funding directed into the repealed accounts, is deposited into the Capital Account. The Operating Account may be used in the operating budget and the Capital Account may be used in the capital budget for activities that reduce greenhouse gas emissions, increase resilience to the impacts of climate change, result in long-term environmental benefits, or otherwise achieve the purposes of the CCA. Generally, the various allowable uses of the repealed accounts are recreated in one or both of the new accounts, with the following exceptions. The Operating Account: limits funding for Ecology's administrative costs to $25 million per fiscal year, adjusted by the implicit price deflator; makes environmental justice activities an ongoing allowable use; and adds electric vehicles and related costs, and alternative fuel as allowable uses. The Capital Account adds electric vehicle infrastructure, including infrastructure in buildings, as an allowable use.

HB 2253.digest: Foster Care Licensing. When high-potency synthetic opioids or illicit substances are present in the home, DCYF is to immediately terminate a child-specific probationary license. DCYF may issue a child-specific license to a relative or close family friend for the placement of a specific child in the care and custody of another state who is to be placed in Washington State through the Interstate Compact on the Placement of Children. Kinship caregivers do not need to complete blood-borne pathogen training. The licensing exemption for physicians and lawyers is struck. DCYF is authorized to terminate a license when a license has been inactive. DCYF is to develop rules in collaboration with impacted groups, which will include a definition of inactive, a process to assess, and exceptions. Foster home closure due to inactivity is considered an enforcement action and is subject to appeal. Foster home licenses specify the category of care the agency is authorized to provide and the ages and number of persons to be served. Crisis Residential Centers. CRCs are to have one staff member to every four children during working hours and one staff member to every six children during sleeping hours. Child Care Licensing . To qualify for a non-expiring full license, licensees accepting state subsidy must utilize an electronic attendance system that captures the daily check-in and check-out time of each child, verified by a parent authorized guardian's electronic signature or biometric identifier. A license may be denied, or a license may be suspended, revoked, modified, or not renewed by the secretary upon proof that the agency has exceeded its licensed capacity. If DCYF has evidence that an agency has exceeded its licensed capacity, DCYF is to conduct an investigation that may result in the revocation of the agency's license. Any child care licensee who is found to have committed child care subsidy fraud is permanently disqualified from child care licensure.

HB 2255.digest: Third-Party Litigation Funding . A new chapter is created that applies to all third-party litigation funders that enter into a litigation financing agreement in Washington or that is subject to Washington law, provides litigation financing for a legal action in Washington, or provides financing to a party who resides in or conducts business in Washington. Any litigation financing agreement that does not comply with the requirements and limitations is void. A claimant or claimant's attorney who is a party to a litigation financing agreement must: disclose in writing to all named parties to the underlying legal action the name, address, and citizenship or country of incorporation or registration of any person or entity that has a financial stake in the outcome of the legal action; and produce an unredacted and complete copy of the litigation financing agreement creating the contingent right to receive payment. An attorney who enters into a litigation financing agreement in connection with representing a claimant in a legal action must disclose in writing to the claimant: the existence of the litigation financing agreement; the identity of the third-party litigation funder; any rights of the third-party litigation funder under the agreement that may affect the claimant's interests, including any rights relating to settlement, litigation strategy, or recovery; and any compensation, fee, commission, or other benefit the attorney or the attorney's firm may receive in connection with the litigation financing agreement. The required disclosure must be made upon filing the legal action, or within 35 days after the execution of the litigation financing agreement, under penalty of perjury. Any incomplete or inaccurate disclosure must be supplemented and corrected within 35 days of learning of the incomplete or inaccurate disclosure. The existence and terms of a litigation financing agreement are subject to discovery in the legal action to which the litigation financing agreement pertains. Prohibited Practices .

HB 2259.digest: Initiative and Referenda Filing Process . A sponsor of a proposed ballot measure must include in its initial filing with the Secretary a petition containing the signatures of at least 1,000 registered voters in support of the proposed ballot measure. The signatures must be accompanied by the individual's name, address, city, and county were they are registered to vote. The Secretary may not accept an initial filing that does not include such a petition. Prior to submitting the initial filing with the CRO for a certificate of review, the Secretary must verify and canvass the signatures on the petition submitted with the initial filing using statistical sampling or other techniques to verify whether the petition contains the required 1,000 or more signatures. Signature Gathering . A person may not pay or be paid for signature gathering on a pay-per-signature basis, but may provide or receive money or other consideration for signature gathering that is not based directly or indirectly on the number of signatures obtained. A person may bring a cause of action in the name of the state against a petition sponsor for a violation of the pay-per-signature prohibition within two years of the date of the alleged violation. Civil remedies, including penalties not to exceed $10,000 for each violation, may be awarded. Any judgment award in favor of the plaintiff must escheat to the state, but a prevailing plaintiff may recover attorneys' fees and costs from the defendant. If a cause of action is dismissed and the court finds that it was brought frivolously or in bad faith, the court may order the person commending the action to pay all reasonable attorneys' fees incurred by the defendant.

HB 2260.digest: A petition signature gatherer circulating an initiative or referendum must sign and date the declaration on each sheet of the petition. The petition signature gatherer must sign the declaration under the penalty of false swearing, which is a gross misdemeanor. The declaration requires the signature gatherer to swear that every signer reviewed the sheet and signed without any gratuity or promise of gratuity. As part of the declaration, the signature gatherer must also provide the signature gatherer's address and county of registration. For purposes of verifying a signature on an initiative or referendum petition, the Secretary of State must verify that the residence address provided by a petition signer is the same as the residence address provided on the petition signer's affidavit of voter registration. A signature is not counted as valid if: the residence addresses do not match; the petition or paper does not specify the residence address; or the required information is not contained in the petition. A signature is not invalidated because of a minor discrepancy. Address verification as part of statistical sampling is sufficient to meet the requirement of signature verification.

HB 2261.digest: Credentialed health care providers who provide health care services must wear a visible identification badge during all patient encounters. The badge must include the health care provider's name, health care credential, and the initials of any health care-related degrees that they hold. The identification badge requirement does not apply to health care providers providing custodial services or who work in nonpatient settings and do not have any direct patient contact. Any advertisement for health care services that names a health care provider must also include the type of health care credential that the health care provider holds as well as the initials and title of any health care-related degrees. A violation of the identification badge or advertisement requirements is considered unprofessional conduct. Hospitals, assisted living facilities, nursing homes, adult family homes, and ambulatory surgical facilities must provide updated badges to health care providers upon the occurrence of several specified events. An updated identification badge is required: upon hiring a new health care provider to provide health care services; upon a new identification badge photograph being required; upon the name change of a health care provider; upon a health care provider's receipt of a new health care credential or health care-related degree; when a new credentialing period begins; or on January 1, 2030. Persons are prohibited from representing themselves as either an "osteopathic physician surgeon" or a "physician surgeon" unless they: are either a licensed physician or osteopathic physician; have completed a surgical residency or fellowship approved by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education or the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada; are certified or eligible for examination by a surgical board of the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education or the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada; and maintain continuing education and proficiency in their specialty. A violation of the title protection provisions for physicians and osteopathic physicians is considered unlicensed practice.

HB 2262.digest: High School Civics Instruction . Beginning with or before the 2027-28 school year, the content for the mandatory, stand-alone high school civics course must include instruction in producing a legible, repeatable, official cursive signature, and how signatures are used by election officials in election, initiative, referenda, and recall processes. Students are not required to produce a legible, repeatable, official cursive signature as a condition for earning credit for the mandatory civics course. The development of applicable curricula may be coordinated with the Office of the Secretary of State and county auditors in accordance with required community outreach plans. The signature-related instruction should include an historical overview of signatures in a civics context, including how signature practices and exclusions have limited civic participation by historically marginalized communities. Election Reporting Requirements . The statewide survey of voted ballot rejection rates produced in odd-numbered years must include the number and rates of ballots that were rejected for signature mismatch by voter age groupings. The survey must also be provided to the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) for inclusion in their website content pertaining to civic education. Any election reports for the state that are published annually by the Secretary of State must also include the number and rates of ballots that were rejected for signature mismatch by voter age groupings. These reports must also be provided to the OSPI for inclusion in their website content pertaining to civic education. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: In comparison to the original bill, the substitute bill: removes a requirement obligating the State Board of Education to include school district compliance with the signature-related instruction requirements in its annual monitoring of school district compliance with basic education requirements; adds that a student's signature, for purposes of the instruction requirements, may be a personalized, handwritten signature or mark that aligns with the student's primary language or culture; adds that the signature-related instruction should include an historical overview of signatures in a civics context, including how signature practices and exclusions have limited civic participation by historically marginalized communities; and adds that students are not required to produce a legible, repeatable, official cursive signature as a condition for earning credit for the mandatory high school civics course.

HB 2265.digest: Tenant Installation of Portable Cooling Devices . Under both the RLTA and the MHLTA, a landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant from installing a portable cooling device, except in the following circumstances: when the installation of the portable cooling device would violate building codes or state or federal law, violate the manufacturer's written safety guidelines for the portable cooling device, cause unreasonable damage to the premises or render the premises uninhabitable, cause unreasonable damage to the manufactured/mobile home or manufactured/mobile home community, or require amperage to power the portable cooling device that cannot be accommodated by the power service to the building, manufactured/mobile home community, dwelling unit, manufactured/mobile home, or circuit; when the portable cooling device would be installed in a window and: the window is a necessary egress from the dwelling unit or manufactured/mobile home; the portable cooling device would interfere with the tenant's ability to lock a window that is accessible from outside; the portable cooling device requires the excessive use of hardware that would damage or void the warranty of the window or frame, puncture the exterior wall of the building or manufactured/mobile home, or cause significant damages; the installation of the portable cooling device in the window would not allow adequate drainage; or the portable cooling device cannot be secured in a way that prevents it from falling out of the window; or when the dwelling or manufactured/mobile home already has a permanently installed and fully operational heat pump that is capable of cooling the dwelling or home. "Portable cooling device" means air conditioners and evaporative coolers. This term includes devices designed to be mounted in a window or sit on the floor, but does not include devices whose installation or use requires alteration to the dwelling unit or the manufactured/mobile home. A landlord who limits the use of portable cooling devices due to inadequate power service must prioritize allowing the use of portable cooling devices for tenants who require it to accommodate a disability. A landlord is not responsible for any interruption in electrical service that is not caused by the landlord. A landlord must include written information in the rental agreement or lease notifying a tenant of the tenant's rights, responsibilities, and restrictions related to installation and operation of a portable cooling device. A landlord is immune from liability for any claim for damages, injury, or death caused by a portable cooling device installed by a tenant. Landlord Duty to Provide Cooling . Under the RLTA, landlords must provide facilities adequate to supply cooling as reasonably required by the tenant, as well as maintain all cooling facilities and appliances supplied by the landlord in reasonably good working order. The terms "excessive heat warning" and "excessive heat watch" are updated to "extreme heat warning" and "extreme heat watch," respectively. This aligns with changes made to these terms by the NWS. Prohibition on Physical Evictions During Periods of Extreme Heat . Sheriffs are prohibited from executing writs of restitution or physically evicting tenants during periods of extreme heat. A "period of extreme heat" is defined as a period of time beginning 24 hours before the effective time of any heat-related alert announced in advance by the NWS, or beginning at the effective time of any heat

HB 2266.digest: Shelters, Transitional Housing, Emergency Housing, and Permanent Supportive Housing . Cities must allow transitional housing and permanent supportive housing in an zones within an urban growth area in which residential dwelling units or hotels are allowed. Indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing must be allowed in any area within an urban growth area in which hotels are allowed. Indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing must be allowed in additional zones if necessary to meet projected needs identified in the comprehensive plan. Counties planning under the Growth Management Act are subject to the same requirements in urban growth areas. Transitional housing, permanent supportive housing, indoor emergency shelters, and indoor emergency housing (STEP housing) may not be located in an area zoned for industrial use. A county or city is not required to approve a permit application for STEP housing proposed in a critical area in which no residential development is permitted, an area of natural hazards that generally prohibit residential development, or on agricultural, forest, or mineral lands of long-term commercial significance. A county or city subject to this requirement may generally not require any standards, conditions, or requirements for STEP housing that are more restrictive than those required for other types of lodging or residential development in the zone. However, the city or county may apply any objective development regulations, including form-based codes, that are not required for lodging or residential development such as density limits, dimensional standards, height restrictions, floor area ratios, setback, lot coverage, stormwater, and tree canopy and retention requirements. Similarly, the city or county may only apply the same development permit and environmental review processes to STEP housing that apply to lodging or residential development in the same zone, unless otherwise required by state law, such as shoreline regulations and building, energy, and electrical codes. If applying design review for STEP housing, only administrative design review may be required. "Administrative design review" for cities is defined as a development permit process in which an application is reviewed, approved, or denied by the planning director (or designee) based solely on objective design and development standards without a public predecision hearing, unless the review is otherwise required by state or federal law or the structure is a designated landmark or within a historic district established under a local preservation ordinance. A city may approve requests for variances from locally established design review standards. A county or city may require the sponsor or managing agency of an indoor emergency shelter or indoor emergency housing to certify in writing that it has, between the date the permit application was approved and the date the certificate of occupancy was issued: provided the name, if any, of the facility and the headquarters address of the managing entity; provided a description of any other programs operating in the building and copies of the applicable licenses and certifications held by the program; notified residents within 500 feet of the facility; conducted more than one public meeting; designated at least one point of contact authorized to make decisions and take corrective action in emergencies; provided at least one telephone number to be used in emergencies; provided documentati

HB 2271.digest: PCRC 2.0 Products . New minimum PCRC requirements are established for the following products (PCRC 2.0 products): For packaging that is a rigid plastic container, the requirement is 30 percent PCRC for products manufactured after January 1, 2029. This requirement applies to packaging with a minimum volume of 2 ounces, is capable of maintaining its shape when empty, is comprised primarily of one or more plastic resins, and is not used in certain direct food contact applications. For the following rigid plastic products, the requirement is 30 percent PCRC for products manufactured after January 1, 2029: (a) buckets and pails; (b) household storage and organization containers and lids; (c) waste containers and lids other than roll carts; (d) nursery pots or trays; (e) bulk shipping or storage containers; (f) household cleaning containers; and (g) indoor and outdoor furniture. For roll carts, the requirement is 10 percent PCRC for those manufactured beginning January 1, 2029, and 30 percent PCRC for those manufactured beginning January 1, 2031. For film plastics manufactured beginning January 1, 2029, the requirement is 10 percent PCRC. Fifteen categories of container or product types are exempted from PCRC 2.0 product requirements, including packaging in direct contact with certain foods, beverages, and medicines; packaging for infant formula, medical food, and oral nutritional supplements; packaging for hazardous or flammable products; and compostable packaging. Requirements for PCRC 1.0 Products . A variety of changes are made to PCRC requirements for PCRC 1.0 products, including that: PCRC requirements are specified to apply based on the date when a PCRC 1.0 product is manufactured. Plastic beverage container PCRC requirements are specified to apply only to hermetically sealed or otherwise capped and airtight containers other than cups. The minimum size of personal household cleaning and personal care product containers subject to PCRC requirements is reduced from 8 ounces to 2 ounces. Ecology may adjust the minimum thickness of plastic trash bags to a thickness of less than 0.7 mils if a significant portion of the market redesigns to thinner bags. Producers of plastic trash bags must begin labeling the packaging containing the bags with the minimum PCRC content, beginning in 2027. Plastic trash bag producers must submit a third-party certificate of compliance with PCRC requirements to Ecology. A decision by Ecology to adjust the minimum PCRC requirement for a PCRC 1.0 product must take effect 24 months after an Ecology determination to adjust the rate, rather than applicable in the year immediately following the decision. Any exclusions from PCRC requirements for household cleaning and personal care products regulated under the federal Insecticide, Rodenticide and Fungicide Act (FIFRA) must be granted for a minimum period of four years. Provisions Applicable to Both PCRC 1.0 Products and PCRC 2.0 Products . The producer of a PCRC 1.0 product or PCRC 2.0 product is specified to be: the manufacturer, brand or trademark owner or licensee, brand owner, importer into the United States, or distributor into the state, in descending order of responsibility. De minimis producers that have an inflation-adjusted annual global gross revenue of $5 million are not subject to PCRC requirements for PCRC 1.0 products or PCRC 2.0 products, but must register and report to Ecology in the same manner as other producers. HB 2273.digest: The SBCC must adopt and amend rules relating to embodied carbon emissions reduction standards. In developing the rules, the SBCC is required to consult with appropriate state agencies, including the Department of Enterprise Services, the Department of Commerce (Commerce), the Department of Ecology, the University of Washington, an existing technical work group with relevant expertise, and other interested parties. The embodied carbon emissions reduction standards apply to all new construction, additions, and renovations of 100,000 square feet or larger of any building covered by the International Building Code. Building projects may comply with embodied carbon emissions reduction standards through one of three paths. Path One—Existing Building Reuse . Building projects that maintain at least 45 percent of an existing structure and envelope comply with the embodied carbon emissions reduction requirements. A building project that complies under this pathway may not add more than 50 percent to the total area. The SBCC is directed to adopt rules to determine how the 45 percent reuse will be calculated. Path Two—Covered Products . As an alternative to paths one and three, all building projects subject to the embodied carbon emissions reduction standards must demonstrate that the embodied carbon emissions of covered products used for the project meet established reduction requirements. The reduction is measured in terms of global warming potential for at least 90 percent of covered projects and summed up at the project level when compared to the project's summed industry average global warming potential. To achieve the reduction, building products must use project-specific as-built material quantities and product- and facility-specific EPDs to demonstrate compliance. The SBCC is directed to adopt rules defining how covered products are calculated. The SBCC must adopt rules to define covered products, how the 90 percent of covered products will be calculated, and establish how the industry average will be determined. A building's design professional of record must update material quantities and embodied carbon emissions calculations based on product- and facility-specific EPDs from procured products and attest that they are accurate and comply with project documents before substantial completion. Calculations must be verified as accurate within the industry standard of care with a letter stamped by a design professional of record. The SBCC is directed to create a template reporting form for consistent reporting on materials, including guidance on calculating compliance with reduction targets. Path Three—Whole Building Life-Cycle Assessment . As an alternative to paths one and two, a building project may demonstrate the embodied carbon emissions reductions using a whole building life-cycle assessment (WBLCA) as compared against a functionally equivalent reference building. A WBLCA is an assessment covering specified life-cycle stages of a product or system to evaluate the environmental impacts of a building, including global warming potential. The reference building must be of the same size, geographic location, function, type, and thermal performance as the proposed building. The SBCC is directed to adopt rules to require compliance with a quantification standard for building life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions. Alternatively, the SBCC may adopt rules to specify required building element metrics. The design professional of record responsible f

HB 2281.digest: Government-to-Government Consultation . General. The government-to-government consultation process between a state agency and a tribe must be mutually agreed upon. "Indian tribe" is redefined as any federally recognized Indian tribe with traditional lands and territories in Washington. Tribal Traditional Cultural Places. Before taking any agency action that may affect a tribal traditional cultural place, a state agency must comply with the consultation requirements of Executive Order 21-02. "Agency actions" are defined as projects proposed in state-funded construction or acquisition projects covered by Executive Order 21-02. "Tribal traditional cultural place" is defined as any geophysical or geographical place, area, or feature associated with the cultural practices, traditions, beliefs, lifeways, arts, crafts, or social institutions of an Indian tribe. "Traditional" is defined as those beliefs, customs, and practices of an Indian tribe that have been passed down through generations and the places associated with those beliefs, customs, and practices. Cause of Action . A state agency may not impose an undue burden or interfere with an Indian tribe's exercise of traditional cultural practices on a tribal traditional cultural place unless it is in furtherance of a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means of furthering that compelling governmental interest. An Indian tribe may bring a claim in superior court for a violation of this requirement. An action against a state agency must be commenced within three years of the agency action. Burden of Proof. If the tribal traditional cultural place or practice can be disclosed, the tribe has the burden of proving that the agency action poses an undue burden on a tribal traditional cultural practice or on the management, use, or preservation of a tribal traditional cultural place. If the tribe meets this burden, the agency must then prove that the governmental interest in the state action is compelling and that the agency chose the least intrusive means for satisfying that governmental interest. If a tribe's traditional cultural tenets prohibit disclosure about a tribal traditional cultural place or practice, it is the agency's burden to prove that: it has a compelling governmental interest in pursuing the action; it is essential that the agency's compelling governmental issue be furthered as originally proposed; and none of the less intrusive alternatives identified adequately advance that compelling governmental interest. An agency may not proceed with the proposed action if it does not meet its burden of proof. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill redefines "agency action" to mean projects proposed in state-funded construction or acquisition projects covered by Executive Order 21-02. The substitute bill removes the reference to "contemporary" lands in the definition of "Indian tribe." The substitute bill eliminates the consultation requirements for an agency action that may affect a tribal traditional cultural place in the original bill and instead requires state agencies to comply with the consultation requirements of Executive Order 21-02 before taking any agency action that may affect a tribal traditional cultural place. The substitute bill establishes a three year statute of limitation for an action against a state agency for imposing an undue burden on interfering with an Indian tribe's exercise of traditional cultural practices on a tr

HB 2283.digest: Fully insured individual, small group, and large group health plans issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2028, must have a medical loss ratio of at least 90 percent. The Insurance Commissioner may adopt rules necessary to implement this requirement. The Insurance Commissioner may require health carriers to submit information regarding a carrier's calculation of the medical loss ratio as part of a carrier's health plan rate filings for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. This information may include: (1) a carrier's reimbursement or payments to a carrier's owned or affiliated health care providers or facilities, health care benefit managers, or other entities; (2) a carrier's use of nonclaims-based payments; and (3) a carrier's payments for quality improvement, risk mitigation, and other incentive-based activities. Medical loss ratio is defined as a health carrier's incurred claims plus the carrier's expenditures for activities to improve health care quality (e.g., prevent hospital readmissions, improve patient safety, reduce medical errors, promote wellness) divided by the health carriers premium revenue (excluding federal and state taxes and licensing and regulatory fees) accounting for payments or receipts related to risk adjustment, risk corridors, or reinsurance.

HB 2284.digest: The scheduled increase in the minimum thickness of carryout bags made of film plastic from 2.25 mils to 4 mils on January 1, 2028 is eliminated. The temporary 4-cent penalty on carryout bags made of film plastic with a thickness of at least 4 mils is made permanent. Compostable bags eligible to be used as carryout bags are specified to include, but not be limited to, bags made in whole or in part from potato starch. Ecology is directed to convene a task force to provide policy recommendations with the goal of ensuring a net decrease in litter. Ecology may contract with an independent third-party facilitator to convene the task force. The task force must consist of representatives of 15 specified interests, including representatives of eight specified types of associations, and six specified state agencies. This task force must at minimum, consider the following when developing policy recommendations: the results of Ecology's 2022 statewide litter study; how to reduce litter at specific public sites; how to reduce the most common types of litter; and how to reduce the cost-per-mile of litter cleanup along state roadways and the root causes of why the average amount of litter per mile far exceeds the average amount of litter per mile along roadways in other states. Ecology must submit a status update to the appropriate committees of the Legislature by January 15, 2027, and a final report consisting of the recommendations of the task force by November 15, 2027.

HB 2285.digest: An electric utility may satisfy its 2030 and 2045 CETA obligations by using electricity from certain natural gas systems operated with carbon capture and utilization, mineralization, or sequestration (CCUS) technology. The CCUS technology must comply with all local, state, and federal laws and have a capture design capacity of at least 75 percent of the baseline carbon dioxide (CO2) production of the applicable natural gas system. The method for calculating the baseline CO2 production of a natural gas system depends on the date that the gas system was originally placed in service: If the gas system was originally placed into service within a one-year period prior to the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, or the gas system had not yet been placed into service as of the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, the baseline CO2 production is the designed annual CO2 production, by mass, as determined based on an assumed 60 percent capacity factor. If the gas system was originally placed in service between one year and three years prior to the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, the baseline CO2 production is the average annual CO2 production by mass during the period between when the natural gas system was placed in service and when the CCUS construction began. If the gas system was originally placed in service more than three years prior to the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, the baseline CO2 production is the average of the three-year period with the highest annual CO2 production during the 12-year period before the beginning of construction of the CCUs system. An electric utility that has not achieved its 2030 CETA obligations is in compliance with CETA if it demonstrates that it has maximized investments in electricity from natural gas systems operated with CCUS, in addition to maximizing investments in electricity from renewable resources and non-emitting electric generation. Natural gas systems operated with CCUS are given treatment equivalent to renewable resources or non-emitting generation for other purposes under CETA, including for CEIP purposes, and for petitions by an investor-owned utility to the UTC for a declaratory order regarding the compliance of a proposed project with 2030 and 2045 CETA obligations.

HB 2291.digest: The Kratom Consumer Protection Act (Act) is established. Licensing Requirement . A kratom retailer license and a kratom processor license are established to be administered by the Liquor and Cannabis Board (LCB). No person may operate as a kratom retailer or a kratom processor in the state without being licensed; however, no person may hold both a kratom retailer license and a kratom processor license. Operating as a kratom retailer or kratom processor without being licensed is a class C felony. Applications for a license may be submitted to the LCB for approval. The application fee and annual renewal fee for either license is $1,000, and kratom retailers need to pay a license fee for each separate retail location. Age Restriction . Persons under 21 years of age are prohibited from purchasing kratom products. A person under 21 years of age who purchases, possesses, or obtains, or attempts to purchase or obtain, kratom products commits a class 3 civil infraction and is subject to four hours of community service. Licensed retailers must display appropriate signage, designed by the Department of Health, that states: "The sale of kratom products to persons under age 21 is strictly prohibited by state law." Retailers must verify the age of consumers who purchase kratom products with government-issued identification when there may be a question of a person's right to purchase. Unsecured displays open to the general public and self-service displays for kratom products are prohibited, except when a retail establishment only permits persons aged 21 and older to enter. A person who sells or gives, or permits to be sold or given, kratom in any form to an underage person is guilty of a gross misdemeanor. Prohibitions Practices . Kratom products are prohibited from being consumed in public, and a person who violates the prohibition is guilty of a class 3 civil infraction. No person may conduct a delivery sale of, ship, or transport any kratom product ordered or purchased by mail or online. A person who knowingly violates this is guilty of a class C felony, with a maximum criminal fine of $5,000 and a potential civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each violation. The Attorney General may seek recovery in civil action, along with an injunction and reasonable attorney's fees and other costs. If a court finds that a person violated this prohibition, any profits received due to the violation are to be disgorged and paid to the State General Fund. A licensee who violates this prohibition is subject to license suspension or revocation. A violation is also a per se violation of the Consumer Protection Act. Penalties and remedies are cumulative. No person may offer a tasting or free sample of kratom to the public. A violation is a misdemeanor. Labeling Requirements . Kratom products must contain a label that includes information about the processor, directions for use that include recommended serving size, and an ingredient list that includes kratom alkaloids. Kratom products must also have a label with the following: a statement that kratom is illegal for use by persons under the age of 21; a statement that recommends against the use of kratom for individuals who are pregnant or breastfeeding; a statement that kratom may be habit-forming; a recommendation to consult a health professional before use; and a statement that reads, "These statements have not been evaluated by the United States Food and Drug Administration. This product is not intended to diagnose,

HB 2296.digest: Utility Company Rental Housing Energy Investments . The Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC) must allow an electric or natural gas company (utility company) to invest in programs that achieve energy conservation and improve the efficiency of energy end use of single-family and multifamily rental housing (rental housing energy investments), instead of requiring the owner to finance cost-effective measures. The UTC may allow the utility company to earn a return on cost-effective rental housing energy investments over a time period that: reduces the customer's energy burden and minimizes the investment's impact of the customer's bill; and provides a return on equity that incentivizes the utility to make the investment. The utility company must prioritize rental housing energy investments to reduce the energy burden of low-income customers, vulnerable populations, and customers in highly impacted communities while meeting the customer's comfort and productivity needs. Rental housing energy investments must be secured through the meter and recovered through the regular billing paid by the tenant, successor tenant, or owner of the premises. If the bill is paid by the owner, the utility company's rental housing energy investment must be recovered pursuant to a site-specific services agreement. The rental housing energy investment must be: recovered as any other energy charge until the authorized return on the investment has been fully recovered; and designated as an energy savings charge as a line-item on the customer's bill. The utility company must provide the owner sufficient information for the owner to provide to their tenant who is responsible for paying the electric or gas bill. The owner must notify a tenant at least 30 days prior to the commencement of work to install conservation measures at the premises. The notice must include a description of the work to be performed and expected benefits of the conservation measure.

HB 2298.digest: County auditors may develop and implement voluntary fraud title protection programs with the goal of preventing land record fraud. These programs may be coordinated with the county treasurer or excise agent. A voluntary property title protection program may allow property owners the option of recording a protection instrument in order to prohibit the transfer of ownership of the property without the use of a personal identification number or other approved override process, or until a release of the fraud protection instrument is recorded. If an auditor receives an instrument that would transfer ownership or real property for which a fraud protection instrument has been recorded, the auditor can delay the recording of the document transferring ownership for up to five business days. Similarly, a county treasurer or excise agent may delay processing a real estate excise tax refund application for up to five days if the property for which the refund application is submitted is the subject of a recorded fraud protection instrument. The recording of fraud protection instruments, and documents releasing such instruments, are exempt from the covenant homeownership program assessment, the growth management planning and review fund surcharge, and the surcharge related to housing. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill authorizes a county treasurer or excise agent to delay processing a real estate excise tax refund application for up to five days if the property for which the refund was sought is subject to a recorded property fraud protection instrument.

HB 2303.digest: An employer may not request, require, or coerce any employee to have a microchip implanted in the employee for any reason. A "microchip" includes a product, device, or technology subcutaneously implanted in the body of an individual and containing a unique identification number and personal information that can be noninvasively retrieved or transmitted with an external scanning device. It does not include a device used in the diagnosis, monitoring, treatment, or prevention of a health condition, so long as it only transmits information as is necessary to carry out the diagnosis, monitoring, treatment, or prevention of the condition. An employee aggrieved by a violation may bring a civil action in a court of competent jurisdiction. The court may award injunctive relief, actual damages, and punitive damages, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and costs.

HB 2313.digest: Cities are authorized to establish publicly owned grocery stores in underserved areas with food access gaps. In establishing a publicly owned grocery store, a city may acquire land and buildings; construct or rehabilitate an existing building; lease buildings to private or nonprofit operators, including long-term leases; transfer property to a community redevelopment authority for management and operation; and take private property for public use through eminent domain. A city may apply for a capital grant when establishing a publicly owned grocery store. Eligible uses of grant funds include property acquisition, property rehabilitation or tenant improvements, equipment and other operating costs, security and site infrastructure, and establishing food locker systems in underserved areas. A food locker system is a refrigerated or climate-controlled secure locker-based food distribution system that allows for scheduled or on-demand food pickup and operates on a 24-hour basis. A city may also establish a tax increment financing area. Revenue collected may be used for property acquisition, redevelopment of existing grocery store sites, and improving access to existing funds.

Similarly, state and local agencies cannot require mitigation, protection, or replacement of shrubsteppe within an urban growth area. Various bushes and plants, including Wyoming big sagebrush, three-tip sagebrush, Idaho fescue, and Thurber's needlegrass, are deemed to be associated with shrubsteppe. So, too, are certain invasive species such as Russian thistle, tumbleweeds, and cheat grass.

HB 2320.digest: Restrictions on manufacturing various firearms and related components are modified to expressly reference the use of three-dimensional (3D) printers, computer numerical control (CNC) milling machines, and digital firearm manufacturing code. Restrictions are established regarding: (1) the sale, transfer, and distribution of digital firearm manufacturing code; and (2) manufacturing frames and receivers and unfinished frames and receivers through the use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or by other means, subject to various exceptions. Restrictions on Manufacturing Undetectable Firearms, Other Firearms, and Components . No person may manufacture, including by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or other means, any machine gun, bump-fire stock, undetectable firearm, short-barreled shotgun, or short-barreled rifle; or any part designed and intended solely and exclusively for use in the same, or in converting a weapon into a machine gun, short-barreled shotgun, or short-barreled rifle; subject to various exceptions. No person may manufacture, including by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or other means, an untraceable firearm with intent to sell the untraceable firearm. A violation of these restrictions is a class C felony. Restrictions on Manufacturing Untraceable Firearms . No person may manufacture, cause to be manufactured, assemble, or cause to be assembled an untraceable firearm, including by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or other means. A violation of this restriction is a civil infraction. A second violation is a misdemeanor. A third or subsequent violation is a gross misdemeanor. No person may knowingly or recklessly allow, facilitate, aid, or abet the manufacture or assembly of an undetectable firearm or untraceable firearm, including by distribution of digital firearm manufacturing code, by certain prohibited persons. A violation of this restriction is a gross misdemeanor. Restrictions on Manufacturing a Frame or Receiver or Unfinished Frame or Receiver . No person may knowingly or recklessly manufacture a frame or receiver or an unfinished frame or receiver by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or by other means, unless that person is a federal firearms manufacturer or federal firearms dealer for the sole purpose of repairing existing firearms. A violation of this restriction is a civil infraction. A second violation is a misdemeanor. A third or subsequent violation is a gross misdemeanor. A violation involving three or more frames or receivers or unfinished frames or receivers is a gross misdemeanor. A person commits a separate violation for each frame or receiver, or unfinished frame or receiver. Restrictions on Digital Firearm Manufacturing Code . No person may sell, transfer, distribute, or offer to sell digital firearm manufacturing code for a firearm or unfinished frame or receiver to a person who is not licensed to manufacture firearms under federal law. No person may possess digital firearm manufacturing code for a firearm or unfinished frame or receiver with an intent to distribute the code to a person who is not a federal firearms dealer for the sole purpose of repairing existing firearms, or with an intent to manufacture a firearm or unfinished frame or receiver using a 3D printer or CNC milling machine. HB 2325.digest: Tourism Assessment Program . The Authority is authorized to establish a Tourism Assessment Program (TAP), subject to review by the Director of Commerce, that is designed, proposed, and governed by the Ratepayer Oversight Board (ROB), described below. The Authority is required to levy and collect a percentage of a business's gross revenue as an annual assessment. The assessments will be collected on an annual basis, after ratification by the businesses in each industry sector. The membership of the Authority's Board is modified by expanding the number of members from 13 to 17, and specifying the non-legislative membership as follows: eight members must be nominated by the ROB and must represent businesses paying the assessments; two members must represent official state destination marketing organizations; two members must represent tourism businesses subject to the assessment; and one member must represent a trade association that represents businesses that are subject to the assessment. The Authority, with review of the Director of Commerce, is required to approve an annual budget for the TAP. The Authority is required to approve or reject the budget recommended by the ROB and may not amend, replace, or independently adopt policies or provisions not submitted by the ROB. A regular audit of the budget is required to be conducted by the State Auditor. The Authority is required to submit an annual report to the Legislature and the Governor. The rules do not apply to federally recognized Indian tribes, businesses, or enterprises unless the tribe or tribal member has opted to participate in the TAP. The state and its agents are immune from liability for obligations incurred by the Authority or the ROB.
