HB 2332.digest: State and local government agencies are generally prohibited from using ALPR systems. Only certain agencies may access, operate, or use ALPR systems and associated data for specifically authorized purposes. Authorized agencies are prohibited from certain practices and must comply with the registration, reporting, and audit requirements, as well as with prescribed retention periods for ALPR data. Law Enforcement . A law enforcement agency may use an ALPR system for the purpose of comparing ALPR data with: data on any of the specified watch lists maintained by a federal or Washington agency; or license plate numbers that have been manually entered into an ALPR database upon an officer's determination that the numbers are material to an investigation of a stolen vehicle, a vehicle associated with a missing or endangered person, a vehicle registered to a person for whom there is an outstanding felony warrant, or a vehicle involved in a felony. A law enforcement agency that uses a watch list must ensure that the watch list is updated at least once every 24 hours. A positive match by an ALPR system alone does not constitute reasonable suspicion as grounds for a law enforcement officer to stop the vehicle. The officer must: develop independent reasonable suspicion for the stop; or confirm visually that the vehicle license plate matches the license plate image on the ALPR system and confirm by other means that the license plate number is on one of the specified watch lists. Parking Enforcement . An ALPR system may be used for parking or toll enforcement as follows: as a component of a photo toll system; by a parking enforcement agency for the purpose of enforcing time restrictions on the use of parking spaces; or by a parking enforcement agency for the purpose of identifying vehicles on a watch list that contains only vehicles subject to impoundment or immobilization pursuant to a local ordinance and that is updated at least once every 24 hours. Transportation Agencies . A transportation agency may use an ALPR system to provide real-time traffic information, for traffic modeling or traffic studies purposes, or to enforce commercial vehicle systems at Washington State Patrol enforcement sites and weigh stations. Prohibited Practices . It is unlawful for any agency to use an ALPR system for immigration investigation or enforcement, any protected health care services, or to track or monitor an activity protected by the state Constitution and the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.

HB 2333.digest: Funding Sources—Candidates and Elected Officials . Active Campaign Funds. The list of reimbursable direct out-of-pocket expenses is expanded to include personal security measures necessary to address dangers or threats that would not exist but for the person's status or duties as a candidate or elected official, on the condition that the personal security measure is reasonably proportional in scope to the level of danger or threat that exists. Surplus Funds. Expenses related to personal security measures necessary to address dangers or threats that would not exist but for the individual's status as a candidate or elected official are considered public office-related expenses for which surplus funds may be used to purchase personal security measures on the condition that the personal security measure is reasonably proportional in scope to the level of danger or threat that exists. Definitions. Personal security measure includes, but is not limited to: nonstructural security devices, such as security hardware, locks, alarm systems, motion detectors, security camera systems, and subscriptions for security systems; structural security devices, such as wiring, lighting, gates, doors, and fencing, so long as such devices are intended solely to provide security and not to improve the property or increase its value; security personnel and services that are bona fide, legitimate, professional, and provided by a person licensed under state law; and cybersecurity software, devices, and services, including those that remove residential addresses from existing websites, and credit monitoring and identity theft monitoring services. Limitations. Any funds authorized to be used to purchase a personal security measure, or to reimburse an individual for direct out-of-pocket expenses incurred to purchase a personal security measure, may not be used to pay the individual's spouse or registered domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, grandchild, brother, sister, parent-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, nephew, niece, aunt, uncle, or first cousin, or the spouse of any such person, or an entity in which any such person has a personal beneficial interest. Reimbursements for expenses incurred to purchase personal security measures must be for the usual and normal charge for such goods or services. Statutory Protections Against Threats and Violence . Washington State Patrol . The Chief Clerk of the House of Representatives and the Secretary of the Senate may, upon the request of a legislator, contract with the WSP to provide security to legislators at public events that have a legislative nexus where local law enforcement is unable or unwilling to provide security. Address Confidentiality Program. An elected official and any person residing with the elected official may be admitted into to the ACP by submitting an application to the Office of the Secretary of the State that includes: a designation of the Secretary as the agent authorized to receive legal service of process and mail on behalf of the applicant ; the residential address and phone number where the applicant can be contacted by the Secretary; and the signature of the applicant and date on which the application was signed. A person who knowingly provides false or incorrect information on an application or falsely attests in an application that disclosure of the person's address would endanger the safety of any elected official is guilty of offering a false or forged instrument to be filed,

HB 2334.digest: Rounding of In-Person Cash Transactions . The total price or change due of any in-person cash transaction may be rounded to the nearest 5 cent increment as follows: If the final digit of a cash transaction ends in 1 cent, 2 cents, 6 cents, or 7 cents, the final digit may be rounded down to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents. If the final digit of a cash transaction ends in 3 cents, 4 cents, 8 cents, or 9 cents, the final digit may be rounded up to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents. If the final digit of a cash transaction ends in 0 cents or 5 cents, the final digit may not be rounded up or down. Transactions made by another form of payment, including credit and debit cards, may not be rounded. The total price of any transaction, without any rounding adjustment, may be paid by the customer at the customer's option if the customer has the exact legal tender to pay the total price. Mixed-Tender Transactions . For mixed-tender transactions, rounding applies only to the portion of the transaction paid in cash, and must not alter or affect the exact amounts authorized, cleared, or settled through any noncash payment system. Rounding by Agencies . State and local agencies may round in-person cash transactions as authorized when pennies are not available, but must remit to the state any applicable tax, fee, or charge. Tax Obligations . Rounding applies solely to the payment amount tendered and does not alter the sales price, or the amount of tax owed or collected. Any person selling goods or services must calculate and remit all taxes and fees imposed by state or municipal taxing authorities based on the sales price before rounding. The state business and occupation tax does not apply to amounts received from rounding up as authorized, nor is any deduction allowed for rounding down as authorized. The state sales and use tax must be calculated on the selling price of goods, services, or other products subject to such tax without regard to any rounding. The amount of tax due may not be rounded. Preemption and Liability . Rounding as authorized: (1) preempts any inconsistent local ordinance, regulation, or rule; (2) is not actionable under the Consumer Protection Act; and (3) does not violate any state or municipal requirement, law, regulation, or standard. Defined Terms . "Legal tender" means all coins and currencies of the United States. "Total price" means the final amount due and payable by the buyer for the purchase of any good, service, or other product, or combination thereof, after all applicable taxes and fees are applied, as well as any discounts or other adjustments that are made by the seller. "Transaction" means the entire purchase by a buyer from a seller for all goods, services, and other products, at that date and time as is shown on an invoice or receipt. A transaction may include one item or multiple items.

HB 2334.title: Cash transactions/pennies

HB 2349.digest: Notice of Release for Potential Sexually Violent Predators . When the agency with jurisdiction makes a referral to the applicable county prosecuting attorney and the Attorney General to notify them about the release of a person who may meet the criteria of a sexually violent predator (SVP), the agency with jurisdiction must also concurrently provide notice of the person's anticipated release date to the: sheriff of the applicable county; senator and each representative of the applicable legislative district; administrator or manager of the applicable county; and applicable chair of the board of county commissioners or county council. Notice of Conditional Release, Change of Address, Unconditional Discharge, or Escape . The list of persons that the Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) must send written notice to before an SVP's conditional release, change of address while on conditional release, or unconditional discharge, or if the SVP escapes, is expanded to include the: executive authority of the political subdivision in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under a less restrictive alternative (LRA); senator and each representative of the legislative district in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA; administrator or manager of the political subdivision in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA; chair of the city council of the city, if any, in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA; and chair of the board of county commissioners or county council, whichever is applicable, in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA. If the court orders an SVP's conditional release or unconditional discharge, the DSHS must send written notice to all persons who are statutorily entitled to notice of an SVP's conditional release, change of address, unconditional discharge, or escape, no later than seven calendar days after the order is filed.

HB 2354.digest: A common interest community qualifies for the small community exemption if the community's amended declaration—and not just the original declaration—contains the requisite language regarding maximum assessments. Small common interest communities that consist only of middle housing are exempt from most WUCIOA provisions. Specifically, if a plat or miscellaneous community consists of no more than six middle housing units and the average annual assessment of all middle housing units does not exceed $1,000, the community is subject only to the following provisions of the WUCIOA: the requirement of a separate title for each unit as a separate parcel of real estate and a separate tax assessment based on the value of that unit together with its interest in the common elements; the prohibition of discriminatory application of building, fire, health, or safety codes and regulations by local governments against the community property based only on the fact that the property is owned as a common interest community; and general provisions that apply when a unit in a common interest community is taken or partially taken by eminent domain. All middle housing common interest communities are exempt from the requirement to prepare and annually update a reserve study if a community does not, and will not in the future, require the construction, operation, and maintenance of any reserve component to manage wastewater and protect health and safety, as well as ground and service waters. The governing documents of a common interest community may not vary from the WUCIOA on the subject of financial responsibility for electric vehicle charging stations and heat pumps. Only the owner of the charging station or heat pump exclusively serving the owner's unit bears that financial responsibility. The threshold that triggers the requirement for an association to be annually audited by a certified public accountant and that allows unit owners to waive the annual audit is increased from $50,000 to $100,000.

The exceptions include: a person performing casual labor in or about a private residence, unless the work is performed in the course of the hiring entity's trade, business, or profession; a person performing babysitting on a irregular and uncertain basis that is incidental in nature and duration; a person performing pet sitting, dog walking, or house sitting who is not also performing other domestic service work; an individual provider, or any provider employed by a home care agency if the home care agency receives certain state funds; or a person in a family relationship with, or who is a family member of, the hiring entity. Hiring entity means any person, group, or entity that provides payment to a domestic worker for the domestic worker's work or services or acts directly or indirectly in the interest of an employer in relation to an employee.

HB 2360.digest: School Use of Albuterol . Beginning with the 2027-28 school year, school districts, charter schools, state-tribal education compact schools, and private schools may maintain a supply of albuterol aerosol, powder, or solution for use in an inhaler or nebulizer (school-supplied albuterol) in a designated location on school property. School-supplied albuterol may be acquired from donation sources, but must be accompanied by a prescription. School-supplied albuterol prescriptions must be accompanied by a standing order authorizing its administration for the management of respiratory symptoms, including breathing difficulties caused by conditions such as asthma. School-supplied albuterol must be accessed and administered in accordance with the uniform procedure for the management of a student's respiratory symptoms as follows: If the student has a prescription for albuterol on file, a school nurse or designated trained school personnel may administer school-supplied albuterol. If the student does not possess albuterol or have a prescription for albuterol on file, only a school nurse may administer school-supplied albuterol. Albuterol may be maintained, accessed, and administered on public and private school property, including the school building and playground, on a school bus, and during field trips or sanctioned excursions away from school property. A school nurse or designated trained school personnel may transport and carry a reasonable quantity of school-supplied albuterol on field trips or excursions. A school must immediately notify a student’s parent or guardian when a student is administered school-supplied albuterol or a student self-administers albuterol and the school has knowledge of this self-administration. Uniform Procedure . By January 1, 2027, the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction and the Department of Health must include, within the uniform policy addressing school staff training requirements, a uniform procedure governing when school nurses and designated trained school personnel access and administer school-supplied albuterol. If a school district elects to maintain school-supplied albuterol, it must incorporate the uniform procedure into its policies governing asthma rescue procedures for students. Employee Opt-Out . A non-nurse employee who has not agreed in writing to include the management of albuterol as a specific part of the employee's job description may file with the school district, charter school, or state-tribal education compact school a written letter of refusal declining to manage albuterol. The letter of refusal may not serve as grounds for discharge or other adverse action affecting the employee's contract status. "Management of albuterol" means the storage, maintenance, access, administration, documentation, and transportation of albuterol in accordance with a standing order and applicable written policies of the school district, charter school, or state-tribal education compact school. Liability Protections . If a student is injured or harmed due to the administration of albuterol that was lawfully prescribed and dispensed, a licensed health professional may not be held responsible for the injury unless the prescription was issued with a conscious disregard for safety. A school employee or contractor who administers albuterol in substantial compliance with a lawful albuterol prescription or standing order and written school policies is subject to limited civil and criminal liability.

HB 2361.digest: The maximum principal amount of any small loan, or the outstanding principal balances of all small loans made by all check casher or seller licensees to a single borrower at any one time, is increased. The $700 limit is changed to $1,200, adjusted biennially for inflation based upon changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Accordingly, the maximum principal amount of any small loan, or the outstanding principal balances of all small loans made by all licensees to a single borrower at any one time, may not exceed $1,200, adjusted for inflation based upon changes in the CPI, or 30 percent of the borrower's gross monthly income, whichever is lower. Beginning January 1, 2027, and biennially thereafter, the DFI must calculate the inflation-adjusted maximum principal amount of any small loan allowed under the law, by calculating to the nearest cent using the CPI. The DFI must publish the information in the Washington State Register. For the purposes of the bill, the relevant CPI is the CPI for all urban consumers, all items, for the Seattle area as calculated by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics or its successor agency. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: As compared to the original bill, the substitute bill: requires the inflation-adjustment to the maximum principal amount of any small loan to be biennially instead of annually; requires the DFI to publish the inflation-adjusted maximum principal amount of any small loan in the Washington State Register, instead of on the DFI's website and in a press release; removes a reference to the DFI calculating the inflation-adjusted maximum outstanding principal balances of all small loans made by all licensees to a single borrower at any one time; and changes a reference to the DFI determining, instead of calculating, the inflation-adjusted maximum principal amount of any small loan allowed under the law.
HB 2361.digest_source: WA House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2361.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to the maximum principal amount of small loans;
HB 2361.title: Small loans maximum amount

HB 2362.digest: Impaired Driving Offenses . The breath or blood alcohol concentration limit of 0.08 percent or higher is reduced to 0.05 percent or higher for the offenses of Driving While Under the Influence and Actual Physical Control of a Motor Vehicle While Under the Influence, and for the unlawful behaviors of unlawful operation of a vessel in a reckless manner and reckless or impaired driving under the Washington Code of Military Justice. Blood and Breath Tests . An alcohol concentration of less than 0.08 is reduced to 0.05 as evidence that may be considered in determining whether the person was under the influence of intoxicating liquor. The liquid simulator solution external standard or dry gas external standard result is reduced to 0.045 to 0.055 inclusive. Driver's License Suspension . The alcohol concentration of 0.08 is reduced to 0.05 for the license sanctions and disqualifications imposed by the DOL and suspension, revocation, or denial of a driver's license, permit, or privilege following a breath test for purposes of the officer's warning, written notice after arrest, sworn report, and scope of the hearing. Criminal Penalty Probation Conditions . The alcohol concentration limit of 0.08 or more is reduced to 0.05 or more for the probation conditions imposed by a court. Unlawful Sale and Purchase of Liquor . The reduction in the breath or blood alcohol concentration from 0.08 to 0.05 does not change civil law for purposes of civil liability of a licensed commercial or quasi-commercial vendor. Public Information Campaign . The Washington Traffic Safety Commission (Commission) is required to develop and implement a public information campaign related to the reduction in the breath or blood alcohol concentration from 0.08 to 0.05. The Commission is required to ensure media coverage statewide, advertise in multiple issues in each county's largest newspaper, provide content in the top nine non-English languages, consider equity outcomes on overburdened communities, and collaborate with the hospitality industry to educate drivers by developing at least 10 percent of the advertisements with the industry. Washington State Institute for Public Policy Evaluation . The Washington State Institute for Public Policy is required to evaluate the impacts of the reduction in the breath or blood alcohol concentration from 0.08 to 0.05 and submit a report by March 1, 2028. The evaluation is required to include the impact of the reduction on serious and fatal traffic crashes, arrests and adjudications for Driving Under the Influence offenses, equity outcomes on overburdened communities, and business effects on the hospitality industry, breweries, wineries, and distilleries.
HB 2362.digest_source: WA House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2362.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to impaired driving;
HB 2362.title: Impaired driving

HB 2364.digest: The Legislative-Executive WorkFirst Poverty Reduction Oversight Task Force is renamed the Legislative-Executive Economic Justice and Well-Being Task Force (Task Force). The number of voting members of the Task Force are expanded from 8 to 11 to add the following state agencies: the Department of Revenue; the Health Care Authority; and the Workforce Training and Education Coordinating Board. The Task Force cochairs must be selected from the voting members and serve two-year terms. The Task Force representatives from the Governor's Offices of Equity, Indian Affairs, and Financial Management are identified as nonvoting members. The duties of the Task Force are modified to specify that the Task Force: oversees the budget and performance of the WorkFirst program; determines outcome and accountability measures for the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; collaborates with the advisory council to monitor the strategies and recommendations in the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; seeks input for poverty reduction to encourage the development of cross-sector and innovative approaches to poverty reduction; analyzes data with a primary focus on the strategies and recommendations of the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; and collaborates with and seeks advice from the Washington Economic Justice Alliance in supporting the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty. Economic Justice and Well-Being Advisory Council . The Intergenerational Poverty Advisory Committee is renamed the Economic Justice and Well-Being Advisory Council (Council). The Secretary of the Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) is authorized to appoint members to the Council as appropriate (in addition to the current members). The required membership of the Council is modified to: include organizations that address poverty, education, or early childhood education grants that may include faith-based organizations, but is not limited to faith-based organizations; include individuals impacted by poverty; remove a subject matter expert in infant mental health; remove a representative from the Department of Children, Youth, and Families and the DSHS; and add entities representing the workforce system and postsecondary education systems. The duties of the Council are modified to require that it monitor the strategies and recommendations outlined in the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty and recommend to the Task Force priorities and policy options that the Task Force should consider proposing to the Governor and the Legislature to effectively reduce poverty and promote and encourage self-sufficiency.

HB 2365.digest: Statewide Broadband Office Duties . The purpose of the SBO is expanded to include promoting broadband adoption and digital equity. The SBO must coordinate with relevant state agencies and community anchor institutions, in addition to other entities, when developing strategies to promote broadband access, and the SBO must develop strategies to promote broadband adoption. In setting broadband goals and definitions for broadband service, the state's definition for broadband may not be speeds less than 100 mbps download and 20 mbps upload. As part of the SBO's outreach efforts, the SBO must request that broadband providers report cost information for retail service, and the SBO must include such information in outreach materials. The SBO must prioritize translation of outreach materials into the three most commonly spoken non-English languages in areas served by the outreach effort. The outreach effort must be reviewed annually by the Forum, instead of by the Office of Equity. In carrying out its purpose, the SBO must consider collaborating with tribes and relevant state agencies. Plan Implementation . The SBO is required to coordinate implementation of the Plan in consultation with relevant state agencies. The SBO must submit a report to the Governor and the Legislature by January 1, 2027, and every two years thereafter, including an updated version of the Plan and a summary evaluation of progress made in implementing the Plan. Digital Equity Forum Duties and Membership . The purpose of the Forum is modified to include developing recommendations related to broadband adoption and digital equity. In addition to existing requirements, when the Forum is developing recommendations, the Forum must also: strengthen cooperatives and other partnerships that promote digital connectivity, broadband adoption, and digital equity, instead of just public-private partnerships; increase awareness of digital equity needs and resources; work to increase collaboration with tribal governments and other partners; recommend opportunities for sustainable digital equity funding; consider related issues within its scope brought forward by the public or members of the Forum; annually review the SBO's outreach effort; and provide feedback on digital equity grant programs. The Forum may also consult with the SBO and other relevant agencies on the Plan. The Office of Equity is not required to appoint members of the Forum, provide staffing for the Forum, or transmit the Forum's recommendations to the Legislature. Instead, the SBO must consult with the Office of Equity, as well as the chair or cochairs of the Forum, on Forum appointments. The SBO must prioritize appointees representing local agencies, in addition to other priority appointees, and the SBO must also consider appointees representing broadband providers, the technology industry, philanthropy, the health industry, and the legal and justice system. A majority of Forum members may appoint an administrative chair or cochairs, and members of the Forum may receive a stipend for attendance at quarterly meetings. The total number of appointed Forum members should not exceed 25 members, unless it is determined that a larger forum is necessary to ensure adequate representation of underserved communities. Digital Opportunity Program . The Digital Equity Opportunity Program is renamed as the Digital Opportunity Program (Program). The Program must provide grants to digital equity programs, instead of community technology

HB 2373.digest: Low-Income Energy Assistance Under the Clean Energy Transformation Act . Starting in 2028, the number of energy assistance programs that electric utilities with fewer than 25,000 customers must provide is reduced to one. Electric utilities with 25,000 customers or more must continue offering energy assistance programs. At least one of these programs for utilities of all sizes must be a monthly bill discount program (Discount Program) for all low-income customers that is sufficient to meet energy assistance need. Electric utilities must demonstrate increasing energy assistance program participation rates and reduced energy burden in each biennial period. Electric utilities must prioritize assistance to low-income households with a higher energy burden. Monthly Bill Discount Program Details . The Discount Program must include at least five income tiers, with benefit levels in each tier set to approximate the discount needed to meet energy assistance for households in each tier. The Discount Program must rely on a third-party low-income needs assessment to determine the income and benefit levels. The Discount Program must also provide a reasonable discount to low-income households that are not in energy assistance need. Electric utilities may: (1) provide a comparable monthly lump-sum payment to utility customers that are unable to receive a monthly discount on their bills; and (2) maintain prior benefit levels for households, if prior levels are greater than those required under the Discount Program. Outreach and Accessibility Requirements . For all low-income energy assistance programs, electric utilities must: offer in-person, phone, and web page enrollment opportunities; offer streamlined eligibility options, including categorial eligibility and self-attestation. Electric utilities may use Community Action Councils or other third parties to audit incomes, and may not require eligibility recertification by an energy assistance program participant more than once every two years; establish application requirements limited to what is necessary to enroll households and effectively implement energy assistance programs; codesign outreach materials and campaigns with community-based organizations, including local low-income service providers that specialize in serving low-income Black, indigenous, and people of color. Electric utilities may enter into an agreement with Commerce to use outreach materials and Commerce-developed strategics, and conduct outreach and enrollment for the purposes of enhancing participation of eligible households in utility low-income programs; develop their energy assistance webpages and energy assistance program materials for multiple languages, and have their webpages and energy assistance program materials reviewed and approved by first language speakers in the state; and provide quarterly bill inserts or emails to customers with program eligibility and enrollment information. Electric utilities may use model bill inserts or text produced by Commerce for this purpose. Reporting . An additional component is added to each utility’s required energy assistance reports to Commerce; utilities must now also report the amount of money used to mitigate rate impacts to low-income customers and a description of any other benefits provided to ratepayers from the sale of no-cost allowances under the Climate Commitment Act, as applicable. HB 2381.digest: The SBCC is directed to adopt a mandatory appendix to the International Building Code as adopted by Washington to establish a performance-based code compliance pathway for low-rise residential buildings with residential occupancy. The appendix applies to buildings of one to six stories that are not classified as high-rise buildings under the International Building Code. Rules adopted must ensure that the performance-based compliance pathway supports integrated and harmonized compliance across specified codes and rules. The SBCC must also adopt rules establishing criteria under which housing systems and plan certifications issued by independent, nationally recognized third-party evaluation or certification organizations may be recognized for purposes of demonstrating compliance with the State Building Code. The SBCC must convene a technical advisory group (TAG) to recommend performance-based code amendments. The TAG must include subject matter experts and appropriate state agencies. The TAG must develop and recommend performance criteria categories and targets and must consider existing and emerging nationally recognized standards and certification frameworks. Recommendations from the TAG must be provided to the SBCC in time for the SBCC to adopt or amend codes as necessary for implementation in the first substantive code update to the State Building Code. The SBCC must adopt section R406 of the international energy conservation code as part of the appendix. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The International Building Code is specified as the International Building Code as amended by Washington. The State Building Code Council must adopt rules allowing demonstrated reductions in embodied carbon associated with building materials to offset or substitute for modeled operational energy use intensity requirements in performance-based compliance pathways applicable to buildings subject to the International Building Code.

HB 2384.digest: A new requirement is added to the application standards for registration as a continuing care retirement community (CCRC). Beginning July 1, 2027, if an applicant for registration as a CCRC offers life care contracts, it must provide an actuarial analysis to the Department of Social and Health Services (Department). A "life care contract" refers to a contract between a CCRC and a person to whom the CCRC agrees to provide lodging and any combination of nursing, medical, or personal care services for at least one year and up to the entirety of the person’s life. The contract is conditioned on payment of an entrance fee in lieu of, or in addition to, other recurring charges that do not change based on the care setting or services. The actuarial analysis requirement begins with the applicant's second registration renewal and applies to every other subsequent registration renewal application. The actuarial analysis must have been prepared by a qualified actuary and include an actuarial memorandum and certification. Upon receipt of an actuarial analysis in application materials, the Department must transmit it to the Office of the Insurance Commissioner (Office) for review. The Department must adopt standards for the contents of the actuarial analysis materials to be submitted. The Office must adopt standards for the review of the actuarial analyses, the qualifications of the actuaries preparing the analyses, and the administration of appeals of determinations that an applicant's actuarial balance is not satisfactory. The Office's standards must include a process for determining the applicant's ability to meet its overall contract obligations under its life care contracts in accordance with actuarial standards of practice. The standards must consider whether the applicant's actuarial balance is satisfactory and reflects liabilities that are sufficient to cover obligations under moderately adverse conditions during the testing period. The term "moderately adverse conditions" is defined as anticipating unfavorable, but not extreme, events with a reasonable probability of occurring during the testing period. Upon concluding its review, the Office must determine whether the applicant's actuarial balance is satisfactory under the review standards and notify the Department and the applicant of the results. If the Office's review finds that the applicant has not satisfied the review requirement, it will notify the applicant of its right to appeal the decision to the Office and provide the reasons for the determination in sufficient detail to allow the applicant to attempt to cure the deficiencies. For those CCRC applicants required to submit an actuarial analysis, the Department's decision to issue a registration depends on the receipt of a notice of completion of the actuarial analysis review from the Office. The Department's online listing of registered CCRCs must include a link to the results of any actuarial analysis review received by the Department from the Office. The Department may issue a provisional registration in situations in which an applicant has submitted sufficient materials for registration, but the results of the review of the actuarial analysis are pending. The Department's registration must be set at a level sufficient to cover the costs to reimburse the Office for its actuarial review activities. HB 2389.digest: Suspended Disposition Alternatives . The court must grant a suspended disposition alternative (Option B or Option C) when a juvenile is eligible unless the court makes an independent finding supported by a preponderance of the evidence that commitment to juvenile rehabilitation is needed because remaining in the community on community supervision would not adequately protect the community for juvenile offenses with a standard range term of confinement over 30 days (except for Murder in the first degree and second degree, Homicide by Abuse, Manslaughter in the first and second degree, Assault in the first degree, Kidnapping in the first degree, Rape in the first degree, Assault of a Child in the first and second degree, violent offenses with certain criminal history, sex offenses, Hit and Run resulting in death, and Vehicular Homicide). In making the finding described above, the court must consider certain factors, including: the severity of the offense(s); the juvenile's criminal history; whether the programming offered in a juvenile facility is appropriate to meet the needs of the juvenile; whether the goals of rehabilitation and community safety can be met in a less restrictive environment; whether the goals of rehabilitation and community safety can be met in a less restrictive disposition that is available; and the juvenile's age, developmental maturity, mental and emotional health, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and any disabilities or special needs impacting the safety or suitability of institutional commitment. The court may place juveniles on electronic monitoring for up to the minimum of a juvenile's standard range when the court does not make a finding described above. Suspended Disposition Alternative (Option B) . Eligibility for the Option B disposition alternative is expanded to include individuals adjudicated of Assault in the second degree, Robbery in the first degree and Attempted Robbery in the first degree, Unlawful Possession of a Firearm, certain felony offenses where there is an allegation that the juvenile was armed with a firearm during commission of the offense, and those with a prior Option B disposition alternative. Substance Use Disorder or Mental Health Disposition Alternative (Option C) . The eligibility for a substance use disorder or mental health disposition alternative, also known as "Option C," is expanded to all juveniles except those adjudicated for an offense that is excluded from the finding described above. In addition, individuals with certain prior criminal history are now eligible for this disposition alternative (current law prohibits individuals with a prior A-, B++, or B+ offense). Appeal of Juvenile Dispositions . Individuals may appeal juvenile dispositions with a term of confinement over 30 days, except for standard range dispositions that do not require the independent finding described above. The Court of Appeals must make certain findings to uphold a finding that commitment to juvenile rehabilitation is needed, as follows: that the reasons supplied by the disposition judge are supported by the record; and that those reasons by a preponderance of the evidence support the conclusion that commitment to juvenile rehabilitation is needed because a community-based placement would not adequately protect the community. HB 2394.digest: Insurance Fraud Program. The personnel that the Commissioner may employ must be qualified by training and experience in the areas of detection, investigation, or prosecution of fraud and other other crimes in which the insurance industry or an insurance consumer or beneficiary is a victim or impacted, instead of qualified by training and experience in the areas of detection, investigation, or prosecution of fraud in which the insurance industry is a victim. Program Purpose . The Program's purpose is revised to make a purpose to confront the problem of insurance fraud and other crimes that impact the insurance industry, or insurance consumers or beneficiaries in Washington by updating definitions to address recurring or technologically sophisticated fraud schemes, and making a concerted effort to: detect such crimes, reduce their occurrence through criminal enforcement and deterrence; require restitution of expenses incurred by an insurer in investigating or paying fraudulent claims or resulting from other crimes; and require restitution to insurance consumers victimized by insurance fraud and other insurance-related crimes. The primary focus of the insurance fraud program is on organized or collusive criminal schemes that are fraudulent activities committed against impact insurance companies or insurance consumers, rather than on organized fraudulent activities committed against insurance companies. Insurance Fraud Program—Definitions and Crime of Insurance Fraud . The definition of "insurance fraud" is revised and restructured as a crime of Insurance Fraud, punishable as a class B felony. Willful embezzlement, abstracting, purloining, or conversion of moneys, funds, premiums, credits, or other property of an insurer or person engaged in the business of insurance is changed to embezzling, abstracting, purloining, or engaging or conspiring in conversion of moneys, funds, premiums, credits, benefits, or other property of an insurer or person engaged in the business of insurance, or insurance consumer or beneficiary.

HB 2400.digest: Business Registration—Vloggers . A vlogger with a substantial nexus with Washington who, within the previous 12-month period, received a total of $12,000 or more in compensation from compensated social media video content, is deemed to be engaged in business activity and must register with the Department of Revenue (DOR). For this purpose, compensation must be determined without any deduction on account of any costs, interest, discount, taxes, or any other expense whatsoever paid or accrued and without any deduction on account of losses. A violation of the registration requirement is punishable by a civil penalty of $1,000, enforceable by the DOR or the Attorney General. Trust Account Requirements—Social Media Services and Third-Party Advertisers . Establishing the Trust Account. A social media service or any third-party advertiser with a substantial nexus with Washington must establish a trust account for the benefit of a minor child of a vlogger when the minor child's likeness, name, or photograph is present in a video segment published by the vlogger and the social media service or third-party advertiser compensates the vlogger in relation to the video segment. The funds in a trust account must be preserved for the benefit of the minor, made available to the former minor upon reaching age 18, and paid into an account of the former minor's choosing upon request. Funding the Trust Account. A social media service and a third-party advertiser must fund the trust account. For any video segment that includes the likeness, name, or photograph of the vlogger's minor child, the social media service or third-party advertiser must withhold a pro rata percentage of the total compensation the social media service or third-party advertiser would otherwise provide to the vlogger in relation to the video segment and deposit the withheld funds in the minor's trust account. "Pro rata percentage" means an amount equal to the percent of time the vlogger's minor child appeared or was referenced in a video segment. Where more than one minor child's likeness, name, or photograph is included in a vlogger's video segment, the compensation with respect to that video segment must be equally divided between the minor children under the pro rata percentage requirement, regardless of differences in percentage of content provided by the individual children. Penalties for Trust Account Violations. A violation of the trust account requirements is enforceable through a civil cause of action in district or superior court by an individual in whose benefit a trust account was or should have been established. Upon finding a violation, a court may award actual damages or impose a statutory penalty, whichever is greater, to be awarded to the harmed individual, in addition to their costs of the suit, and a reasonable attorney's fee. A court may also provide injunctive relief and any other relief the court finds just and equitable to enforce the trust account requirements. Actual damages for a violation of trust account requirements is the amount of compensation a social media service or third-party advertiser should have deposited to an individual's trust account, plus a reasonable amount of interest to be determined by the court. Statutory damages for a violation of trust account requirements are: (1) $50,000 for a failure to establish a trust account; and (2) $50,000 for each video that includes the likeness, name, or photograph of the vlogger's minor child visually or as

HB 2401.digest: The Washington State Boys and Men Commission (Commission) is established as a stand-alone agency, contingent upon the receipt of nonstate contributions in an amount sufficient to fully fund the Commission's operational costs through December 31, 2029. The Office of Financial Management (OFM) must, by June 30, 2026, determine the amount by fiscal year that would be necessary to fully fund the operating costs of the Commission through December 31, 2029. The OFM must also seek nonstate contributions, place any contributions received into the newly created Boys and Men Commission Account, and notify interested parties whether sufficient funds have been received to fully cover the Commission's operational costs through December 31, 2029. The Commission would consist of nine members appointed by the Governor. At least one member must be from a federally recognized Indian tribe. The Governor must consider nominations for membership based on maintaining a balanced and diverse distribution of ethnicity, geographic representation, sexual orientation, age, socioeconomic status, and occupational representation, but the majority of members must self-identify as male to maintain sufficient representation of individuals with direct lived experience. The Commission is administered by an executive director.

HB 2402.digest: Beginning January 1, 2030, a person may not manufacture, sell, or distribute into Washington, IV solution containers made with intentionally added DEHP or that contain unintentionally added DEHP in a quantity that equals or exceeds 0.1 percent weight per weight. Beginning January 1, 2035, a person may not manufacture, sell, or distribute into Washington IV tubing made with intentionally added DEHP or that contains unintentionally added DEHP in a quantity that equals or exceeds 0.1 percent weight per weight. Human blood collection and storage bags, apheresis and cell therapy blood kits and bags, including tubing, are exempt from these prohibitions. A person or entity may not replace DEHP in revised or new products with other ortho-phthalates. If the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or the Department of Health (DOH) determine that there is an industry shortage of FDA-approved IV solution containers and tubing, FDA-approved IV solution containers and tubing with DEHP may be manufactured, distributed, and sold in Washington until the FDA or DOH determines the supply chain interruption is terminated. A person or entity, due to pending FDA approval for the DEHP-free IV solution containers or due to the manufacturer not having adequate equipment to manufacture the DEHP-free IV solution containers by January 1, 2030, may meet the requirement by January 1, 2032, if: the person or entity notified its Washington customers, no later than January 1, 2027, that it has commenced development of the DEHP-free IV solution containers; and the person or entity provides notice to its customers and posts to its website, no later than January 1, 2028, that it will not meet the 2030 deadline. A new chapter in Title 70A is created.

HB 2403.digest: Changes to Failure to Register Offenses . Felony Failure to Register as a Sex Offender is a seriousness level I offense and an unranked class C felony, and the elevation to a class B felony for a third or subsequent felony Failure to Register offense is removed. The definition of "sex offense" in the SRA is also modified to not include a second or subsequent felony Failure to Register offense. Reentry Plans and Community Custody . For anyone under the DOC's jurisdiction for a sex offense or Failure to Register offense, the DOC must utilize existing resources and methods to support compliance and improve functioning in the community as part of developing a person's individualized reentry plan. Modifications are also made to community custody requirements for Failure to Register violations. Regardless of a person's risk classification and whether the person has been sentenced to more or less than one year of confinement, courts must impose varying lengths of community custody for felony and misdemeanor Failure to Register violations for both sex offenses and kidnapping offenses. Specifically, courts may impose up to one year of community custody for a first misdemeanor or felony Failure to Register as a Sex Offender violation or Failure to Register as a Kidnapping Offender violation. Courts must impose two years of community custody for a second or subsequent violation of a Failure to Register. Model Policy . The Washington Association of Sheriffs and Police Chiefs is required to review its model policy regarding Adult and Juvenile Sex Offender Registration to identify opportunities to utilize technology, report its findings to the Legislature by December 1, 2026, and update the model policy by June 1, 2027.

HB 2405.digest: The Department of Labor and Industries (Department) is authorized to use funds allocated for return-to-work programs to provide funding for workplace behavioral health programs focused on occupations that have a high risk of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The Department may determine appropriate organizations eligible for awards. A pilot program is established to increase access to care for workers seeking workers' compensation coverage for PTSD as an occupational disease. The Department must provide eligible workers with the opportunity to participate in the pilot program, and the workers may opt in. The Department and participating self-insured employers must authorize treatment for PTSD prior to claim adjudication for a worker who opts in to the pilot program, regardless of whether the claim for benefits is ultimately allowed. A diagnostic interview and up to 11 treatment sessions within 90 days of diagnosis may be authorized prior to claim adjudication. A worker may receive treatment prior to claim adjudication from a provider outside the medical provider network if the provider agrees to be paid in accordance with the Department's medical aid rules and fee schedules and signs a nonnetwork provider agreement. The Department must contact nonnetwork providers who agree to provide treatment as part of the pilot program to better understand barriers to entering the medical provider network. Once a claim is allowed, the worker must seek treatment within the medical provider network. Costs for treatment prior to adjudication on state fund claims that are ultimately rejected will be spread across all risk classes for which there is a presumption of coverage for PTSD as an occupational disease. Costs for treatment on self-insured claims that are ultimately rejected will be paid by the self-insured employer. The Department and participating self-insured employers must authorize up to six additional PTSD treatment sessions within one year of claim closure when necessary to maintain a worker's level of functioning at the time of claim closure. The supervisor of industrial insurance may authorize continued treatment of up to 12 sessions, if a claim has not been allowed within 90 days. The Department may enter into agreements with healthcare organizations and providers for workers to receive services and may modify administrative requirements such as documentation, timelines, reporting, or prior authorization for workers and treating providers participating in the pilot program. Self-insured employers must produce upon request a report of all workers' compensation claims subject to the pilot. If the pilot program provisions conflict with an existing statute, the pilot program supersedes the conflicting statute for the duration of the pilot. The Department has rulemaking authority to implement the program. By July 1, 2030, the Department must provide recommendations to the Legislature based on the pilot.

HB 2406.digest: General Notices and Communications from the Department of Labor and Industries . Numerous statutes governing how the Department sends notices in various programs are amended to allow notices to be sent electronically. Before using an electronic method for the first time, the Department must provide recipients the option to receive notices nonelectronically. Notices Under the Industrial Insurance Act . Notices of orders closing a claim may be sent electronically if the recipient chooses. The copy of the order must contain a statement saying the order is final within 60 days from the date the order is communicated through nonelectronic means and 65 days from the date the order is communicated through electronic means. Notices and Appeals Under the Washington Industrial Safety and Health Act . The Department has a total of 75 working days in which to make a redetermination when there has been an appeal, instead of a 30-day period with a 45-day extension period. The Department must provide information about public hearings for rulemaking to the newspapers, rather than publishing in the newspaper, at least 20 days, rather than 30 days, prior to the hearing. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill removes certain sections from the bill, thereby restoring current law on notices related to: (1) transportation network companies and drivers; (2) petitions to de-certify a self-insured employers; (3) elections for third-party actions in workers' compensation cases; and (4) other workers' compensation orders, except that the bill still allows for closing orders to be sent electronically if the recipient chooses.

HB 2409.digest: Covered Employees and Employers . Collective bargaining for agricultural employees is placed under the jurisdiction of PERC. "Agricultural employee" means any person engaged in agriculture, any individual engaged or permitted by an agricultural employer to work on a farm, and any person engaged in the canning, processing, preserving, freezing, drying, marketing, storing, packing for shipment, or distributing of agricultural produce, meat and fish products, or perishable foods. Cannabis agricultural employees or other employees covered under the NLRA are not included. Covered employers are any persons who employ agricultural employees and includes any person acting directly or indirectly as an agent of an agricultural employer. PERC Enforcement . The PERC has concurrent jurisdiction with the courts to enforce state law prohibiting employers from interfering, restraining, or coercing employees from engaging in concerted activities for purposes of collective bargaining. The PERC has authority to issue cease and desist orders and take other affirmative action, such as order the payment of damages and reasonable attorneys’ fees and the reinstatement of an agricultural employee. Certification of the Exclusive Bargaining Representative and Bargaining Unit Determinations . In each application for the certification of an exclusive bargaining representative or unit clarification, PERC must determine the appropriate bargaining unit. If there is disagreement as to the merger of two or more bargaining units, PERC must be invited to intervene. If there is a disagreement between the employer and employees as to the selection of a bargaining representative, a farmworker labor organization must invite PERC to intervene. The PERC must determine the bargaining representative by either a cross-check or secret ballot election. Cross-check is available in limited circumstances and applies when a farmworker labor organization seeking to be certified is already recognized by the U.S. Department of Labor, is the only organization seeking to be certified, and there is a showing of interest supporting the selection of the exclusive bargaining representative by more than 50 percent of the employees. If cross-check is not appropriate, PERC must conduct a secret ballot election upon a request of a farmworker labor organization showing written proof of at least 30 percent of the employees within the unit. Procedures and timelines are established for PERC to conduct the election and certify the exclusive bargaining representative. Timelines are also established for when the question of representation and decertification can be raised. Dispute Resolution and Interest Arbitration Provisions . If the employer and exclusive bargaining representative fail to come to an agreement within three months of certifying the exclusive bargaining representative, or within three months of an expired collective bargaining agreement, all unresolved matters must be submitted for resolution through interest arbitration. The parties may agree to continue negotiations beyond the three-month deadline before going to arbitration. Procedures are established for parties to select an arbitrator, select hearing dates, submit their last and final proposals, and split the arbitration fees and expenses. Provisions are also created regarding evidence and other factors the arbitrator may consider when coming to a decision. The arbitrator’s decision is final and binding on the parties, subject to supe

HB 2410.digest: Establishment of the Washington State Commercial Truck Safety and Education Council . The Washington State Commercial Truck Safety and Education Council (Council) is established in the Washington Traffic Safety Commission (Commission) to recommend programs and projects that improve the safety of the commercial trucking industry. The Council may: recommend programs and projects that carry out the purpose of the Council, including enhancing safety and training, providing for research and development, and educating the public; request the authorization of the payment of Council costs; coordinate Council activities with industry associations and others to provide the efficient delivery of services; recommend procurements for contracts with entities to carry out the purpose of the Council; recommend the Commission apply for, receive, and accept grants, loans, and gifts; and recommend grants targeted at improving commercial motor vehicle safety and training. The Council must meet at least quarterly, with an initial meeting to be convened by the Commission no later than January 2027. Beginning December 31, 2027, the Council is required to annually report its activities, findings, and recommendations during the preceding year to the Transportation Committees of the Legislature. Council Membership . The following Council members are required to be appointed by the Governor: the Chief of the Washington State Patrol, or the Chief's designee; the Director of the DOL, or the Director's designee; the Secretary of the Washington State Department of Transportation, or the Secretary's designee; the Executive Director of the Washington Trucking Associations (WTA) or the Executive Director's designee; the Director of the Commission, or the Director's designee; the Executive Director of the Washington State Board for Community and Technical Colleges, or the Executive Director's designee; one member of the general public; three members from a trucking industry association or associations, with consideration given to a list of six nominees submitted by the WTA; the Executive Director of the Workforce Training and Education Coordination Board (WTECB), or the Executive Director's designee; and one member from a labor organization recommended by the Washington State Labor Council (WSLC). The Council may consult with other governmental entities or individuals from the public or private sector who have a unique interest or expertise in commercial vehicle safety, training, and efficient operations. Funding for Council Activities . The Commercial Vehicle Safety Enforcement Fee assessed on commercial motor vehicles is increased from $16 to $32. The additional revenue is directed to the Commercial Truck Safety and Education Account (Commercial Truck Safety Account), which is created as a non-appropriated account to be used only for activities recommended by the Council to improve the safety of the commercial truck industry and related administrative costs. Only the Director of the Commission or the Director's designee may authorize expenditures from the account. Commission costs associated with support of the Council are to be reimbursed for the Commercial Truck Safety Account.

HB 2415.digest: Fatality Reviews of Unexpected Deaths of Department of Social and Health Services Facility Residents . The DSHS must conduct an unexpected fatality review (review) upon the unexpected death of any resident of a DSHS facility or in any case identified for a review by the DD Ombuds or the Patient Rights Ombuds. The primary purpose of the review is to develop recommendations to the DSHS and Legislature regarding changes in practices or policies to prevent fatalities and strengthen safety and health protections for residents in DSHS facilities. Reviews must not take precedence over investigations being conducted by adult protective services, child protective services, residential care services, or law enforcement. Scope of Reviews. The DSHS facilities included in the review requirement include all facilities operated by the DSHS that provide care on a residential or inpatient basis. This includes residential habilitation centers, state-operated living alternatives, transitional care facilities, state hospitals, the Child Study and Treatment Center, the Special Commitment Center, secure community transition facilities, and other DSHS facilities that provide inpatient services to individuals who are placed in the care of the DSHS under the provisions governing involuntary treatment, competency to stand trial, and not guilty by reason of insanity commitment. An unexpected fatality includes any death of a resident of a DSHS facility, regardless of where the death actually occurred, that was not the result of a diagnosed or documented terminal illness or other debilitating or deteriorating illness or condition where the death was anticipated, or that occurred within one year of a report of abuse or neglect of the resident. Review Team. The DSHS must convene an unexpected fatality review team (review team) made up of individuals with appropriate expertise who do not have previous involvement in the case. The review team must include a representative from the Health Care Authority. If the unexpected fatality concerns a resident of a residential habilitation center or state-operated living alternative, the review team must include the DD Ombuds or their designee. For unexpected fatalities of persons not residing in either of these settings, the review team must include a representative from the Office of the Patient Rights Ombuds. During the course of the review, the DSHS and the review team must have access to all records and files regarding the person or otherwise relevant to the review that have been produced or retained by the DSHS including, but not limited to, critical incident reviews, root cause analysis, and mortality review committee reports. If the report concerns a person who was the subject of one or more reports of abuse or neglect within the last year, the report must also describe the nature of any reports of abuse or neglect. HB 2416.digest: For emissions through 2030, Ecology must allocate no-cost allowances to a WTE facility constructed prior to 1992 that becomes a CCA covered entity at the beginning of the second compliance period, if the facility is operated in compliance with federal laws and regulations and meets state air quality standards. Relative to the facility's baseline average annual GHG emissions from 2021 through 2025, Ecology must allocate no cost allowance equal to 100 percent of baseline emissions for emissions year 2027 and 2028, 93 percent of baseline emissions for emissions year 2029, and 86 percent of baseline emissions for emissions year 2030. Forty percent of the allowances allocated to the WTE facility must be consigned to auction, with proceeds to be used, with Ecology approval, for investments in projects or programs that reduce GHG emissions associated with the WTE facility. The owner or operator of a WTE facility must submit a proposal to Ecology of how the investments in projects or programs will reduce GHG emissions before expending proceeds from consigned allowances. Ecology must review this proposal within 90 days, and the WTE facility owner or operator must address Ecology's comments, gain Ecology approval of its proposal, and take reasonable steps towards implementation of the proposal. If a WTE facility’s GHG emissions exceed the no-cost allowances allocated to the facility for 2027 through 2030, the WTE facility owner or operator must acquire additional compliance instruments equal to its compliance obligation. The WTE facility may bank unused allowances. Ecology must withhold or withdraw the relevant share of no-cost allowances to the WTE facility if the WTE facility ceases production and closes, with the withheld or withdrawn allowances being transferred to the CCA’s Emissions Containment Reserve. If the WTE facility curtails production, it may retain but not trade allowances during the period of curtailment. Ecology may not allocate no-cost allowances to electric utilities for GHG emissions associated with electricity produced by a WTE facility for which the WTE facility has a CCA compliance obligation. By December 1, 2030, the owner or operator of the WTE facility constructed prior to 1992 must provide a two-part plan to Ecology and the Department of Commerce. One portion of the plan is a greenhouse gas emission reduction plan that must outline how the facility will achieve emissions consistent with the state emissions limits for 2040 and 2050 through any combination of GHG emission reduction strategies. The other portion of the plan is a waste reduction and material recovery plan that must be consistent with the state's waste management hierarchy, take into consideration the organic material management policies that apply to local governments and businesses and the expected impacts of the 2025 Recycling Reform Act, and align with the county's local solid waste plan. Ecology may provide technical assistance and guidance for the development and implementation of the plan. The owner or operator of the WTE facility must consider social, environmental, and health factors in overburdened communities and vulnerable populations, and consult with local municipally created sustainability advisory groups. The facility owner or operator must submit the plan for review by Ecology in consultation with the Department of Commerce, and must address comments received from the agencies within 120 days. HB 2418.digest: A permit issued based on compliance with state and local building codes is not a project permit. Nor is a special purpose district's or public utility district's determination of service available, system capacity, infrastructure requirements, or review of proposed ware, sewer, or stormwater civil plans. Determination of Completeness . A determination of completeness must be based on whether an application is procedurally complete. A determination of completeness is not a substantive review and cannot be conditioned on the adequacy, accuracy, or sufficiency of the information submitted. Permit Review Deadlines . Periods during which an applicant has not paid an applicable fee or posted a required notice, periods in which a draft of a final environmental impact statement is being prepared following a determination of significance under SEPA, and periods between the issuance of a final decision and the expiration of the applicable administrative review period are not included when determining the number of days a project permit application has been in review with a local government. Nor are periods in which a local government has completed all possible work on the application but is waiting on necessary action from another government entity. Any government entity other than a local government, special purpose district, or public utility district that imposes a fee on an applicant for the review of a project permit application related to a residential project must complete its review within the project permit review timelines applicable to a local government. The time period that a government entity has taken to conduct its review of the application is exclusive of the time period that the local government or another public agency has taken to review the application. If the review is not completed within the applicable timeframe, then the government entity must refund 20 percent of the permit review fee that it collected. If a government entity does not impose a fee for its review, then no refund is required. An applicant may, in writing, waive the permitting review deadlines applicable to a government entity's review of a project permit application. If an applicant does so, then provisions related to project permit review deadlines and to a potential refund do not apply to the application. Similarly, if an applicant agrees to the extension of the deadlines for a county or city to issue a decision on a project permit application, then the deadlines and refund provisions do not apply to that application. An applicant may agree to waive or extend the deadlines for a government entity or a local government at any time prior to the denial or the application or the expiration of the deadlines. Special purpose districts and public utility districts (districts) have different permitting deadlines for project permit applications related to residential projects than do local government or other government entities. For a district, the time for conducting a review of an application begins after it receives a complete application referral from the local government. A referral is complete if it provides civil plans and related materials that are based on the district's adopted engineering and design standards, and all materials required to constitute a complete application under the district's procedures are included. A district has 15 calendar days from the day it receives the application referral to determine if the application is complete. If it is

HB 2421.digest: Beginning January 1, 2035, the manufacture, sale, and distribution of new vehicle tires containing 6PPD or regrettable 6PPD substitutes identified by Ecology by rule is prohibited. These restrictions do not apply to products that are certified, regulated, or specified by the following federal agencies: the United States Federal Aviation Administration, the United States Department of Defense, the United States Department of Homeland Security, or the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. In adopting rules, Ecology must consider information generated by other states or nations to identify regrettable 6PPD substitutes, and must, at minimum, identify as a regrettable 6PPD substitute any alternative that is evaluated under Safer Products and determined not to be a safer alternative to 6PPD. Ecology may adopt rules to implement, administer, and enforce requirements related to 6PPD and regrettable 6PPD substitutes in vehicle tires. Violations are subject to civil penalties of up to $5,000 for a first offense and $10,000 for repeat offenses. Penalties are appealable to the Pollution Control Hearings Board and must be deposited in the Model Toxics Control Operating Account. The restrictions on 6PPD and regrettable 6PPD substitutes in vehicle tires do not limit the authority of Ecology under Safer Products. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: Substitute House Bill 2421 as compared to the original bill: eliminates the new 6PPD mitigation fee on motor vehicle tires that contain 6PPD; specifies that the 2035 restriction on 6PPD and regrettable 6PPD substitutes in tires applies only to vehicle tires; and excludes, from the new 2035 restrictions on 6PPD in vehicle tires, products that are certified, regulated, or specified by the following federal agencies: (1) the United States Federal Aviation Administration; (2) the United States Department of Defense; (3) the United States Department of Homeland Security; or (4) the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

HB 2425.digest: Nurse Delegation . An RN may delegate tasks to other individuals in any setting where an RN determines it is in the best interest of the patient and within the nurse's scope of practice. When delegating a task, the nurse must determine the competency of the individual to perform the tasks, including verifying certification or documentation as required by rule; evaluate the stability of the patient and appropriateness of the delegation; and supervise the task. Setting specific requirements and restrictions are eliminated as are specific requirements related to the injection of insulin. A nurse may delegate tasks to credentialed medical assistants. If trained and delegated the task by an RN, a nursing assistant or home care aide may administer medications, including those that pierce the skin through subcutaneous injections, and may perform capillary blood sticks. An RN may not delegate the administration of medication through intramuscular or intravenous means, tasks involving piercing or severing tissues, or acts that require substantial skill or nursing judgement. Requirements that an RN verify that a nursing assistant or home care aide has completed the required nurse delegation training before authorizing delegation are removed (however, the RN must verify any certification or documentation required by rule prior to delegating a task). Education and training provided by an RN to a parent, guardian, or family member designated to provide care for a patient is not delegation of a nursing care task. By January 1, 2028, the Board of Nursing must adopt rules to address appropriate delegation parameters. Accepting Delegation of Nursing Care Tasks . Requirements that nursing assistants and home care aides complete a specialized diabetes nurse delegation course before administering insulin and requirements to provide certificates of completion of the nurse delegation core training and diabetes delegation course to the delegating nurse are eliminated. Nursing assistants and home care aides accurately following delegation instructions, rather than written delegation instructions, from a nurse are immune from liability regarding the performance of their duties. No facility or employer (rather than a provider of community-based care or in-home services agency) may discriminate or retaliate against a person because the person made a complaint or participated in an investigation. Nursing assistants and home care aides are not subject to any liability, reprisal, or disciplinary action when administering medication in an emergency response situation if the patient has a prescribed and available medication for that specific type of emergency event.

HB 2428.digest: Life Insurance Policy—Written Notice of Possible Termination for Nonpayment of Premium . Subject to three exclusions, at least 30 days before the day on which coverage under an individual life insurance policy will lapse based on nonpayment of the premium, the insurer must send a written notice of possible termination of coverage to the policyholder at the policyholder's last known address and a third party designated on the account as authorized under the bill. An insurer must obtain and, upon request, demonstrate proof of delivery for each notice the insurer sends under this requirement. Proof of delivery may include records sufficient to show that notices are sent first-class mail using an intelligent mail barcode, or a certified mail receipt, read-receipt for electronic delivery, or tracking confirmation from a shipping service. The requirement to send the written notice does not apply to: (1) group life insurance policies; (2) life insurance policies for which payment of premium is due monthly or more frequently; or (3) term life insurance policies that have a term of one year or less. Life Insurance Policy—Applicant Designation of Third Party to Receive Notice . Subject to the same three exclusions, an insurer that delivers or issues for delivery an individual life insurance policy in Washington must notify the applicant for the policy, in writing at the time of application for the policy, of an applicant's right to designate a third party to receive notice of lapse or termination of the policy based on nonpayment of the premium. An applicant may make a designation at the time of application for the policy, or at any time the policy is in force, by submitting a written notice to the insurer containing the name and address of the third-party designee. The designation of a third party does not create or constitute acceptance of any duty or liability on the part of the third party related to: (1) informing or not informing the policyholder or any other person about a notice received by the third party; (2) making a payment of any premium on behalf of the policyholder; (3) compensating the policyholder, beneficiary, or any other person in relation to a lapse or cancellation of a life insurance policy; or (4) taking any lawful action upon receiving a notice. The designation of a third party also does not create or constitute acceptance of any liability on the part of the insurer as to the third party. Prospective Application of Bill . The bill applies prospectively only and not retroactively. It applies to life insurance policies issued on or after the effective date of the bill.
