SB 5915.digest: In selecting health technologies to be reviewed under the Health Technology Assessment Program, the Health Care Authority (Authority) must give priority to an additional category of health technologies. The new priority category relates to health technologies that have patient access established or recommended for a patient population under Medicare or in nationally recognized expert treatment guidelines, including guidelines adopted by specialty physician organizations or patient advocacy organizations. When the health technology pertains to a life-threatening or rare disease, the Health Technology Clinical Committee (Committee) must: evaluate all applicable clinical trials regarding the technology, as published in peer-reviewed clinical literature, including randomized control trials; and consider information submitted by clinical experts indicating that a randomized control trial or other specific trial design would be unethical, impractical, or impossible for the technology within a specific patient population. Re-reviews of health technologies are not limited to evidence made available since the previous determination. Re-reviews must consider new evidence in combination with, and within the context of, the clinical evidence the Committee had previously considered. The Authority must publish on its website the receipt of submissions for new technology assessments and re-review assessments with 30 days of receipt. The Committee must review the submissions and communicate its decision to review or re-review within 180 days. If the Committee issues an adverse determination, it must provide the submitting party with a written, substantive explanation of the rationale for the adverse determination within 180 days from the date of submission.

SB 5934.digest: The bill as referred to committee not considered. Summary of Bill (Proposed Substitute): The court must grant a motion requesting DNA testing if the motion is in the proper form, unless the state shows by clear and convincing evidence that the DNA evidence could not demonstrate a likelihood of innocence. When evaluating whether the state has met its burden by clear and convincing evidence, the court shall presume the test results most favorable to the convicted person in light of all the evidence presented at trial. Within 90 days after a motion, the state may oppose DNA testing by providing an explanation as to why the DNA evidence could not demonstrate a likelihood of innocence. A court order or request for laboratory examination authorizing DNA testing does not create or indicate any position of the court or any party regarding the legal significance of the DNA test results. When a motion is granted or when a request for testing is agreed to by the state, the convicted person is entitled to discovery consistent with the laws and court rules that apply at trial. DNA Testing . DNA testing may be performed by the WSP crime lab, or it may be contracted to be performed by the WSP crime lab. Items subject to testing shall be transferred to the WSP crime lab in installments. The WSP crime lab shall consult with parties to determine: the order in which the evidence will be tested; the evidence items that will be transferred to the WSP crime lab with each installment; and the total number of installments necessary to complete DNA testing. The court may consider a motion to revise the order for DNA testing if testing has begun and: the crime laboratory determines that an evidence item is unsuitable for DNA testing, and the crime lab submits written notice to the parties and the court explaining how the scientist reached that determination, and why the evidence is unsuitable for DNA testing; or the results suggest the requirements that form the basis of the motion are no longer met. Biological material or evidence samples must be preserved in accordance with laws on DNA evidence, a sentencing court's order, and any court rule adopted for the preservation of evidence. The court no longer has to specify the samples to be maintained and the length of time the samples must be preserved.
SB 5934.digest_source: WA Senate Bill Report (Orig.) (Summary of Bill)
SB 5934.last_action: First reading, referred to Law & Justice.
SB 5934.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to reducing litigation costs by removing barriers to postconviction DNA testing;
SB 5934.title: Postconviction DNA testing

SB 5936.digest: Business Liability for Trafficking or Coercion . A business may only be prosecuted for Trafficking or Coercion of Involuntary Servitude when the business knowingly engages in Trafficking, or when an employee or agent engages in Trafficking, the conduct is a pattern of activity that meets one of the offenses, the conduct directly benefits the business, and the entity knew the conduct was occurring and failed to take effective action to stop it. When a business is prosecuted for Trafficking or Coercion of Involuntary Servitude, the court may consider the severity of the business's conduct, and may order additional penalties. The additional penalties may include: a fine up to $1 million per offense; profit disgorgement from the conduct; and debarment from state and local government contracts. Victim Confidentiality . Law enforcement officers and prosecuting agencies are required to keep the identity, pictures, and images of the alleged victim and the victim's family confidential for investigations and prosecutions of Trafficking or Coercion of Involuntary Servitude. Disclosure is permitted when it is necessary for the investigation or prosecution, required by law or a court order, or necessary to ensure services or benefits are provided for the victim or victim's family. Public Records Exemption . An exemption is added to the Public Records Act for the identity, pictures, and images of the alleged victim or victim's family in an investigation or prosecution for Trafficking or Coercion of Involuntary Servitude. Alien Crime Victims . If a state or local law enforcement agency, prosecutor, administrative judge, hearing office, or other authority determines that an individual does not meet the requirements for the certifying agency's determination regarding helpfulness to the detection, investigation, or prosecution, then the certifying agency is required to inform the individual of the reason for its determination. The individual may make another request for a determination and submit additional evidence.

SB 5937.digest: Alternative Key Requirements . Upon request, a landlord must offer a tenant an alternative key that does not use biometric identifier information or a software application operated on the tenant's mobile phone or similar electronic device. Examples of alternative keys include, but are not limited to, key fobs, key cards, physical keys, other forms of physical access, or keypads or similar devices that use manual entering of a coded sequence of numbers, letters, or both. "Biometric identifier information" means a physiological, biological, or behavioral characteristic that is used to identify, or assist in identifying, an individual including, but not limited to: a retina or iris scan; a fingerprint; a voiceprint; or a scan or record of a palm, hand, or face geometry. Smart Access Systems . Smart access system data collection and privacy policy requirements are added to the RLTA. "Smart access system" means any system that uses electronic or computerized technology, such as a radio frequency identification card, a mobile phone application, biometric identifier information, or any other digital technology that is designed to gather information in order to grant entry to a building containing a dwelling unit, its elevators, its common areas, or to an individual dwelling unit. A smart access system does not include methods of entry that solely rely upon a keypad or similar device that uses the manual entering of a coded sequence of numbers, letters, or both. "Smart access building" means a building containing a dwelling unit that uses a smart access system. Data Collection. A smart access building landlord or third party may collect only the minimum amount of authentication data and reference data necessary to enable the use of a smart access system for the purpose of granting a user access to a building, its elevators, its common areas, or to a user's dwelling. "User" means a tenant of a smart access building. "Authentication data" means the data generated or collected at the point of authentication in connection with granting a user entry to a smart access building, common area, or dwelling unit through such building's smart access system, excluding data generated or collected by a video, audio, or camera system that is used to monitor entrances but not grant entry. "Reference data" means the information against which authentication data is verified at the point of authentication by a smart access system in order to grant a user entry to a smart access building, dwelling unit, or common area. A smart access system may collect, generate, or use only the following information: a user's name; the dwelling unit number and other doors or common areas that the user can access; a user's preferred contact method; a user's biometric identifier information if used by the smart access system; the identification card number or any identifier associated with the physical hardware used to facilitate building entry including radio frequency identification card, Bluetooth, or other similar technical protocols; passwords, passcodes, usernames, and contact information used singly or in conjunction with other reference data to grant a user entry to a smart access building, dwelling unit, or common area through the building's smart access system, or to access any online tools used to manage user accounts related to a building; lease information, including move-in and move-out dates if available; and the time and method of access, solely for security and oper

Up to 50 youth are eligible for the program if they are receiving foster care services and are experiencing homelessness. Youth who are at risk of experiencing homelessness are eligible as well, subject to appropriation. Rental assistance is to be provided to eligible youth based on the following criteria: rental assistance is provided for up to 24 months, not to exceed a youth's 21st birthday; the amount of rental assistance must be based on fair market rent in the youth's location; youth shall pay no more than 30 percent of their adjusted gross income toward rent, including the extended foster care subsidy; and if the youth's rent and utilities exceed the fair market rent for that location, the youth's contribution is not to exceed 40 percent of their monthly adjusted gross income, including the extended foster care subsidy.

SB 5945.digest: Persistent offender is defined to include convictions for murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, or any sex offense considered a most serious offense at any age, or most serious offenses in which the person was 18 years of age or older at the time of the offense date for three strikes. A resentencing hearing is required in any case that the person has been sentenced as a persistent offender, if one of the convictions occurred with an offense date before the person turned 18 years old. A resentencing hearing is not required for a person that was convicted of murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, or any sex offense considered a most serious offense, at any age. The prosecuting attorney for each county must review each sentencing document for any person sentenced as a persistent offender. The prosecutor must, or the person that was sentenced as a persistent offender with a conviction that occurred for an offense while under the age of 18 may, make a motion for relief from sentence to the original sentencing court. The prosecutor must make reasonable efforts to notify victims and survivors of victims of the motion for resentencing and the date of the resentencing hearing. Victim advocates must be made available to the victim or their survivors, and the court must provide an opportunity to the victim or their survivors to present a statement personally or through representation. All notice requirements must comply with the requirements under state law. The sentencing court shall grant the motion if it finds that a conviction for an offense that was committed when the person was under the age of 18 was used as a basis for a finding that the person was a persistent offender, unless the person was convicted of murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, or any sex offense considered a most serious offense. The court must set an expedited resentencing date. At resentencing, not withstanding the requirement that any sentence imposed be determined by the law in effect at the time of the offense, for purposes of resentencing, any conviction for an offense under the age of 18 must be sentenced as if it were not a most serious offense, regardless of if the offense happened before, on, or after the 2019 law that removed robbery in the second degree from qualifying as a strike offense. Applies retroactively to persons incarcerated in total confinement as persistent offenders on the effective date of the bill, regardless of the date of offense or conviction that resulted in the person being sentenced as a persistent offender. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY HUMAN SERVICES COMMITTEE (First Substitute): Requires victims and survivors of victims of any crimes committed by the offender to be notified of the motion for resentencing and the date of the resentencing hearing. Permits victims and survivors to present a statement either personally or by representation. Requires the prosecuting attorney and court to comply with chapter 7.69 RCW. Includes persons convicted of murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, or any sex offense considered a most serious offense at any age as persistent offenders. Restores the two-strikes definition of persistent offender. Resentencing is not necessary for any person that has been convicted of murder in the first or second degree, or any sex offense considered a most serious offense.

SB 5951.digest: Authorization for a School Supply of Albuterol. Beginning in the 2027-28 school year, school districts, charter schools, state-tribal education compact schools, and private schools are authorized to maintain a supply of albuterol at each school in a designated location. Albuterol may be acquired from donation sources, but it must be accompanied by a prescription. Albuterol from the school or school district supply authorized must be accessed and administered in accordance with a uniform procedure for the management of a student's respiratory symptoms, including breathing difficulties caused by conditions such as asthma, as follows: if the student has a prescription for albuterol on file, a school nurse or designated trained school personnel may administer albuterol; or if the student does not have albuterol or a prescription for albuterol on file, only a school nurse may administer albuterol. Albuterol may be maintained, accessed, and administered on private school or school district property, including the school building, playground, and school bus, as well as during field trips or sanctioned excursions away from school property. The school nurse or designated trained school personnel may transport and carry a reasonable quantity of the school or school district supply of albuterol on field trips or excursions. School employees who are not licensed for nursing care and who have not agreed in writing to the use of albuterol as a specific part of their job description, may file a written letter of refusal to use albuterol. This letter may not serve as grounds for discharge, nonrenewal of an employment contract, or other action adversely affecting the employee's contract status. Student Asthma Policy. By January 1, 2027, the Superintendent of Public Instruction and Secretary of Health must update the student asthma policy to include a uniform procedure for when school nurses and designated trained school personnel access and administer the school or school district supply of albuterol. School districts may adopt policies regarding the use of albuterol from a school or school district supply. If a school district chooses to adopt a policy, it must include the uniform procedure. Liability protections are included for a licensed health professional prescribing albuterol and a pharmacist dispensing it; and a school nurse or other school employee or contractor administering albuterol in substantial compliance with a prescription and in accordance with policy. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY EARLY LEARNING & K-12 EDUCATION COMMITTEE (First Substitute): Removes the section directing the Secretary of Health to issue a statewide standing order prescribing albuterol for school supplies and removes corresponding references.
SB 5951.digest_source: WA Senate Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
SB 5951.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to expanding access to albuterol in public and private schools;
SB 5951.title: Albuterol access in schools

SB 5960.digest: WDFW shall designate an ungulate population as at-risk and initiate predator mitigation within 60 days if any population within the federal delisting area experiences a population reduction of 25 percent or more below its ten year rolling average. Ungulate populations include mule deer, white-tailed deer, elk, moose, mountain goat, mountain caribou, and bighorn sheep. If a population is designated at-risk, WDFW shall implement predator mitigation actions, including: seasonal or geographic predator reduction around sensitive ranges; translocation of gray wolves within Washington; and targeted removal or nonlethal mitigation. WDFW must also monitor ungulates to determine population increases over time. Mitigation actions must continue until mule deer and white-tailed deer populations meet or exceed 2004 harvest levels for two consecutive years and exceed their ten year rolling average. WDFW shall conduct and resume annual population counts of white-tailed deer in partnership with sportsmen. Survey methods shall be collaboratively designed and publicly transparent. A report of the population counts and the annual deer season harvest reports shall be published annually by March 31st or two weeks before the current seasons can be set. WDFW must report annually to the Legislature by March 31st ungulate population trends, at-risk designations, mitigation actions, and progress toward 2004 population benchmarks.

SB 5965.digest: Beginning in 2028, a retail establishment must collect a passthrough charge of $0.15 for reusable film plastic carryout bags. The passthrough charge for reausable film plastic carryout bags increases to $0.18 in 2028. Restaurants are not required to collect the passthrough charge for carryout bags provided for off-site consumption. A retail establishment that uses a third-party platform must list the applicable passthrough charges associated with each customer order. The requirement that reusable film plastic carryout bags increase to 4 mils in thickness beginning in 2028 is eliminated. Retail establishments are prohibited from collecting passthrough charges and the establishments customary fee for paper carryout bags for any customer using WIC, cash, or food assistance program benefits. Violations of the chapter are civil penalties of up to $250 for a retail establishment. Any carryout bag ordinance by a local government enacted as of April 1, 2020 is preempted by this chapter. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY WAYS & MEANS COMMITTEE (Second Substitute): Retains current law allowing the sale of reusable plastic film bags and specifying postconsumer recycling requirements. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY ENVIRONMENT, ENERGY & TECHNOLOGY COMMITTEE (First Substitute): Maintains the passthrough charge for paper carryout bags at $0.08. Specifies that carryout bags provided by restaurants for off-site consumption are exempt. Eliminates new civil penalties for manufacturers and distributors. SB 5966.digest: Medically tailored meals means a fresh or frozen meal that is designed by a qualified medical professional for the treatment of one or more medical conditions of a client. If DSHS or HCA contracts with entities to provide medically tailored meals to enrollees of medical assistance programs, the entities must be, to the extent possible, Washington State-based, nonprofit organizations. Medically tailored meal vendors are to comply with the enrollee's nutrition care plan and have a qualified medical professional review and approve the menus. All medically tailored meals provided to enrollees of medical assistance programs must: align with evidence-based nutritional practice guidelines for treating the specific condition; offer accommodations in dietary needs, allergy restrictions, and cultural preferences; prioritize local, whole foods or from scratch prepared meals unless otherwise required to appropriately meet the needs of the enrollee; provide at least 500 calories, or otherwise meet a client's or enrollee's medically appropriate energy needs; and provide one-third of the recommended dietary reference intakes for carbohydrates and protein as established by the Food and Nutrition Board of the National Academy of Medicine, unless otherwise permitted. A medically tailored meal vendor is a vendor that provides medically tailored meals according to specifications from a qualified medical professional. A qualified medical professional is a person who holds a credential issued by a disciplining authority regulated by the Department of Health and whose credential includes the authority to establish and tailor nutrition care plans to meet the medical needs of enrollees of medical assistance programs.

SB 5973.digest: Signature Gathering. It is unlawful to provide or receive money or other consideration for signature gathering based on the number of signatures obtained on an initiative or referendum petition. A person who has reason to believe that a person is providing or receiving money or other consideration for signature gathering based on the number of signatures may bring a citizen's action in the name of the state for an appropriate civil remedy, including civil penalties, against any initiative or referendum measure sponsor or signature-gather entity that violates the prohibition. If the person who brings the citizen's action prevails, the judgment awarded must go to the state, but the person must be entitled to recover reasonable attorneys' fees and costs from the defendant as fixed by the court. In the case of a citizen's action that is dismissed and that the court also finds was brought frivolously or in bad faith, the court may order the person bringing the action to pay all reasonable attorneys' fees incurred by the defendant. Civil penalties may not exceed $10,000 for each violation. The action for violation of the prohibition may be brought in the superior court of the county of residence or principal place of business of the initiative or referendum measure sponsor or signature-gathering entity or the superior court of the county in which a violation occurred. Any action must be commenced within two years after the date when the violation occurred. A signature-gathering entity is a person or entity that is employed, paid, or otherwise receives consideration or gratuity for the purpose of soliciting or procuring signatures of voters on an initiative or referendum petition. Minimum Signature Requirement. If any legal voter of the state, either individually or on behalf of an organization, desires to petition the Legislature to enact a proposed initiative measure, or submit a proposed initiative measure to the people, they must file with SOS a petition, bearing the signatures of at least 1000 legal voters in support of the proposed measure, including the legal voter's name and the address, city, and county at which they are registered to vote. SOS must, prior to submitting a copy of the proposed measure to the CRO, verify and canvass the signatures and names of the legal voters. SOS must by rule establish procedures to implement this signature requirement. SOS may use statistical sampling techniques to verify whether a petition contains the required number of signatures of legal voters. SOS may not accept for filing any proposed measure if the legal voter failed to submit a petition bearing the required signatures or if the petition clearly bears insufficient signatures. The signature sheets used to collect signatures must meet all formatting and content requirements, except for the inclusion of the title.

SB 5975.digest: The definition of covered cookware is modified to exclude the electrical components of electronic cooking devices. Beginning January 1, 2027, no manufacturer may sell, offer for sale, distribute for sale, or distribute for use aluminum or brass cookware, utensils, or cookware components that contain lead which was intentionally added. The 90 parts per million lead level limit is applicable to cookware manufactured on or after January 1, 2026. The 10 parts per million lead content standard is eliminated. Ecology must develop and make available guidance to manufacturers regarding covered items, testing methods, compliance, and enforcement. Safer Products . Cookware containing lead is added as a priority product under the Safer Products program beginning with the June 1, 2029 review cycle. Ecology must adopt a lead content standard that is either ten parts per million of the lowest lead limit that is feasible. In evaluating cookware as a priority product, to the extent feasible, Ecology must consider the entire lifecycle of the product, including when surfaces become damaged, scratched, or heavily used. Ecology may also consider the end-of-life management and recyclability of the product. Ecology may order cookware manufacturers to submit data on lead levels in their products. To the extent practicable, Ecology must make the data publicly available. Manufacturers that fail to comply may be subject to per product penalties.

SB 5976.digest: Narrowing the Application of the Commercial Electronic Mail Act. A sender must have a reliable basis, rather than reason, to know that an email is held by a Washington resident for the sender to be in violation of the Act. A commercial email's subject line must be likely to mislead a recipient, acting reasonably, about a fact material to the relevant transaction and be material to the recipient completing the transaction. A recipient of a commercial email in violation of the Act may only claim damages if they received, reviewed, and detrimentally relied upon the email, rather than just received the email. Repealing Specified Per Se Violations of the Consumer Protection Act. The following per se CPA violations are repealed: initiating or conspiring with another person to initiate the transmission of a commercial email that: uses a third party internet domain name without the third party's consent; misrepresents or obscures any information in identifying the point of origin or transmission path of the email; or contains false or misleading information in the subject line; and assisting in the transmission of a commercial email when the person knows, or consciously avoids knowing, that the initiator of the commercial email is engaged, or intends to engage, in any act or practice that violates the CPA. Lawsuits filed on or after the effective date are subject to the provisions, regardless of when the conduct occurred.
SB 5976.digest_source: WA Senate Bill Report (Orig.) (Summary of Bill)
SB 5976.last_action: First reading, referred to Business, Trade & Economic Development.

SB 5979.digest: In a dependency proceeding, if the petitioner is not seeking removal of the child from a parent, guardian, or custodian, the petition must contain a clear and specific statement as to the harm that will occur if the child or family does not receive court-ordered services, and the facts that support that conclusion. DCYF is to establish policies for the initiation of dependency proceedings, giving great weight to the presence of high-potency synthetic opioids; the lack of a parent, guardian, or custodian capable of adequately caring for a child, such that the child is in circumstances which constitute a danger of substantial damage to the child's psychological or physical development; and a parent's substance use as evidence of negligent treatment or maltreatment as defined in state law; and the amount or frequency of prior referrals within the preceding five years. Unless otherwise required by law, nothing is to preclude DCYF from initiating a dependency preceding where a child is dependent in state statute. DCYF must engage judicial officers, court administrators, child welfare professionals, and parents impacted by the child welfare system, to develop practice guidelines and training on the use of in-home dependencies as an option to provide ongoing services, support, and protective supervision in: situations where a child is not at risk of imminent physical harm, but the circumstances pose a danger of substantial damage to the child's psychological or physical development; situations where a child is abused or neglected by a person legally responsible for the care of the child; situations where substance use or mental health issues, by a person legally responsible for the child, may not otherwise fit the mandatory time limits of a child protective services investigation or family assessment response; and repeated or frequent prior referrals. DCYF is also to engage the same group of stakeholders to develop practice guidelines and training focused on removing children from in-home dependencies when the immediate danger to a child is not mitigated after a disposition of a dependency. SB 5982.digest: Amended Definitions. Under CETA, the definition of consumer-owned utility is expanded to include port districts (ports) engaged in the business of distributing electricity. A consumer-owned utility must have at least one, rather than more than one, retail electric customer in Washington. A consumer-owned utility does not include a PUD with only one customer, provided the customer remains the same as of January 1, 2026, and the PUD continues to receive 100 percent of its electricity from the Bonneville Power Administration. A market customer is redefined as a nonresidential consumer of electricity, rather than a customer of an electric utility, that purchases electricity from an entity that is not a utility subject to CETA; or generates electricity for its own consumption, its lessee’s consumption, or both. A consumer no longer has to generate enough electricity to meet 100 percent of its own needs to meet the definition of market customer. An affected market customer is also defined as an electricity consumer, rather than the customer of a utility. An affected market customer does not include a nonresidential customer that prior to May 7, 2019, generated electricity to meet less than 100 percent of its own needs continues to consume electricity with the same or greater percentage of CETA-compliance electricity, for the same end uses. It is clarified that, for electric utilities, retail electric load is the amount of megawatt hours of electricity delivered in a given calendar year to its customers. For an affected market customer, retail electric load is newly defined as the amount of megawatt-hours of electricity purchased from an entity that is not a utility subject to CETA, or self-generated for its own consumption. Reporting and Compliance for Affected Market Customers. The Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC) must adopt rules to establish reporting requirements for affected market customers to demonstrate compliance with CETA. Reporting requirements must be consistent with current law to the extent practicable. The UTC may waive these reporting requirements for affected market customers that: only procure power from nonemitting electric generation or renewable resources; or generate electricity using de minimis amounts of fossil fuels exclusively for emergency backup requirements. The UTC must, on its own motion or if requested, enforce affected market customers' compliance with CETA. Commerce must establish reporting requirements for ports, but it may waive reporting requirements that do not pertain to customers served by ports. For ports, the consumer-owed utility interim performance report is due July 1, 2030, rather than July 1, 2026.

SB 6008.digest: Flexible Demand Programs. Electric utilities with more than 100,000 electric customers must implement a flexible demand program by December 31, 2026. All other electric utilities may choose to implement a flexible demand program. A flexible demand program is defined as an electric utility program that encourages consumers to shift or modulate their electricity demand in ways that benefit the electric utility's electric system. This may include incentives, time of use rates, virtual power plants, and other mechanisms for signaling end use load and customer energy storage systems to respond to price signals. To be approved for a residential battery incentive program (incentive program), a flexible demand program must: provide an upfront battery incentive payment; a plan for incorporating residential battery energy storage systems and connected distributed energy resources into a flexible demand program and financially encourage customers to manage their electricity by responding to time of use rates or demand charge price signals to reduce costs to the electrical system, or provide the utility with the means to manage batteries collectively to benefit the grid; allow a user of a net metering system to fully participate in the program; not allow for battery energy storage system leases to customers unless they are utility-owned rent-to-own, or owned by a electric utility and leased at no cost to low-income or moderate-income customers; be designed to lower a customer's current total annual electric utility expenses; and reserve at least 40 percent of the program funding for low-income, moderate-income, or tribal households. Residential Battery Incentive Grant Program. Subject to the availability of amounts appropriated, a residential battery incentive grant program (grant program) is established to improve access to residential battery energy storage systems for low-income and moderate-income customers, and maximize system benefits for all retail electric customers. The Department of Commerce (Commerce) must award grants to electric utilities with qualified incentive programs. In a biennium, no more than 35 percent may go to a single utility and no more than 40 percent may be awarded to investor-owned utilities. If Commerce awards funds in multiple rounds, the funding caps do not apply in a final funding round. Commerce's application process for electric utilities establishing an incentive program must include: plans for how the utility's incentive program will encourage low-income participation; an example of customer application that requires one of several specified income verification processes at the time of enrollment; a statement on the types of utility rent-to-own or leased agreements for residential battery energy systems; expected monthly savings to participating customers' electrical bill expenses; descriptions for prioritizing customer applications to the flexible demand program and using customer feedback to design the incentive program; documentation of utility expenses and upgrades proposed as part of program implementation, which may not exceed 20 percent of total grant funds received by a utility during a biennium, and may include advanced metering infrastructure and subscription fees paid by the utility to operators of an electric utility-owned virtual power plant; and a notarized signed and sworn statement that customer data will not be sold or aggregated for any purposes beyond the direct operation of its flexible deman

SB 6009.digest: Administrative Procedure Act . A petition for direct review of a final agency decision by an environmental board that relates to a clean energy project must be certified by the superior court for transfer to the court of appeals upon a finding that the judicial review can occur based upon the agency record developed before the administrative body. The provisions for direct review of a final agency decision that was not by an environmental board that required the superior court to make certain findings for the decision to be eligible for direct review are repealed and the current provisions are retained that allow for direct review of an agency decision that does not relate to a clean energy project if the superior court finds: that transfer would serve the interest of justice; it would not cause substantial prejudice to any party; and that the judicial review can occur based upon the agency record developed before the administrative body. Land Use Petition Act . The provisions of the LUPA for transfer of judicial review of a land use decision to the court of appeals upon the superior court finding that all parties have consented to the transfer and agreed that the judicial review can occur based upon an existing record are retained and will not expire on July 1, 2026. A party's withholding of consent to transfer for direct appeal is inadmissible as evidence at trial. The withholding of consent may not be used against the party in any proceeding.

The Public Records Act . Records filed with, or maintained by, the Department of Labor and Industries (Department) are confidential and not open to public inspection if they reveal the identity of, or contain any personal information about, an employee or applicant who has filed a complaint, requested assistance, or participated in an investigation relating to workplace pregnancy accommodations. SB 6017.digest: Victim Witness Questioning. Upon the motion of a prosecuting attorney or the victim in any criminal proceeding involving sexual assault or domestic violence in which the defendant is proceeding pro se, the court may conduct, appoint standby counsel to conduct, or appoint an investigator to conduct the questioning of the victim witness on behalf of the defendant if certain conditions are met. The court must make particularized findings on the record articulating the the factors which the court based its decision. Nonfatal Strangulation. A minor age 13 years or older may consent to a forensic examination for the purpose of gathering evidence for possible prosecution for domestic violence assault involving nonfatal strangulation. Rights of Sexual Assault Survivors. The term sexual assault survivor is changed to sexual violence survivor. Victims of female genital mutilation are afforded the same statutory rights as sexual violence survivors. Sexual Assault Forensic Examination Best Practices Advisory Group. The SAFE Advisory Group is redesignated and reauthorized until July 1, 2028. The purpose of the SAFE Advisory Group is shifted to recommending actionable, trauma-informed, victim-centered policies related to preventing and addressing sexual violence. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY WAYS & MEANS COMMITTEE (Second Substitute): Allows the victim witness to move for the court to either conduct or appoint standby counsel to conduct all examination of the victim witness on behalf of the defendant. Adds a member representing children's advocacy centers to the SAFE Advisory Group.

SB 6019.digest: Home Care Agency Vendor Rate . The home care agency vendor rate is the sum of the portion of the vendor rate dedicated to the wages, benefits, and required employer contributions of premiums for home care agency workers who provide direct care and the home care agency administrative rate. For fiscal year 2027, the Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) shall determine, in its sole discretion, the portion of the total vendor rate dedicated to wages, benefits, and required employer contributions for home care agency workers who provide direct care. Beginning in fiscal year 2028, this portion of the rate is equal to the previous fiscal year plus the incremental changes calculated using the current process. The portion of the vendor rate calculated for training may only be used for training, testing, and certification costs, as well as costs associated with the administration of training, testing, and certification scheduling and compliance for home care agency workers who provide direct care. The board must review the projection from the DSHS of the portion of the vendor rate dedicated to the wages and benefits for home care agency workers who provide direct care and the required employer contributions or premiums. Verification of Expended Funds . Beginning July 1, 2027, the DSHS or its designee must verify that the home care agencies have expended funds in accordance with the wages and benefits, health care rate, and training rate requirements. Each home care agency must submit one of the following to assist the DSHS in this verification process: an independent third-party audit conducted by a qualified, accredited firm to validate compliance with requirements; or a written attestation from the labor organization that is the exclusive bargaining representative of the home care workers who provide direct care that are employed by the agency, confirming that the home care agency has complied with the wages and benefits, health care rate, and training rate requirements. Through a transparent process that includes public notice and public comment opportunities, the DSHS may adopt rules to establish reasonable objective criteria to temporarily exempt a home care agency determined to be facing extraordinary circumstances that prevent compliance. Consumer Directed Employer Labor Rate and the Rate-Setting Board . The consumer directed employer (CDE) labor rate must include a specific hourly amount that the CDE may only use for training, testing, and certification costs, and associated costs for the administration of training, testing, and certification scheduling and compliance for individual providers. When the board determines a proposed labor rate, it must include a specific amount for training benefits. If an agreement on a proposed CDE labor rate is not reached by a majority of the members on the board prior to August 1, then the labor rate must be determined by a majority of the voting members of the board, including a vote of the chair member. If an agreement over the labor rate is not reached prior to September 1, then the labor rate must be determined by the sole vote of the chair member. Administrative Rates and the Rate-Setting Board . The DSHS must determine a home care agency administrative rate. SB 6036.digest: DSHS may exempt certain former foster care providers from AFH licensure when certain conditions are met. Adult Family Home Licensing Exemption for Those with a Former Foster Care License. An individual is exempt from AFH licensure when the individual: has had an active license to operate a foster family home in Washington for at least three years; provided personal care services for the former foster care youth in the individual's care for at least three years on the date the youth exited foster care; does not have any founded or substantiated findings by child protective services or adult protective services; and is not the subject of a pending adverse licensing action at the time the youth in their care exits the foster care system, and the only unrelated adults the individual provides personal care to in the home are the former foster youth or youths that lived with the individual prior to exiting foster care. Adult Family Home Licensing Exemption for Those with a Former Child-Specific Foster Care License. An individual is exempt from AFH licensure when the individual: is or has previously been approved by DCYF for a child-specific license; does not have any founded or substantiated findings by child protective services or adult protective services; and is not the subject of a pending adverse licensing action at the time the youth in their care exits the foster care system, and the only unrelated adults the individual provides personal care to in the home are the former foster youth or youths for whom the individual received the child-specific license.

SB 6037.digest: The requirement that a city’s or town’s property tax levy must be reduced as a part of the formation of a district after July 1, 2026, is removed. Instead, a city or town creating a fire protection district must reduce its statutory maximum tax rate by the combined tax rate imposed by the newly formed fire protection district, with the exception of cities with a population over 500,000. For the city or town participating in a district formed after July 1, 2026, with the exception of cities over 500,000 in population as of 2025, the city's or town's property tax levy may not exceed $5.90 per $1000 of assessed valuation. Districts may impose up to a $0.25 per $1,000 of assessed value levy that is outside of the $5.90 per $1,000 limit in statute. Notice of the public hearing on a resolution adopted by the legislative authority of a city or town must be published on a city website or local newspaper, rather than a newspaper of general circulation, for three consecutive weeks. The legislative authority may provide additional notice of the hearing by mail or other manner deemed necessary by the authority to notify affected persons. Prior to adopting a resolution, the legislative authority of the city or town must include labor organizations representing employees who perform fire prevention, fire suppression, and emergency medical services within the city or town, to consult on development of the proposed financing plan, governance structure, and anticipated impacts on service delivery and employment conditions; and if the city or town is located within the boundaries of a public hospital district, the city or town must consult with the public hospital district on any impact of the financing plan on the public hospital district property tax levy. If a district formed by resolution is governed by a board of fire commissioners, the fire commissioners must be independently elected at the same election where the resolution to authorize the formation of the district is submitted to voters. A district may contract with the city or town within its boundaries for services including, but not limited to, administrative services like information technology, financial, and human resources functions. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY WAYS & MEANS COMMITTEE (Second Substitute): Requires a city or town, prior to adopting a resolution, to consult with labor organizations on the development of the proposed financing plan, governance structure, and anticipated impacts on service delivery and employment conditions. Requires a city or town located within the boundaries of a public hospital district, prior to adopting a resolution, to consult with the public hospital district on any impact of the financing plan on the public hospital district property tax levy. Makes a technical clarification. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY LOCAL GOVERNMENT COMMITTEE (First Substitute): Requires that a city or town participating in a district may not have the city’s or town’s property tax levy rate exceed applicable rates in statute. Specifies that a district may levy of up to $0.25 per $1,000 of assessed value that is outside of levy limits established in statute.

SB 6037.title: Fire protection districts

SB 6041.digest: The personality rights of every individual and personality is expanded to include the use of the individual's or personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in any medium in any manner. Personality rights in any medium in any manner as transferable, assignable, and licensable, in whole or in part, by contract or transfer. Voice is defined as a sound in a medium that is readily identifiable and attributable to a particular individual, regardless of whether the sound contains the actual voice or a simulation of the voice of the individual. The culpability for infringement of personality rights is a knowing standard. Infringement is expanded to included instances where any person, without express or implied written or oral consent of the owner of the right, knowingly publishes, performs, distributes, transmits, or otherwise makes available to the public a living or deceased individual's or personality's voice or likeness in any medium in any manner. The civil penalty for infringement of personality rights is increased to $3,000 and is an additional remedy in addition to a civil action to recover actual damages. The right to bring a civil action and recover actual damages against an infringer of personality rights is clarified to extend to the successors, heirs, or other transferee of the living or deceased individual or personality. Such persons may bring a civil action regardless of if the infringement did not result in any profits. Existing processes to obtain court injunctions to prevent infringing use are updated to include personality rights in any medium in any manner. Existing exceptions and exemptions to liability for the infringement of personality rights are updated to include personality rights in any medium in any manner.

SB 6042.digest: Safe school plans must include the creation and maintenance of school maps that are made available to local and state first responder agencies that provide emergency services to the mapped schools. This requirement is subject to the availability of amounts appropriated. The school maps must be made available to local and state first responder agencies in digital formats that: are interoperable with the software platforms in use by each local and state first responder agency, without requiring the agencies to purchase software, obtain licenses or subscriptions, or incur any cost to access, view, or use the maps; conform to and integrate with security software platforms in use by the mapped school; and permit printing, electronic distribution, and integration into interactive mobile and web-based platforms. School maps must reflect accurate floor plans oriented to true north and must include site-specific labeling of interior features, exterior access, elevation-related features, exterior structures and spaces, and safety and security features. The maps must have controls that prevent independent modification or updating without corresponding updates to the underlying data within the software platforms used by emergency services. All school mapping data must be collected, accessed, analyzed, aggregated, produced, transmitted, shared, used, modified, maintained, and stored within the United States. School mapping data are not subject to public disclosure and are specifically excluded under the Public Records Act.

SB 6049.digest: Exempt Employment Information . Survivor of Crimes . The PRA exemption pertaining to agency employees who are survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, sexual abuse, stalking, or harassment is expanded to exempt an agency employee's name or other personally identifying information from public disclosure if the employee provides a sworn statement to their employer attesting that they or their dependent is a survivor of a hate crime. Voluntarily Submitted Demographic Details and Survey Responses . For purposes of voluntarily submitted demographic details, circumstances when such data is not exempt under the PRA are expanded to include when the information is anonymized. A new exemption is added to the PRA to exempt from public disclosure individual survey responses voluntarily provided by a state employee, vendor, or contractor in response to a voluntary survey administered by or on behalf of a public agency for the purpose of engagement and improving state government. Survey information that is deidentified, anonymized, or aggregated is not exempt. Data is considered "aggregated" when data is combined from many individuals and reported in a summary form such that individual-level information is not disclosed. "Anonymized" data is processed so that an individual can no longer be identified directly or indirectly by any party, making reidentification effectively impossible. "Deidentified" data is data that has been stripped of personal identifiers or redacted so that it cannot reasonably be linked to a specific individual. Healthy Youth Survey . Records containing individual student responses to the Healthy Youth Survey are exempt from public inspection and copying under the PRA.

SB 6053.digest: The bill establishes labor protections for domestic workers. Definitions. The term domestic worker includes any employee or independent contractor working in a private residence for four or more hours in a month as a nanny, child care provider, home care worker, personal care provider, housekeeper or cleaner, cook, gardener, or household manager, subject to certain exceptions. The exceptions include: a person performing casual labor in or about a private residence, unless the work is performed in the course of the hiring entity's trade, business, or profession; a person performing babysitting on a irregular and uncertain basis that is incidental in nature and duration; a person performing pet sitting, dog walking, or house sitting who is not also performing other domestic service work; an individual provider, or any provider employed by a home care agency if the home care agency receives certain state funds; or a person in a family relationship with, or who is a family member of, the hiring entity. Hiring entity means any person, group, or entity that provides payment to a domestic worker for the domestic worker's work or services or acts directly or indirectly in the interest of an employer in relation to an employee.

SB 6061.digest: Declaring the Legislature's Intent. Among other things, the Legislature declares that a stable and predictable funding mechanism, developed and governed by the industry through a self-supported assessment, can generate substantial economic returns for the state and empower local businesses, destinations, and communities to compete on a level playing field with neighboring states and national leaders such as California, Oregon, and British Columbia. Defining Terms. Various terms are defined; for example, tourism business means businesses that derive a significant portion of revenue from tourism activity in Washington in the following sectors: lodging, travel services, attractions, recreation, beverage producers, full-service restaurant locations with revenues exceeding $5 million per year, and retailer locations with revenues exceeding $5 million per year. Authorizing a Tourism Assessment Program. The Legislature authorizes the WTMA to establish a tourism assessment program by rule, subject to ratification by the tourism businesses. The assessments shall be calculated as a percentage of gross revenue and collected annually. An unpaid assessment constitutes a debt to the state, subject to a penalty of up to 10 percent of the unpaid assessment, and may be recovered by civil action. When designing the program, the WTMA must give substantial weight to the recommendations made by the Tourism Self-Supported Assessment Advisory Group in its October 31, 2025, report to the Legislature, and the design developed by the Rate Payer Oversight Board. Creating a Rate Payer Oversight Board. The WTMA is required to appoint members of a Rate Payer Oversight Board (Oversight Board) consisting of at least ten members, with at least two representatives from each of the identified tourism businesses. For the initial Oversight Board, the Tourism Self-Supported Assessment Advisory Group, shall prepare a list of nominees for appointment, all of whom must be employees or officers of businesses subject to any proposed assessment. Initial terms of the Oversight Board shall be six months or until completion of the initial referendum. Subsequent appointments shall be made under the process designed by the Oversight Board and properly ratified. Describing the Duties of the Rate Payer Oversight Board. The ratepayer oversight board shall design the assessment program, which shall include the following components: sector-specific classifications; assessment methodology and the rates for each business sector; a referendum process for ratification; opt-out provisions, if applicable; revenue thresholds for businesses assessed in each sector, where applicable; program term length; and appointment process for the ratepayer oversight board following the initial appointments of the Oversight Board. The Oversight Board shall govern the activities of the tourism assessment program. Additional duties of the Oversight Board include: approving an annual budget and expenditure plan; providing an annual report to the WTMA and the Legislature; and monitoring program effectiveness and recommend adjustments. Describing the Ratification Process. The timing and process for ratifying the proposed assessment program is described, including how weighted votes are calculated. The Oversight Board shall conduct a referendum among affected businesses to ratify the proposed assessment program within three years of the passage of this legislation. SB 6062.digest: Juvenile Sentencing. A court is required to grant a suspended disposition alternative under Option B or Option C when a juvenile is eligible, unless the court makes an independent finding supported by a preponderance of the evidence, that commitment to the department is needed because remaining in the community and being placed on community supervision with a suspended disposition, would not adequately protect the community. This applies to all juveniles that have a standard range term of confinement over 30 days. Excluded offenses from consideration of a suspended disposition alternative include, murder in the first degree and second degree, homicide by abuse, manslaughter in the first and second degree, assault in the first degree, kidnapping in the first degree, rape in the first degree, assault of a child in the first and second degree, violent offenses with certain criminal history, sex offenses, hit and run resulting in death, and vehicular homicide. When making the finding on whether commitment to a JR facility is appropriate as described above, the court must consider certain factors, including: the severity of the offense or offenses; the juvenile's criminal history; whether programming, treatment, and education offered and provided in a JR facility is appropriate to meet the needs of the juvenile; whether the goals of rehabilitation and community safety can be met by assigning the juvenile to a less restrictive disposition that is available to the court; the juveniles age, developmental maturity, mental and emotional health, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and any disabilities or special needs impacting the safety or suitability of institutional commitment; and whether the juvenile and the community will benefit from use of this disposition alternative after considering any examinations ordered under this section and the victim's opinion regarding whether the juvenile should receive a suspended disposition under this section. The court is allowed to extend a suspended disposition for an additional one-year period for good cause. The court may also impose a determinate sentence of electronic monitoring if it is available in the jurisdiction, for up to the minimum of the juvenile's standard range. All conditions the juvenile must follow to maintain the suspended disposition must be in writing. Robbery in the first degree when committed at age 15 or under is reduced from A (103 to 129 weeks) to A- (30-40 weeks) on the grid. Robbery in the first degree committed at age 16 or 17 is moved from A++ (129 to 260 weeks) to A (103-129 weeks) and any attempt, conspiracy, bailjump, or solicitation is moved from A (103-129 weeks) to B+ (15-36 weeks). Robbery in the second degree is moved from B+ (15-36 weeks) to B (local sanctions) on the grid. Suspended Disposition Alternatives. Option B Suspended Disposition Alternative. Expands eligibility for juveniles to receive an Option B sentence for anyone adjudicated of robbery in the first degree or an attempt, conspiracy, or solicitation to commit robbery in the first degree, assault in the second degree, unlawful possession of a firearm, certain offenses involving a motor vehicle, certain felony offenses where there is any allegation that the juvenile was armed with a firearm during the commission of the offense, and those with a prior Option B disposition alternative in their juvenile history. SB 6065.digest: Interest-Free Interfund Loans. A school district that is in binding conditions or under enhanced financial oversight may take a temporary, interest-free interfund loan from its transportation vehicle fund, subject to the same conditions as temporary, interest-free loans authorized from its capital projects fund. Interfund Transfers. A school district that is in binding conditions or under enhanced financial oversight may petition OSPI for permission to transfer money from its transportation vehicle fund to another school fund. If a school district has taken a temporary interfund loan from its transportation vehicle fund, the petition may include a request to convert the temporary interfund loan to a permanent transfer with no requirement for repayment. OSPI may only approve the petition if the transfer is not detrimental to any function or project for which the transportation vehicle fund was established. OSPI rulemaking authority is modified to allow for such transfers to take place.

SB 6066.digest: Until January 1, 2029, the legislative body of a county, city, or town, or WSDOT may create a crash prevention zone (zone) within its jurisdiction on the portion of U.S. Highway 395 from milepost 23 to milepost 32 between Pasco and Mesa. Beginning January 1, 2029, the legislative body of a county, city, or town may create a zone within its jurisdiction by identifying public roads where the incidence of collisions resulting in serious injuries or fatalities is greater than expected for similar roads. WSDOT may create a zone within its jurisdiction by identifying public roads where the incidence of collisions resulting in serious injuries and fatalities is greater than expected for similar highways over the previous five-year period using adopted processes in the Highway Safety Manual as published by the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials. A county, city, or town, or WSDOT may consider and implement safety improvement approaches in designated zones. A county, with the approval of a city or town, may designate a zone that includes roadways that include public roads within the county and city or town. A county, city, or town may designate a zone that includes roadways managed by WSDOT with the approval of WSDOT. WSDOT may designate a zone on a state highway without the approval of a county, city, or town. A public hearing on the zone map must be held before the establishment of a zone. Once a zone has been designated, the jurisdiction that established the zone must conduct an engineering and traffic investigation of the public roads in the zone to identify safety improvements, including any adjustments to the speed limits. A county, city, or town may contract with WSDOT to conduct an engineering and traffic investigation of the public roads in the zone. The Washington State Patrol (WSP) and local law enforcement agencies must coordinate, within existing resources and to the extent practicable, increased enforcement of traffic laws within the zone in a manner intended to reduce collisions in the zone. WSDOT may use speed reduction methods, approaches, and technologies to reduce speeding within any zone it establishes. A city, town, or county may use automated traffic safety cameras to detect speed violations committed within a zone, subject to current requirements and conditions on the use of such cameras, with an authorized penalty amount of up to $290 for each infraction. For each zone created by a city, town, or county, a corresponding local account must be created and administered by the jurisdiction. Any revenue generated from the use of automated traffic safety cameras to detect speeding violations committed in a zone must first be used to cover the costs of camera administration, including the cost of processing infractions, with any remaining revenue to be deposited into the corresponding local account. The base penalty amount for unlawfully using a personal electronic device while driving is doubled if the infraction occurs within a zone. The total penalty amount, including statutory assessments, may not be waived, reduced, or suspended. Fifty percent of the penalty amount collected must be deposited into the highway safety fund for such infractions committed in a zone established by WSDOT, to be used only for the same zone purposes applicable to a local corresponding account. The zone must be dissolved once safety improvements have been implemented. Until January 1, 2029, a zone may also be dissolved

SB 6068.digest: The bill as referred to committee not considered. Summary of Bill (Proposed Substitute): Liability for Unpaid Wages and Benefits. An owner and a direct contractor that enter into a construction contract are jointly and severally liable for any unpaid wages, including fringe benefit contributions, compensation for missed meal and rest periods, reimbursements, penalties, and damages, owed to any unrepresented employee of the direct contractor and any unrepresented employee of a subcontractor at any tier for labor performed on a project within the scope of the construction contract. The unrepresented employee or an authorized third party representative may bring a civil action against an owner, a direct contractor, or a subcontractor to recover unpaid wages, including fringe benefit contributions, compensation for missed meal and rest periods, reimbursements, interest, penalties, double damages, noneconomic damages, attorney fees, expert witness fees, and costs incurred in connection with the action. Penalties and double damages are mandatory and must be awarded regardless of whether the failure to pay wages was willful. The civil action must be brought within three years from the date the unpaid wages, benefit contributions, compensation for missed meal and rest periods, reimbursements, penalties, and damages became due. Prior to commencing a civil action, a person must send written notice of the alleged violation by first-class certified mail to the owner and direct contractor that: sets forth the alleged violation and the nature of the claim; and states that the owner and the direct contractor have 21 calendar days from the certified delivery date to correct the alleged violation. A civil action may not be initiated until after the 21 days have expired and may not be brought if the owner or direct contractor corrects the violation within the 21 day time period. Any agreement to waive or release an owner or direct contractor from liability, or to indemnify an owner or direct contractor for liability under the bill is invalid. An owner or direct contractor may not avoid liability under this section by claiming that a person performing labor on a project within the scope of a construction contract is an independent contractor unless the person qualifies as an independent contractor under the Minimum Wage Act. There is a rebuttable presumption that any person performing labor on a project is an employee.

SB 6069.digest: Shelters, Transitional Housing, Emergency Housing, and Permanent Supportive Housing. Cities and counties—within urban growth areas—must allow STEP housing in certain zones as follows: transitional housing or permanent supportive housing in any zones in which residential dwelling units or hotels are allowed; and indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing in any zones in which hotels are allowed. A city or county may not require STEP housing to be located in a zone within an urban growth area zoned for industrial use. Nothing in the requirements under the act allows a county or city to limit indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing in a manner where the capacity of indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing is insufficient to meet the projected needs under their comprehensive plan. A county or city must allow indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing in additional types of zones when necessary to meet projected needs under their comprehensive plan. A city or county subject to this requirement may generally not require any standards, conditions, or requirements for STEP housing that are more restrictive than those required for other types of development in the zone. The city or county may apply any objective development regulations, including form-based codes, that are required for residential development such as setback, lot coverage, stormwater, and tree canopy and retention requirements. The city or county may only apply the same development permit and environmental review processes to STEP housing that apply to other types of lodging and residential development in the same zone, unless otherwise required by state law, such as shoreline regulations and building, energy, and electrical codes. If applying design review for STEP housing, only administrative design review may be required. Administrative design review for cities is defined as a development permit process in which an application is reviewed, approved, or denied by the planning director—or designee—based solely on objective design and development standards without a public pre-decision hearing, unless the review is otherwise required by state or federal law or the structure is a designated landmark or historic district established under a local preservation ordinance. Nothing in the act requires a city or county to approve a permit application for STEP housing that is proposed in a critical area in which no residential development is permitted, an area of natural hazards that generally prohibit residential development, or on agricultural, forest, or mineral lands of long-term commercial significance. Certification Requirements. For an indoor emergency shelter or indoor emergency housing, a city or county may require the sponsor or managing agency to certify in writing that it has, between the date the permit application was approved and the date the certificate of occupancy was issued: notified residents within 500 feet of the indoor emergency shelter or indoor emergency housing; conducted no more than one community meeting; designated at least one point of contact and provide at least one telephone number to be used in emergencies; and provided documentation of the sponsor's or managing agency's operational policies or procedures for health, fire, safety, and occupancy. A city or county may not require the sponsor or managing agency to provide additional certifications outside of what is allowed under the act. Permitting Requ

SB 6070.digest: Pen Registers, Trap and Trace Devices, and Cell Site Simulator Devices . The circumstances where a law enforcement officer may be authorized by court order to install and use a pen register, trap and trace device, or cell site simulator device are expanded to include when the device is necessary to fulfill community caretaking functions, subject to certain conditions. The court must authorize the installation and use of the device if the court finds that the information likely to be obtained is necessary for law enforcement to fulfill community caretaking functions and there is probable cause to believe that the device may aid in locating a missing endangered person. The court may consider the following nonexaustive list of factors when determining whether there is probable cause for a law enforcement officer to perform community caretaking functions to help locate a missing endangered person: the person has a recent history of suicidal ideation; the person has an apparent lack of access to prescribed medications; the person left behind personal items that one would expect the person to take if the disappearance was voluntary; the disappearance involves an unusual and unexplained absence from work, school, or other regularly scheduled activity; the person is a minor who lacks the skills for long-term self-care and safety; there is evidence to suggest the person is suffering a significant mental health crisis leaving them unable to manage the person's care and safety; the person was the primary caregiver for another person or animal and made no effort to arrange for a continuation of care; the location and conditions in the area where the person is suspected to be located, combined with their available resources, are not consistent with long-term survival; the person has a developmental disability; the person is a vulnerable adult; the person is a minor for whom law enforcement can identify multiple risk factors that are indicative that the minor is a current victim of human trafficking or commercial sexual exploitation; or the person is believed to have Alzheimer's disease or other age-related dementia that inhibits the person's ability to manage the person's care and safety. The existing gross misdemeanor for a law enforcement officer's knowing and unauthorized installation or use of a pen register, trap and trace device, or cell site simulator device is limited to circumstances where the device was installed or used in an ongoing criminal investigation. A law enforcement agency must take all steps necessary to permanently delete any information or metadata collected from the unauthorized use of a cell site simulator device, and may not transmit, use, or retain such information or metadata for any purpose whatsoever, if: the agency has not obtained a court order approving the use of the device within 48 hours; or the application for the court order is denied. Search Warrants . The statutory provision authorizing magistrates to issue search warrants is expanded. Any magistrate with power to issue a warrant for the arrest of a person charged with a crime may, when satisfied that there is probable cause and upon application supported by oath or affirmation, issue a search warrant to search for and seize any evidence that may aid in locating a missing endangered person. SB 6081.digest: Department of Licensing Records . The DOL is prohibited from displaying, transmitting, or otherwise making available any record or supporting documentation of a person's sex designation change unless the person provides consent for a specific purpose. Credentials and digital records issued after a change to a person's sex designation may not include any indicator that the person's sex designation has been changed, including credentials and digital records transmitted for purposes of voter registration and to WaTech in the DOL's annual transmission of its electronic data file on all drivers and identicard holders. Public Records Act Exemption. Exemptions under the PRA relating to driver's license and permit records are expanded to include any record or information used to prove sex designation when applying for, renewing, or making changes to a driver's license, instruction permit, or identicard. Further, any record pertaining to a confidential vehicle license plate, driver's license, or identicard that, alone or in combination with any other records, may reveal the sex designation of an individual performing an undercover or covert law enforcement, confidential public health work, public assistance fraud, or child support investigative activity, is exempt from disclosure under the PRA. Disclosure of Records to Another Jurisdiction . Records and supporting documents contained in a person's Washington driver's record that include the person's sex designation change may not be shared with another jurisdiction that requests the driver's record unless the person gives consent for a specific purpose. Vital Records . Personal information collected from individuals who have requested a change to their sex designation in a vital record is exempt from disclosure under the PRA. Supporting documentation related to sex designation changes must be sealed by the state registrar and may not be disclosed, and any supporting documentation transferred to the State Archives related to sex designation changes may not be made publicly available. The reasons for which the DOH may deny a request for vital statistics data or records are expanded to include a determination by the DOH that there is a reasonable possibility of the data being used to cause or enable harm or disenfranchisement; that its use could reasonably result in disparate impact on the data subject; or that otherwise fulfilling the request would not be in the public interest. The DOH is prohibited from releasing a certification of birth to any government agency or court for the same reasons. Except for certifications and informational copies of vital records, all vital records, reports, supporting documentation, vital statistics, data, and information contained in these records that are maintained by the DOH are confidential and not subject to state or federal discovery, subpoenas, or other compulsory process.
