SB 6094.digest: State Plan Amendment. The Health Care Authority (HCA), using existing resources, must develop and submit a state plan amendment by July 1, 2027, to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to allow for facility-based payments to residential pediatric recovery center as provided in SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Act. HCA, using existing resources, must submit a status report by January 1, 2027 to the appropriate policy and fiscal committees of the Legislature detailing the feasibility of an approval for the state plan amendment. Until the submitted state plan amendment's approval and subject to amounts appropriated, HCA must provide grant funds to the specific facility that was subject of the pilot project created by the Legislature to ensure availability of services to infants with a history of substance exposure. The Legislature's intent is to appropriate funds from the Opioid Abatement Settlement account for this purpose. Non-Medical Bundled Payment Model. The Department of Children, Youth, and Families (DCYF), in coordination with HCA, must develop and implement a bundled funding model, which is subject to appropriation, for nonmedical maternal and child health programmatic services provided by residential pediatric recovery centers to infants born substance exposed and their families. DOH must identify allowable service components, which may include, but are not limited to: caregiver coaching, education, and skill building related to infant care, feeding, soothing, safe sleep, and developmental support; dyadic services that promote bonding, attachment, and caregiver-infant interaction; family support services, including peer navigation, case management, and coordination with child welfare and community-based providers; respite, overnight accommodations, and on-site supports for caregivers while the infant is receiving services at a residential pediatric recovery center; and discharge and transition planning, including linkage to early intervention, home visiting, substance use disorder treatment, primary care, and community supports. "Residential pediatric recovery center" means a health care facility licensed or certified by DOH to provide pediatric transitional care services that is able to provide medically necessary recovery services to infants affected by neonatal abstinence syndrome, neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, or prenatal substance exposure, as well as nonmedical treatment and wraparound support services for infants born substance exposed and their families. Pediatric Transitional Care Services. "Pediatric transitional care services" means any medical and nonmedical treatment and wraparound support services for substance-exposed infants and one or more parents of the infant according to the requirements of this chapter and provided in an establishment licensed by DOH. An establishment providing pediatric transitional care services to substance-exposed infants and their parents must demonstrate that it is capable of providing services for infants who: have been exposed to substances before birth; have been determined by the clinical director or medical director of the establishment to respond favorably developmentally to specialized care to assist bonding and attachment from 24-hour continuous residential care treatment services including nursing and infant care services as a result of prenatal substance exposure; and are referred to the establishment by DCYF, regional hospitals, and private parties. SB 6096.digest: Cities and towns collecting water or sewer connection charges must, by 2030, adopt and maintain a system for the deferred collection of connection charges for single-family detached, single-family attached, and multifamily—qualifying—residential construction. The deferral system must include a process by which an applicant for a building permit for a qualifying residence may request a deferral of the full payment of connection charges. The deferral system offered by a city or town must include one or more of the following options: deferring collection of the connection charges payments until final inspection; or deferring collection of the connection charges payments until certificate of occupancy or equivalent certification. Cities and towns utilizing the deferral process must withhold certification of final inspection, certificate of occupancy, or equivalent certification until the connection charges have been paid in full. For the purposes of the bill, connection charges are defined as the one-time capital and administrative charges that are imposed by a utility for physical connection to existing infrastructure for a single-family detached, single-family attached, or multifamily residence. The deferral system requirements under the act do not apply to cities and towns that have implemented a system for the deferred collection of connection charges as of the effective date of the act. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY HOUSING COMMITTEE (First Substitute): Specifies that a deferral option must be for the collection of the connection charge, as opposed to deferral of the impact fee payment. Modifies the definition of connection charge to mean the one-time capital and administrative charges imposed by a utility for physical connection to existing infrastructure, rather than for a new utility service and costs borne or assessed by a utility for the labor, materials, and services necessary to physically connect a designated residence to the respective utility service. Limits the deferral system requirements under the act to cities and towns that have not implemented such a system by the effective date of the act.

SB 6102.digest: Beginning July 1, 2026, the annual QAF rate will be the rate in effect as of July 4, 2025. Until June 30, 2026, the QAF rate shall be calculated by a ratio—the product of the projected aggregate fee schedule amount and the State Medical Assistance Percentage divided by 90 percent of the projected total annual emergency ambulance transports by all ambulance transport providers. The annual QAF rate is calculated as a percentage of annual gross revenue for participating ambulance transport providers. HCA must annually calculate the add-on rate and the add-on rate must be adjusted annually to reflect the available fee amount. The fee-for-service add-on shall be equal to the quotient of the available fee amount projected by the authority for the previous fiscal year divided by the total Medicaid emergency ambulance transports that HCA projected for the previous fiscal year. If, during a state fiscal year until June 30, 2026, the actual or projected available fee amount exceeds or is less than the actual or projected aggregate fee schedule amount by more than 1 percent, HCA must adjust the annual QAF rate so that the state fiscal year's available fee amount is approximately equal to the state fiscal year's aggregate fee schedule. If, during a state fiscal year after July 1, 2026, the actual or projected available fee amount exceeds or is less than the actual or projected aggregate fee schedule amount by more than 1 percent, HCA must adjust the QAF add-on rate so the state fiscal year's available fee amount is approximately equal to the state fiscal year's aggregate fee schedule amount. If the difference between the state fiscal year's available fee amount and the state fiscal year's aggregate fee schedule amount constitutes less than 1 percent of the state fiscal year's aggregate fee schedule amount, the available fee amount is considered equal to the aggregate fee schedule amount.

SB 6118.digest: Beginning in the 2026-27 school year each school district must develop a cardiac emergency response plan (plan) for every school within the district and every athletic facility on a school campus, to the extent state funding is appropriated for the purpose. Each plan must be updated annually and include the following core elements. Cardiac Emergency Response Team. The plan must designate a cardiac emergency response team (response team) comprised of school staff, including coaches, school nurses, athletic trainers, teachers, counselors, and administrators. The plan must establish procedures for activating the response team if a person experiences a cardiac arrest on school property, and establish a regular schedule for response team training in cardiopulmonary resuscitation, first aid, and AED use. The plan must also establish dates, at least annually, where the plan will be rehearsed in each school. Automated External Defibrillator Locations and Maintenance. The plan must designate locations for the installation of AEDs throughout campus, including at each campus athletic facility, with the goal of being able to place an AED on a person within three minutes of becoming aware of a cardiac arrest. AED locations must be identified with clear signage and stored in an unlocked location on school property that is easily accessible during the school day and during school-sponsored athletic events or team practices in which students of the school are participating. The plan must include the regular maintenance schedule for AEDs, aligned with the manufacturer's operational guidelines. School officials must notify local emergency service providers of AED locations and types. Emergency Response and Procedures. The school district must work to integrate the plan into the community emergency response protocols, and the plan must describe how this coordination and integration will be achieved. The plan must also establish procedures for responding to incidents of cardiac arrest that occur off-campus during school-sponsored events. Each plan's core elements, the school staff training, and the locations for AEDs must all follow guidelines set by the American Heart Association or another evidence-based organization focused on emergency cardiovascular care. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY EARLY LEARNING & K-12 EDUCATION COMMITTEE (First Substitute): Provides that school districts must develop cardiac emergency response plans and fulfill all other related bill provisions only to the extent state funding is appropriated for that purpose.

SB 6129.digest: Taxation of Nicotine Products. Beginning January 1, 2027, the various OTP tax rates and the vapor products tax are each repealed and replaced with a single tax rate of 95 percent of the taxable selling price for all nicotine products. "Nicotine product" means any product that contains nicotine or a nicotine analogue, whether derived from tobacco or created synthetically, and is intended for human consumption or placement in the oral or nasal cavity or absorption into the human body by any other means. The term does not include cigarettes or therapeutic nicotine cessation products approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration. "Nicotine analogue" means a substance that has a chemical structure substantially similar to the chemical structure of nicotine or which has, or is represented to have, an effect on the central nervous system that is similar to or greater than the effect on the central nervous system of nicotine. Vapor Product Tax Revenue Distributions. Revenue from the tax on vapor products must be deposited as follows: 50 percent to the match transfer account and 50 percent into the FPHS account until distributions to the match transfer account reach $10 million each fiscal year; any additional revenue collected from the tax on vapor products must be deposited to the FPHS account until the total amount of distributions to the account reach $20 million each fiscal year; and the remainder of revenue collected from the tax on vapor products each fiscal year must be deposited into the state general fund. Beginning January 1, 2029, DOR must annually adjust for inflation distribution amounts to the match transfer account and the FPHS account using the consumer price index for the Seattle area as calculated by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics or its successor agency. The inflationary adjustment may not result in a distribution amount that is less than the distribution amount for the prior year. Preexisting Inventories. The nicotine products tax established in the bill does not apply to any nicotine product for which the OTP tax was paid by the distributor prior to July 1, 2027. Cigarette Tax. Beginning January 1, 2028, an additional tax is imposed on the sale, use, consumption, handling, possession, or distribution of cigarettes at a rate of $0.09875 per cigarette. The additional tax on cigarettes results in a total tax rate of $5 per package of 20 cigarettes. Beginning January 1, 2032, the additional tax on cigarettes must be adjusted for inflation once every four years using the consumer price index for the Seattle area as calculated by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics or its successor agency. DOR may not adjust the tax rate if the adjustment would result in a tax rate that is lower than the applicable tax rate for the prior year. All revenue from the additional taxes on cigarettes must be deposited to the state general fund. Tribal Compacting. The Governor may seek government-to-government consultations with federally recognized Indian tribes to renegotiate cigarette and vapor product tax compacts to include the taxation of flavored nicotine products and flavored cigarettes. Any tribal tax imposed on flavored nicotine products or flavored cigarettes must be equal to the state rate imposed on such products. The Governor may delegate the authority to renegotiate cigarette and vapor product tax contracts with federally recognized Indian tribes to DOR. Section 301, Chapter 422, Laws of 2025. The OTP t

SB 6130.digest: National Voter Registration Day. Each public high school must observe National Voter Registration Day on or about the third Tuesday of September each year. On this date, or within a two-week period before or after that date, as resources allow, public high schools must coordinate a voter registration event in history or social studies classes. During these events, as part of the future voter program, teachers must make voter sign up and registration available to all students 16 years of age and older. The event must include adequate time for students to complete the registration process in class and paper registration forms must be provided to students who cannot use the online registration. The Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI), in consultation with the Secretary of State, must annually update and distribute youth voter registration materials for eligible students to register to vote at school and notify high school principals and social studies teachers of these materials' availability. OSPI and the Secretary of State must collaborate to provide registration methods that enable the electronic collection of information on the number of students who registered to vote on National Voter Registration Day. Each year, OSPI must report on the goal of achieving at least 50,000 annual new voter registrations of high school students. As resources allow, county auditors may participate in National Voter Registration Day events. Temperance and Good Citizenship Day. Each year on Temperance and Good Citizenship Day, public high schools must, as resources allow, coordinate a voter registration event in alignment with the requirements of National Voter Registration Day. The primary focus of these events must be to support eligible students who missed the opportunity to become future voters or registered voters on National Voter Registration Day earlier in the school year. SB 6131.digest: The bill as referred to committee not considered. Summary of Bill (First Substitute): The Commission is designated as a public health authority, as defined under the federal HIPPA Privacy Rule, to promote and protect public health and safety and to identify contributing factors that most commonly lead to motor vehicle collisions resulting in death or serious injury. The Commission is tasked with: conferring with federally recognized tribes deemed eligible under the federal Highway Safety Act; receiving crash reports, toxicology reports, and related investigation information from state and local law enforcement agencies; receiving driver licensing records from DOL for motor vehicle collisions resulting in a fatality; reviewing traffic crashes resulting in the death of a pedestrian, bicyclist, or other active transportation users, and including members of the Council in these reviews if attendance is less than a quorum of the Council membership; and presenting reports of such traffic crash reviews to the Council. The Commission may, as a public health authority, collect certain health care information, which is exempt from public inspection and copying. Such health care information must also only be used for Commission purposes, including for anonymized fatal or serious injury collision reports and for providing such reports and underlying data to the University of Washington's Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation. The Commission may compile and link data, store information in a secure database, and perform statistical and epidemiological analyses to identify causes and trends in traffic fatalities.

SB 6147.digest: Notice Requirements. Certain grocery establishments located in geographic areas designated as food deserts using United States Department of Agriculture criteria, or in certain low-income census tracts, must provide written notice at least four months before closing to the city council, county council or commission, local health department, state legislators representing the location of the grocery establishment, and Office of the Attorney General (AG). The grocery establishment must also provide notice of its intention to close to its customers and the public by posting prominent written notices at all public entries and exits to the grocery establishment. Good Faith Engagement. During the closure notice period, the grocery establishment must, upon reasonable request, meet and work in good faith with the local city council, county council or commission, health department, state legislators, collective bargaining organization if applicable, and AG to find alternative outcomes allowing for continued availability of grocery establishment products and services at the closure location. This requirement may be satisfied by attending at least one community meeting convened by a neighborhood association or neighborhood organization representing the interests of neighborhood residents and one meeting with a collective bargaining organization, if applicable. Alternative outcomes may include identifying strategies or resources to allow the grocery establishment to remain open, assisting residents in organizing a cooperative, or identifying another grocery establishment capable of continuing similar products and services at or near the closure location. Reduced Notice. A grocery establishment may close for business having provided less than four months’ notice if the closure is due to a natural emergency or disaster or if, as of the time notice would have been required, the grocery establishment was actively seeking capital or business which, if obtained, would have enabled the grocery establishment to avoid or postpone the closure and the grocery establishment reasonably and in good faith believed that giving the required notice would have precluded obtaining the needed capital or business. A grocery establishment relying on reduced notice must give as much notice as practicable and, at the time notice is given, must articulate in writing the basis for having reduced the notice period. Enforcement. The AG may institute civil proceedings for injunctive and monetary relief, including civil penalties, for violations of the closure notice requirements and meeting obligations. A collective bargaining organization representing impacted employees, or the city attorney or county prosecuting attorney for the jurisdiction where the grocery establishment is located, may bring a civil action to enforce compliance and may seek injunctive or declaratory relief and a writ of mandamus. In an action brought by these parties, the court may award reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs to a prevailing plaintiff. Negative Use Restrictions. A negative use restriction that would prohibit a grocery establishment from operating at a location where such a use would otherwise be allowed is void and unenforceable. SB 6159.digest: The bill as referred to committee not considered. Summary of Bill (Proposed Substitute): Public Hospital Districts. Public hospital districts that are not affiliated with a nonpublic entity may enter into cooperative agreements and contracts with other public hospital districts and publicly owned or operated health care entities to provide for the health care needs of the people serviced by the hospital districts. Any authorized public hospital district or publicly owned or operated health care entity are defined as participants for the purposes of WHCFA. Annual Coverage Assessment. An annual coverage assessment (assessment) will be assessed on insurers and other businesses subject to the insurance premium tax with initial assessments due and payable on or before March 1, 2027. The assessment equals $0.75 per coverage month in the prior calendar year. Funds collected shall be deposited into the Public Hospital Infrastructure Account (account.) Each insurer or taxpayer subject to the insurance commissioner on or before March 1st of each year, an annual coverage month assessment statement indicating the number of coverage months associated with premiums or prepayments for health care services subject to the insurance premium tax. "Coverage month" means each month of coverage under an insurance policy or each month of prepayment for health care services where premiums or prepayments are subject to the insurance premium tax. This assessment must be borne solely by the insurer or taxpayer and may not be passed through to enrollees in premiums, rates, plan design, or otherwise. Any insurer or taxpayer failing to file its annual coverage month assessment statement and pay the assessment: by March 31st, the insurer or taxpayer must be assessed a penalty of 5 percent of the assessment amount; within 45 days after the due date, the insurer or taxpayer must be assessed a total penalty of 10 percent of the assessment amount; and within 60 days of the due date, the insurer or taxpayer must be assessed a total penalty of 20 percent of the assessment amount. Interest accrues on the amount of the unpaid assessment at the maximum legal rate of interested permitted by state law commencing 61 days after the assessment is due until the assessment is paid. The assessment may be collected by distraint, and the penalty recovered by any action instituted by the insurance commissioner in any court of competent jurisdiction. The amount of any penalty collected must be paid to the state treasurer and credited to the Public Hospital Infrastructure Account. The insurance commissioner may revoke the certificate of authority or registration of any delinquent insurer or taxpayer, and the certificate of authority or registration will not be reissued, until all assessments, interest, and penalties imposed have been fully paid and the insurer or taxpayer has otherwise qualified for the certificate of authority or registration. In the event that any insurer or taxpayer has paid to the insurance commission any annual coverage assessment in error or in excess of that which it is lawfully obligated to pay, the insurance commissioner must, upon written request, make a refund thereof. An insurer or taxpayer may only request a refund of assessments within six years of the end of the calendar year for which the assessments are owed. SB 6162.digest: Retired Persons Property Tax Relief Program. Property owners qualifying under the Program are exempt from 100 percent of part 1 of the state levy. Therefore, property owners are exempt from the state property tax in its entirety. The qualifying income threshold percentages under the Program are increased by 10 percentage points. The qualifying income threshold percentage for the Deferral Program is increased by 15 percentage points. The amount of assessed value used in determining the amount of regular property tax relief under income thresholds 1 and 2 are increased as follows: applicants qualifying under income threshold 1 receive an exemption from regular levies on the greater of $80,000 or 80 percent of the assessed valuation; and applicants qualifying under income threshold 2 receive an exemption from regular levies on the greater of $70,000 or 45 percent of assessed valuation with a $200,000 maximum. A standard deduction option is provided for determining combined disposable income equal to $7,500 for individuals and an additional $7,500 for spouses and domestic partners. Combat-related special compensation is excluded from the determination of disposable income. Up to $6,000 in rental payments may be deducted in the calculation of combined disposable income if the payments are derived from renting a living space in the person's principal place of residence. State Property Tax Rate. Parts 1 and 2 of the state levy are consolidated into a single, integrated state property tax. For calendar year 2026, the rate is initially set at $2.075355. Property Tax Statements. Tax statements must identify the state property tax as the state school levy. Tax Preferences. The changes to the Program do not expire and are not subject to review by JLARC.

SB 6174.digest: The bill as referred to committee not considered. Summary of Bill (Proposed Substitute): Textile and Apparel Coordinating Organization. By January 31, 2027, producers of textiles and apparel (covered textile products) must join a textile and apparel coordinating organization (TACO) that registers on behalf of the producers with Ecology, or must register independently with Ecology. If applications for more than one TACO are submitted to Ecology, Ecology must determine and register the proposed TACO that can most effectively implement the requirements of a TACO. For each covered textile product, a single specified person, either the product's manufacturer, brand licensee, brand owner, importer, distributor of the material in Washington, or another person assigned contractual responsibility as a producer is defined as the producer responsible for participation in a TACO. Producers do not include sellers of only secondhand products or sellers with less than $1 million, in annual aggregate global turnover, as adjusted for inflation and measured following a specified process. By March 15, 2027, Ecology must approve a TACO that meets enumerated requirements, including having a governing board of specified composition, and financial responsibility and financial controls. By June 1, 2027, each producer must be a member of a registered TACO. By June 15, 2027, each TACO must provide Ecology a list of brands of covered textile products of each member producer. Needs Assessment. The TACO must prepare and cover the costs of a needs assessment for covered textile products, in consultation with Ecology. The needs assessment must be designed to determine the necessary steps and investment for successful implementation of a future EPR program for covered textile products, and be based on specified assumptions, including: assumptions about the covered textile product collection system convenience standards; assumptions about the processes for the transport of collected covered textile products; and assumptions about the post-collection management standards an EPR program would be required to meet.

SB 6182.digest: Assessment on Health Carriers . Each health carrier offering health plans on the Health Benefit Exchange is subject to an annual coverage assessment which is initially due and payable on or before March 1, 2027. This does not include carriers offering dental only or vision only plans. The assessment is set at 82 cents per coverage month in the prior calendar year for the first year of the assessment, and annually thereafter, 16.5 cents per coverage month in the prior calendar year. Coverage month means each month of coverage under an insurance policy or each month of prepayment for health care services where premiums or prepayments are subject to the premium tax, not including coverage for Medicaid services rendered by licensed providers on a prepaid capitated basis that meets the federal requirements for Medicaid managed care organizations. Each health carrier must file an annual coverage month assessment statement with the OIC indicating the number of coverage months associated with premiums or prepayments for health care services subject to the premium tax. Any health carrier that fails to file their annual coverage month assessment statement or pay the assessment: by March 31st, will be assessed a total penalty of 5 percent of the assessment amount; within 45 days after the due date, will be assessed a total penalty of 10 percent of the assessment amount; and within 60 days of the due date, will be assessed a total penalty of 20 percent of the assessment amount. The assessment must be borne solely by the health carrier and may not be passed through to enrollees in premiums, rates, plan design, or otherwise, unless the OIC determines that to do so would create a significant risk of carrier insolvency or consumer harm. Interest accrues on the amount of the unpaid assessment at the maximum legal rate of interest permitted by the state beginning 61 days after the assessment is due until paid. The OIC may revoke the certificate of authority or registration of any delinquent health carrier, and the certificate of authority or registration may not be reissued until all assessments, interest, and penalties imposed under this section have been fully paid and the health carrier has otherwise qualified for the certificate of authority or registration. If any health carrier pays the OIC any assessment in error or more than what it is lawfully obligated to pay, the OIC shall upon written request make a refund thereof. A health carrier may only request a refund of assessments within six years of the end of the calendar year for which the assessments are owed. Refunds may be made either by crediting the amount toward payment of taxes, assessments, or other charges due or to become due from such health carrier, or by making a cash refund. If the waiver is granted, DSHS is to prohibit the purchase of candy and sweetened beverages with SNAP benefits. If a waiver is not granted, then DSHS is to request a waiver annually until a waiver is granted. Unhealthy foods include candy and sweetened beverages. Candy means a preparation of sugar, honey, or other natural or artificial sweeteners in combination with chocolate, fruits, nuts, or other ingredients, or flavorings in the form of bars, drops, or pieces. Candy does not include any preparation containing flour and does not require refrigeration. Sweetened beverages means any nonalcoholic beverages that contains natural and artificial sweeteners. Sweetened beverage does not include any beverages: that contain milk or milk substitutes; that are greater 50 percent vegetable or fruit juice by volume; that require preparation before consumption, such as powders or concentrates; commonly referred to as infant or baby formula; marketed primarily as sports drinks for hydration; or suitable for human consumption and manufactured as a source of necessary nutrition due to a medical condition or for use as an oral rehydration electrolyte solution for infants and children formulated to prevent or treat dehydration due to illness.

SB 6192.digest: Star Teacher Award. Each ESD must select six high-performing teachers each year to receive an ongoing annual Star Teacher bonus, subject to appropriations. Three of these Star Teachers must be mathematics teachers and three must be English language arts teachers. At least one awardee in each subject area must be selected based on improvement in kindergarten to sixth grade scores and one must be selected based on improvement in seventh to twelfth grade student scores over the previous two years. When assessing student improvement, the ESD must account for the difficulty level of the courses taught. The third awardee in each subject area must be selected at the ESD’s discretion, incorporating consideration of the teacher’s engagement with students, knowledge of teaching materials, ability to implement best practices for teaching, and student outcomes. Beginning in the year in which a teacher is selected as a star teacher, the star teacher will receive a $10,000 bonus for each year that he or she is a full-time educator teaching in his or her awarded subject area. This bonus is increased to $20,000 if the star teacher teaches in a school that meets the definition of high poverty school established by OSPI or in a school where at least 70 percent of the student body qualifies for the free and reduced-price lunch program. Structured Literacy Programs. School districts, charter schools, and state-tribal education compact schools must implement a structured literacy program that uses evidence-based instructional practices to promote the literacy of students in kindergarten through twelfth grade, beginning no later than the 2028-29 school year. A structured literacy program must: include at least semantics or comprehending written language, reading and writing fluency, orthographic knowledge or phonics, phonology and phonemic awareness, and vocabulary or oral language knowledge and proficiency; be systemic, sequential, and cumulative; provide direct, explicit, and rigorous instruction that is high quality and knowledge rich; be diagnostic of and responsive to individual student needs, including by being multisensory and multimodal; provide instruction and services, including dyslexia interventions, within a multitiered system of supports; use screening assessments and other tools to identify at-risk readers in kindergarten through twelfth grade, including dyslexia screenings for students in kindergarten through second grade; implement intensive reading improvement strategies for third-graders reading below grade level; use research-based family involvement and engagement strategies to help families and guardians assist in improving students’ reading and early literacy skills at home; and offer the parents of a student who performs below grade level on any reading assessments a reading improvement strategy. SB 6195.digest: Revenue Thresholds and Tier Conversions. At the time of license renewal, a tier three producer must demonstrate minimum gross sales reported to the Department of Revenue of $24,000 per month or $288,000 annually throughout the two-year period prior to renewal. If a tier three producer fails to meet this revenue threshold throughout the two-year period prior to renewal, the license is converted to a tier two producer license and the producer’s maximum amount of space for cannabis production is limited to 10,000 square feet. At the time of license renewal, a tier two producer must demonstrate minimum gross sales reported to the Department of Revenue of $8,000 per month or $96,000 annually throughout the two-year period prior to renewal. If a tier two producer fails to meet this revenue threshold throughout the two-year period prior to renewal, the license is converted to a tier one producer license and the producer’s maximum amount of space for cannabis production is limited to 4000 square feet. Tier one producers are not subject to the revenue threshold requirements and tier conversions. The bill defines tier one, tier two, and tier three producers based on the licensed production area. Two-Year Lookback Period. When determining the two-year period prior to renewal, time prior to the effective date of the new section must be included if the time is within two years of a license renewal occurring on or after the effective date of the new section. Exemptions. A tier three producer or tier two producer may request, and the LCB in its discretion may grant, a one-year exemption from the application of the new section if extenuating circumstances exist and the request is submitted to the LCB within 30 days of license renewal. Extenuating circumstances include, but are not limited to, natural disasters or other extraordinary events beyond the producer’s control. Conforming Changes. Cannabis producer licenses are subject to annual renewal and the revenue threshold and tier conversion requirements established in this bill. Renewal of a cannabis producer license is subject to those requirements. EFFECT OF CHANGES MADE BY LABOR & COMMERCE COMMITTEE (First Substitute): Revises the revenue-threshold framework for cannabis producer tiers by replacing the bill’s two-year, monthly-or-annual gross sales structure with cultivation-method-specific annual thresholds measured over a one-year evaluation period. Adds cultivation method categories used to determine which annual revenue threshold applies, including indoor cultivation, mixed-light cultivation, light deprivation, and outdoor cultivation. Applies specified annual revenue thresholds by cultivation method. Defines the one-year evaluation period as the 12 months immediately preceding the month in which the producer license renewal is due, and provides a limited lookback for certain renewals. Requires LCB to determine a producer’s cultivation method designation based on the predominant cultivation method reflected in the producer’s approved floor plan, and allows a producer to request reclassification by submitting an amended floor plan. Treats multiple cannabis producer licenses operated under a shared UBI as a single entity for purposes of meeting the applicable revenue thresholds by aggregating gross sales across those licenses, and directs LCB to verify UBI information through DOR records. Provides an 18-month grace period following an approved transfer or sale of a cannabis producer license before

SB 6200.digest: "Portable cooling device" is defined as an air conditioner, portable heat pump, or evaporative cooler, including a device mounted in a window or designed to sit on the floor, but does not include devices whose installation or use requires excessive alteration to the dwelling unit. "Window-mounted portable cooling device" is defined as a portable cooling device that is installed to sit in the window but does not include a saddle-mounted portable cooling device, a u-shaped portable cooling device, or a floor-mounted device that is connected to a window for air exchange or ventilation. "Saddle-mounted portable cooling device" is defined as a portable cooling device that hangs over the windowsill with interior and exterior components rather than sitting on top of it, such that the window view is not fully obstructed and the device will not fall when the window is opened, and includes u-shaped portable cooling devices. Tenant Use of Cooling Device under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. Under the RLTA, a landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant from installing a portable cooling device of any type unless: the dwelling already has a permanently installed and fully operational heat pump; or installation of the device would violate state or local building codes, state law, or federal law, violate the device manufacturer's written safety guidelines for the device, cause unreasonable damage to the premises or render the premises uninhabitable, or require an electrical supply to power the device that cannot be accommodated by the existing power service to the building, dwelling unit, or circuit. A landlord may also prohibit or restrict a tenant from installing a window-mounted portable cooling device if: the window is a necessary egress and the device would interfere with its use as egress; the device would interfere with the ability to lock the window; the device requires excessive use of brackets or other hardware that would damage or void the warranty of the window or frame, puncture the exterior wall of the building, or otherwise cause significant damage; the device cannot be secured in a way that prevents it from falling out of the window; or the landlord's insurance policy for the dwelling occupied by the tenant expressly restricts or prohibits the use of window-mounted portable cooling devices, this restriction or prohibition has been communicated to the tenant, and the landlord has provided written evidence of insurance policy restrictions or prohibitions to the tenant. As a condition of installing a portable cooling device, a landlord may require that the device be adequately drained to prevent damage to the dwelling unit or building. A landlord may also require that a window-mounted portable cooling device be subject to inspection or servicing by the landlord after installation. Nothing in the act shall preclude a landlord from charging for the rental of a portable cooling device rented by the tenant from the landlord, nor for any damages arising out of a tenant's use of a portable cooling device. Notice and Limitations under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. A tenant must provide at least two days' notice to a landlord prior to the installation of a window-mounted portable cooling device. A landlord must notify tenants in their lease of their rights, responsibilities and restrictions related to installation and operation of a portable cooling device. SB 6201.digest: Real Estate Excise Tax Exemption. Adds a social housing agency to the list of qualifying grantees for the purpose of qualifying for a REET exemption. Social housing agency means a public corporation created for the purpose of developing, maintaining, and operating social housing. Social housing means mixed income housing that is made available by a social housing agency for a period of at least 99 years to primarily serve low or moderate-income households. The social housing agency must record a covenant at the time of transfer that the property will primarily be used for low-income housing for a period of at least 15 years. Property Tax Exemption. The real and personal property owned or used by a social housing agency in providing rental housing for qualifying households is exempt from taxation if at least 50 percent of the occupied dwelling units are occupied by a qualifying household and the rental housing was insured, financed, or assisted in whole or in part through one of the following: federal or state housing program administered by the Department of Commerce; federal housing program administered by a city or county; an affordable housing levy; the Washington State Housing Finance Commission; the covenant homeownership and housing related surcharges; or city or county funds designated for affordable or social housing. If less than 50 percent of the units are occupied by a qualifying household a partial exemption may be allowed for each dwelling unit occupied by a qualifying household. If at initial application the property is unoccupied, or subsequent to the initial application the property is unoccupied because of renovations, and the property is not currently being used for the exempt purposes but will be within three years the property is eligible if: a commitment for financing to acquire, construct, renovate, or otherwise convert the property to provide housing to qualifying households has been obtained; the social housing agency has manifested its intent in writing to construct, remodel, or otherwise convert the property to housing for qualifying households; and only the portion of the property that will be used to provide housing or lots for qualifying households is exempt. Qualifying household means a single person, family, or unrelated persons living together whose income is at or below 80 percent of the median income, at the time of move in, adjusted for family size for the county in which the property is located. If a currently exempt rental housing unit was occupied by a qualifying household at the time the exemption was granted and the income of the household subsequently rises above 80 percent of the median income but remains at or below 115 percent of the median income, the exemption will continue as long as the housing continues to meet the certification requirements. If a dwelling unit or lot becomes vacant or is subsequently rerented, the income of the new household must be at or below 80 percent of the median income. The social housing agency may agree to make payments to the city, county, or other political subdivision for improvements, services, and facilities furnished for the benefit of the rental housing as long as the payments do not exceed the amount last levied as the annual tax of the city, county, or political subdivision upon the property prior to exemption. SB 6204.digest: Home Cultivation Authorization. A person 21 years of age or older may produce and possess up to six cannabis plants, and the cannabis and cannabis products derived from those plants, on the premises of the housing unit occupied by the person. No more than 15 plants may be produced at any one time on the premises of a single housing unit, regardless of the number of residents living on the premises. Visibility and Odor Restrictions. A class 3 civil infraction applies when a person produces or knowingly possesses plants, cannabis, or cannabis products derived from those plants, as otherwise authorized, and the plants, cannabis, or cannabis products can be readily smelled from a public place or the private property of another housing unit, or are visible within the ordinary public view. Penalties for Exceeding Plant Limits. A class 1 civil infraction applies when a person produces and knowingly possesses more than six but fewer than 16 plants, unless otherwise authorized under commercial or medical cannabis law. A class C felony applies when a person produces and knowingly possesses 16 or more plants, unless otherwise authorized under commercial or medical cannabis law. Enforcement and Liquor and Cannabis Board Authority. An investigating law enforcement officer or agency may seize and summarily destroy plants produced or possessed in excess of the six-plant limit when the person is not otherwise authorized to produce and possess the additional plants under commercial or medical cannabis law. The Liquor and Cannabis Board (LCB) has no authority or responsibility to investigate or enforce the home cultivation requirements. LCB’s authority to enforce state laws related to commercial cannabis production, processing, or sales is not limited when there is evidence of a violation of other state controlled substances law provisions. Extraction and Processing. Extraction or separation of resin from cannabis and production or processing of cannabis concentrates or cannabis-infused products must be performed in accordance with rules adopted under medical cannabis law. Additional Limitations. The home cultivation authorization does not apply in a housing unit used by a family day care provider to provide early childhood education and early learning services or used as a foster family home. The authorization also does not apply to a person supervised for a criminal conviction when the supervising corrections agency or department, including local governments or jails, determines the home cultivation provisions are inconsistent with and contrary to the person’s supervision. Nothing prevents or restricts a property owner from prohibiting cultivation by a renter or lessee upon or within the property under the terms of a rental agreement, lease, or other contract. Definitions. For purposes of the controlled substances possession statute, the bill defines housing unit—by reference to medical cannabis law, ordinary public view, public place, and use of a controlled substance. The definition of cannabis products in the Uniform Controlled Substances Act is expanded to include any product containing only THC content. Forfeiture of Real Property. Real property forfeiture based on cannabis-related activity is limited to cases in which the cannabis is possessed for commercial purposes that are unlawful under Washington State law, the amount possessed is 16 or more plants or, except as authorized under the home cultivation provision, one pound or more of cannabis,

SB 6206.digest: Subject to appropriations, Commerce must establish a pilot program to incentivize and make child care more accessible to first responders. "First responders" means firefighters, law enforcement officers, public safety telecommunicators, emergency medical personnel, as licensed or certificated by this state, and human service professionals that respond to emergency situations involving behavioral health crises and people experiencing complex medical needs including, but not limited to, social workers, behavioral health clinicians, advanced practice registered nurses, registered nurses, community health workers, and peer support specialists. Commerce must award grants with funds appropriated to local jurisdictions to provide incentive payments to licensed or certified child care providers who care for children of paid and volunteer first responders. Incentive payments must be prioritized for licensed or certified child care providers that offer child care during nonstandard work hours, on short notice, and when a child has an illness. Commerce must select at least four local jurisdictions, which can be counties, cities or incorporated towns, with one in each of the north and south regions of Washington State and on each side of the Cascade mountains to receive state grants. Selected local jurisdictions must be able to provide a plan of how they can equally match state grants for incentive payments with nonstate resources. The plan may include future nonstate resources including a sales and use tax for criminal justice purposes. By November 1, 2029, Commerce must submit a report that includes the outcomes of this pilot program. At a minimum, the report must describe the impact on recruitment of personnel, personnel retention, and discernable job satisfaction, resulting from program benefits and accessibility. SB 6209.digest: Gainful Employment Standard. The Washington Student Achievement Council must adopt rules establishing a gainful employment standard for private, for-profit institutions of higher education that wish to participate in the WCG and CBS. At minimum, to be eligible to participate in those financial aid programs, debt payments for graduates must be no more than 8 precent of annual earnings or 20 percent of discretionary earnings, which is defined as annual earnings minus 150 percent of the federal poverty guideline for the individual. In developing this standard, WSAC must take into consideration programs completion, and work with the Education Research and Data Center on data development and measures. Maximum Washington College Grant and College Based Scholarship Awards for Private, For-Profit, Four-Year Institutions. Beginning in the 2026-27 academic year, the maximum WCG award amounts for students attending private, for-profit, four-year institutions is 50 percent of the average of the awards for the same academic year granted to students at the public research institutions in Washington. Beginning in the 2026-27 academic year, the maximum WCG award amounts for students attending two-year for-profit institutions is 50 percent of the maximum award for students attending public two-year institutions. Beginning in the 2027-28 academic year, the maximum CBS award amounts for students attending private, for-profit, four-year institutions is 50 percent of the average of the awards for the same academic year granted to students at the public research universities. Beginning in the 2027-28 academic year, the maximum CBS award amounts for students attending private, two-year for-profit institutions is 50 percent of the maximum award for students attending public two-year institutions. SB 6214.digest: The bill as referred to committee not considered. Summary of Bill (First Substitute): Land Bank Authorities. The legislative authority of a city or county may authorize the establishment of a land bank authority by a public corporation, a public housing authority, or a nonprofit organization exempt from federal income taxation under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. A land bank is defined as the inventory of real property acquired, held, leased, or transferred by a land bank authority for purposes consistent under the chapter created by the bill. Authorizing Ordinances or Resolutions. A city or county legislative authority must adopt an ordinance or resolution authorizing an entity to establish and operate a land bank. At a minimum, the ordinance or resolution must: state the public purpose of the land bank authority, including acquiring, holding, managing, and transferring property for affordable housing consistent with adopted local housing plans and the Growth Management Act; describe the governance or oversight structure applicable to the land bank authority; and authorize the land bank authority to acquire, hold, lease, and transfer real property, including transfers at less than fair market value in exchange for affordability requirements authorized under the chapter created by the bill. SB 6216.digest: Procedures for notifying the public for land sales are modified. Notice of the sale of lands managed by DNR no longer has to be posted in conspicuous places in DNR's Olympia office or in the office of the county auditor, but must be posted on DNR's public website. The list of lands and the appraised values that DNR must produce for all land sales no longer needs to be in pamphlet form. The list should be made available prior to the date of the sale, including on the Internet. Clarifying language is added that lands acquired by escheat, deed of sale, gift or through the land bank may only be sold after appraisal and for at least fair market value, and the transaction is in the best interest of the state or affected trust. The manner in which DNR must publicize the sale of valuable materials valued at $250,000 or less is modified. DNR may publicize valuable materials sales through the agency's website or through other methods deemed most practical by DNR. Valuable materials sales may take place either at DNR's applicable region headquarters or at an alternate location designated by DNR. DNR is no longer required to publicize such sales at DNR's Olympia office or at the office of the county auditor of the county in which the materials are located. DNR is no longer required to print a paper copy of the list of all valuable materials on public lands to be sold, but must make the list available upon request. A sale of valuable materials that has been offered, but for which no bids have been received, may be reoffered consistent with existing statutory requirements.

A community scaled project is a weatherization project that includes multiple dwelling units in the same neighborhood or area where overlapping factors such as environmental, social, or economic conditions may adversely impact residents, as determined by Commerce. A community scaled project may provide for full or partial weatherization, energy efficiency measures, or structural rehabilitation and repairs. A project sponsor must identify priority communities using indicators that include data reflecting environmental health disparities, housing vulnerability, and pollution exposure. Community scaled projects are excluded from the requirement that all units receiving weatherization services in a project be occupied by low-income households. When selecting community scaled projects, Commerce must consider socioeconomic data to prioritize those that serve low-income households. Commerce must approve or deny a proposal for grant funding for a community scaled project within 90 days of the closing application period. SB 6224.digest: The Children and Youth Behavioral Health Leadership Council (leadership council) is created through the Governor to address children and youth health and wellness issues and coordinate efforts to implement WTSP. The leadership council must include representation from representatives from state agencies involved in children and youth behavioral health or wellness activities identified by the Governor; representatives with lived experience caring for individuals with behavioral health issues experienced as a child or youth; and individuals representing a federally recognized Indian tribe or tribes whose traditional lands and territories included parts of Washington. Duties of the leadership council include reporting to the Governor on state agency practices and recommendations for changes in state policy that will help implement the WTSP; providing easily accessible and publicly available updates regarding the actions, decisions and recommendations of the leadership council; and notifying the Governor and appropriate committees of the Legislature when it believes that the executive coordination officer has accomplished the goals of that position and is no longer needed. The work group is allowed to advise and provide recommendations to the leadership council. The work group is required to use the WTSP to guide the priorities and efforts of the work group. The work group is extended for an additional two years from 2029 which is now set to expire in 2031. To the extent possible with existing resources, the Governor must support and facilitate coordination between various state agencies to follow the framework of the WTSP, and is allowed to use private funding sources to support the WTSP. The Governor must maintain an executive coordination officer for the children and youth system of care to: coordinate and monitor the implementation of the WTSP; build any infrastructure described in WTSP; coordinate private funding used for WTSP; and monitor in coordination with the Washington State Office of Equity any equity impacts of implementation of WTSP. All agencies are required to ensure that children and youth behavioral health activities and planning efforts align with WTSP and are implemented in an equitable manner.

SB 6228.digest: The preferential B&O tax rate of 0.138 percent for warehousing and reselling of prescription drugs is repealed. Beginning January 1, 2027, the gross income of businesses warehousing and reselling drugs for human use pursuant to a prescription is subject to a B&O tax rate of 0.5 percent. The term "warehousing and reselling drugs for human use pursuant to a prescription" is defined in the bill as the buying of drugs for human use pursuant to a prescription from a manufacturer or another wholesaler and reselling of the drugs to persons selling at retail or to hospitals, clinics, health care providers, or other providers of health care services by a wholesaler or retailer who is registered with the federal Drug Enforcement Administration and licensed by the state Pharmacy Quality Assurance Commission. The gross income of critical access pharmacies is subject to a preferential B&O tax rate of 0.25 percent. The term "critical access pharmacy" means a pharmacy in this state that is further than a 25-mile radius from any other pharmacy, is the only pharmacy on an island, or provides critical services to vulnerable populations, as identified by the health care authority. If a pharmacy is in a rural area or serves vulnerable populations, as defined by the health care authority, and the 25-mile radius intersects with another pharmacy, both are considered critical access pharmacies.

SB 6230.digest: For purchases made by legal tender, if the total price ends in $0.01, $0.02, $0.06, or $0.07, the amount must be rounded down to the nearest $0.05. SB 6239.digest: Claims Commission. A claims commission is established within the office of administrative hearings for the purpose of adjudicating claims against the state and its political subdivisions, or against their officers, employees, or volunteers, acting in such capacity, for damages arising out of tortious conduct. Claims for personal injury must be brought in the commission before filing suit where the claim occurred ten or more years before the filing of the claim or when the claimant has reached the age of 18, whichever is later. Claims for personal injury may be brought in the commission where the claim injury occurred fewer than ten years before filing or when the claimant has reached the age of 18, whichever is later. The Office of Administrative Hearings shall administer and provide staff support to the claims commission. Claims shall be heard and determined using the Administrative Procedure Act. Members of the claims commission shall be appointed by the Governor and shall consist of: a representative of the Office of the Attorney General; a victim advocate; a mental health professional; a representative of the Washington State Association for Justice; a single representative for all state agencies; a single representative for all counties; a single representative for all school districts; a representative of the Office of Financial Management, who may assign a state actuary; and a representative from the Department of Enterprise Services. The duties of the members of the claims commission include, but are not limited to: appointing neutral hearing officers; maintaining a registry of neutral hearing officers; adopting rules governing the procedural conduct of hearings, consistent with the Administrative Procedure Act; and delivering annual reports on the commission's work to the appropriate committees of the Legislature by December 15th of each year. Neutral Hearings Officer. A neutral hearing officer may set and conduct hearings, determine credibility, and issue written decisions and awards. The neutral hearing officer shall be a retired Washington superior court judge, retired appellate court judge, or former administrative law judge with substantial experience adjudicating tort claims. The neutral hearing officer shall be trained in trauma-informed practices, including recognizing the impacts of trauma on participants and conducting proceedings in a manner that promotes fairness, safety, and respect. Claims. Before filing a claim with the claims commission, a claimant must comply with the presentment and filing requirements outlined in law for state and local agencies. The filing of a claim with the commission shall toll the applicable statute of limitations. Neutral hearing officers shall be assigned on a rotating or random basis, subject to disqualification for cause. Each party shall be entitled to one peremptory strike of an assigned neutral hearing officer, exercised within ten days of assignment. At the time of filing, a claimant shall select either the expedited examiner track or the hearing track. Expedited Examiner Track. Claimants electing to proceed on the expedited examiner track shall submit with their claim a statement signed under penalty of perjury identifying the location and approximate dates of abuse, the name of the perpetrator or perpetrators, if known, witnesses, if any, and claimed damages as well as any information in the claimant's possession or control substantiating the claim. There is a filing fee of $25

SB 6241.digest: In every watershed resource inventory area (WRIA) with a native steelhead population, WDFW must implement a steelhead wild broodstock conservation program. The program shall include volunteers that deliver live broodstock to a hatchery or rearing facility, and the WDFW must rear the wild fish for release at the appropriate time. WDFW must conduct rule making to develop hatchery management plans that utilize wild broodstock to sustain wild populations in each WRIA that contains a native population of steelhead trout. The rules must include fish health, wild broodstock requirements, and population size targets. The rules must also include strategies to reduce risk of inbreeding and methods to maximize survival of fish to spawning. The program shall identify effective population size targets and other strategies to reduce risk of inbreeding depression, genetic drift, and domestication. WDFW must also establish policies for spawning and rearing protocols, release protocols, and predator control. The wild broodstock conservation program must have clear management objectives, including species conservation, watershed health, and fisheries supply.

The Insurance Commissioner (Commissioner) may issue a limited lines travel insurance producer license to an individual or business entity that has filed with the Commissioner an application for a limited lines travel insurance producer license in a form and manner prescribed by the Commissioner. The limited lines travel insurance producer must be licensed to sell, solicit, or negotiate travel insurance through an authorized insurer. No person may act as a limited lines travel insurance producer or travel insurance retailer unless properly licensed or registered, respectively. The grounds for the suspension, revocation, and penalties applicable to resident insurance producers apply to the limited lines travel insurance producers and travel retailers. Travel Retailers. A travel retailer is a business entity that makes, arranges, or offers planned travel and may offer and disseminate travel insurance as a service to its customers on behalf of and under the direction of a limited lines travel insurance producer. A travel retailer may offer and disseminate travel insurance under a limited lines travel insurance producer business entity license only if specified requirements are met: The limited lines travel insurance producer or travel retailer must provide to purchasers of travel insurance: a description of the material terms of the insurance coverage; a description of the process for filing a claim; a description of the review or cancellation process for the travel insurance policy; and the identity and contact information of the insurer and limited lines travel insurance producer. At the time of licensure, the limited lines travel insurance producer must establish and maintain a register, on a form prescribed by the Commissioner, of each travel retailer that offers travel insurance on the limited lines travel insurance producer's behalf. The register must be maintained and updated by the limited lines travel insurance producer and must include the name, address, and contact information of the travel retailer and an officer or person who directs or controls the travel retailer's operations, and the travel retailer's federal tax identification number. The limited lines travel insurance producer must submit the register to the Commissioner annually in a form and manner prescribed by the Commissioner. The limited lines travel insurance producer must certify that the registered travel retailer complies with federal law related to c rimes by or affecting persons engaged in the business of insurance whose activities affect interstate commerce . The limited lines travel insurance producer must designate one of its employees who is a licensed individual producer as the person responsible for the compliance with the travel insurance laws and regulations applicable to the limited lines travel insurance producer and its registrants. The designated employee, president, secretary, treasurer, and any other officer or person who directs or controls the limited lines travel insurance producer's insurance operations must comply with the fingerprinting requirements applicable to insurance producers in the resident state of the limited lines travel insurance producer. SB 6255.digest: The Legislative-Executive WorkFirst Poverty Reduction Oversight Task Force is renamed the Legislative-Executive Economic Justice and Well-Being Task Force (Task Force). The number of voting members of the Task Force are expanded to include the following state agencies: the Department of Revenue; the Health Care Authority; and the Workforce Training and Education Coordinating Board. The Task Force cochairs must be selected from the voting members and serve two-year terms. Legislative members are voting members. The Task Force representatives from the Governor's Offices of Equity, Indian Affairs, and Financial Management are nonvoting members. The duties of the Task Force are modified to specify that the Task Force: oversees the budget and performance of the WorkFirst program; determines outcome and accountability measures for the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; collaborates with the advisory council to monitor the strategies and recommendations in the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; seeks input for poverty reduction to encourage the development of cross-sector and innovative approaches to poverty reduction; analyzes data with a primary focus on the strategies and recommendations of the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; and collaborates with and seek advice from the Washington Economic Justice Alliance in supporting the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty. The Intergenerational Poverty Advisory Committee is renamed the Economic Justice and Well-Being Advisory Council (Council). The secretary of the Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) is authorized to appoint members to the Council as appropriate—in addition to the current members. The membership of the Council is modified to: include organizations that address poverty, education, or early childhood education grants that may include faith-based organizations, but is not limited to, faith-based organizations; include individuals impacted by poverty; remove a subject matter expert in infant mental health; remove a representative from the Department of Children, Youth, and Families and DSHS; and add entities representing the workforce system and postsecondary education systems. The duties of the Council are modified to require that it monitor the strategies and recommendations outlined in the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty and recommend to the Task Force priorities and policy options that the Task Force should consider proposing to the Governor and the Legislature to effectively reduce poverty and promote and encourage self-sufficiency. By December 1, 2026, state agency representatives on the Task Force, the Washington Economic Justice Alliance, and the Advisory Council are to provide a report to the Task Force and Governor regarding their review and update of the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty.

SB 6277.digest: Student Admission. Residency Requirements. A child of a military family meets the residency requirements for enrollment in a school district if a parent or guardian of the child is transferred to, or is pending transfer to, a military installation within Washington or a bordering state, or the military family is transferring due to a military exigency requiring relocation, under official military orders. With regard to a parent or guardian who is transferred to, or is pending transfer to, a military installation within Washington, there is no longer a requirement that the parent or guardian be on active duty. Proof of Military Orders. The parent or guardian must provide proof of official military orders or documentation by their military commander of the directed move. Proof of Residence. Proof of residence must be provided to the school district within 90 calendar days of enrollment. A parent or guardian may use, as proof of residence, the address of a temporary lodging located within the school district where the military family expects to obtain permanent housing. Application for Enrollment. A school district must accept an application for enrollment and course registration for a child of a military family on a conditional basis before the military family arrives in Washington. The school district must accept the application by electronic or other means. A school district is not required to finalize the child's enrollment until the parent or guardian provides both proof of military orders and proof of residency. Special Education Services. Transfer of Education Records. If a child of a military family transfers with an IEP or a plan developed under section 504 of the federal Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (section 504 plan), the school district must take the necessary steps to accept the transfer of the child's education records and any prior evaluations. Continuity of Services and Accommodations. Upon enrollment, the school district must ensure that the child of a military family receives appropriate services and accommodations consistent with the child's existing IEP or section 504 plan, without unreasonable delay. Reevaluation Timeline . If the school district determines that a reevaluation is necessary, the reevaluation must be completed within 30 calendar days after the date of arrival, subject to the parent's or guardian's informed consent. Transportation. A non-resident school district is not required to provide transportation to and from school, unless otherwise required by state or federal law.

SB 6278.digest: Ongoing review of fully approved teacher and principal preparation programs must include the following components as established by the Professional Educator Standards Board (PESB): program standards, educator role standards, evidence submitted by programs, and input from community constituents and prekindergarten through grade 12 partners, including educators who may have direct experience with the program being reviewed. The PESB must regularly update these components to reflect the changing needs of the modern classroom as identified by educators in the classroom and as identified through a review of changes to state and federal requirements. This regular update is intended to promote better continuity, communication, consistency, and coherence across the educator preparation system and the prekindergarten through grade 12 community it serves, and enable educator preparation programs to better respond and adapt in a timely manner to the changing needs of the prekindergarten through grade 12 system. Following review of an educator preparation program using the components, the PESB will determine a response to any areas of practice where the program's performance is out of alignment with standards and requirements, provide the program notice of that response, and require the program to identify actions that will be taken to come into alignment with the standards and requirements. Beginning January 1, 2027, the student teacher field placement plans must be submitted to the PESB on a schedule established by the PESB at a frequency of no less than one submission every three years.

SB 6284.digest: High Risk Artificial Intelligence Systems. Beginning July 1, 2027, each deployer of a high-risk AI system must use industry-standard means to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination. A "high-risk artificial intelligence system" is defined as a system that is intended to autonomously make, or be a substantial factor in making, a consequential decision without meaningful human consideration. Risk Management . Developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, on or after July 1, 2027, must implement and maintain a risk management policy and program. The policy and program must specify and incorporate the principles, processes, and personnel that the deployer uses to identify, document, and mitigate known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination. A deployer must use: a NIST or other nationally or internationally accepted framework; or comply with a framework that the attorney general designates. Impact Assessments . Deployers of high-risk AI systems, on or after July 1, 2027, must complete an impact assessment that evaluates and documents: the systems purpose; an analysis of known or foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination; steps taken to mitigate risks; a description of the data, outputs, and metrics to evaluate the system; and a description of transparency measures, post-deployment monitoring and user safeguards. Consumer Notice . Each time a deployer uses an AI system in making a consequential decision, the deployer must provide notice to the consumer with certain disclosures. In any enforcement action, there is a rebuttable presumption that a deployer used reasonable care if the deployer was in compliance with the requirements of this act. Exemptions. Developers with fewer than 50 full-time equivalent employees are exempt from the risk management requirements under the act. Deployers are exempt from the risk management and impact assessment requirements if they: employ fewer than 50 full time employees; do not use the deployers own data to train the AI system; and the AI systems used by the deployer are used for the intended uses as disclosed by the deployer. The deployer must make available to consumers any impact assessment that includes information that is substantially similar to information in the impact assessment required under this act. The requirements in the act must not be construed to apply to federal agencies, the use of AI for research, performance of work in contract with certain federal agencies, HIPAA covered entities under certain circumstances, insurers regulated by the Office of the Insurance Commissioner or a comparable federal body, certain financial institutions, and other entities under specific conditions as provided in the act. Enforcement. The attorney general may bring an enforcement action under the Consumer Protection Act. Before commencing an enforcement action, the attorney general must provide 45 days written notice to a deployer or developer that is out of compliance with the act. Government Disclosure. A government agency that makes available an AI system intended to interact with consumers must provide certain disclosures to each consumer, before or at the time of interaction, that the consumer is interacting with an AI system.
